title: Understand DEP
text: DEP separates the ability to use an identifier from the ability to read it. Start with the clinic below, then follow the chapters from SQL to a working application. Basic SELECT, INSERT and JOIN knowledge is enough. Summary What is DEP? DEP (Database-Enforced Privacy) is a database-enforced privacy model, implemented by the experimental DEP Engine in which privacy protection is part of the type system, the query semantics, and the execution engine, rather than a layer added on top of the data. What is the core idea? A column declared PROTECTED can be used by the database to find a record, update it, and connect it to related records, but its value is never returned by an ordinary query. The principle. > The ability to use a value for an operation does not require the ability to read it. The promise. > Protected values remain inside the database unless released through an explicitly declared disclosure. The four decisions. DEP separates four decisions that most databases fold into a single privilege: Decision What it means In DEP --- --- --- Matching Using a protected value to find, update, or connect the records of one value Authorized equality lookups on the operational path; protected joins need a single-value anchor Linking Connecting whole datasets through a protected value Allowed only inside a function declared LINKS Returning Sending a protected value back to a client Never done by an ordinary query; the value comes back as NULL Disclosing Releasing a protected value deliberately Allowed only inside a function declared DISCLOSES, the only place where REVEAL is legal In the clinic. A patient's ID number lets reception find her and lets her doctor see her diagnoses, yet neither application ever receives an ID number back from the database. The clinic's dashboard and its AI scheduling assistant connect through the masked read path, where an ID number cannot even be used to search. Why it matters for privacy. Every route by which a protected value can leave the database, and every place where whole datasets are linked through one, is an object in the schema: visible to code review and queryable from the catalog. That turns privacy by design from a policy into something the database enforces on every query (Privacy as Code, privacy by design, and the GDPR). The limits. Permitted matching can still reveal that a record exists and associate it with the data that is returned. Names and other ordinary fields can identify people, aggregates are not automatically anonymous, and the server itself is trusted. Chapter 8 states the guarantees and limits precisely. --- Working with the examples The playground and clinic.sql contain six sample patients. The larger clinic described below illustrates the scale of the problem. Example tables show selected rows; the playground shifts dates to today. For a local setup, use Run the full clinic. The server chapter records implementation limits and version differences. Project components Name Role ------ DEP The Database-Enforced Privacy model DEP SQL SQL constructs that express protection, permitted use and declared exceptions DEP Engine The separate database server that enforces the implemented rules DEP CLI and Hoopeo Studio The SQL shell and graphical client; both can also run an embedded Engine DEP.js The browser simulator behind the playground Project Hoopeo The project containing these components The problem In one sentence: in most databases, the permission to use a value in a query and the permission to read that value are the same permission. The clinic What is the clinic? It is the single example this whole document follows: a small clinic with about 50,000 patients. Its database holds three kinds of information: who the patients are, when they have appointments, and what they have been diagnosed with. Before DEP, the schema is ordinary SQL: sql CREATE TABLE patients ( patient_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, national_id TEXT UNIQUE, phone TEXT, full_name TEXT, health_fund TEXT ); CREATE TABLE appointments ( appointment_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, patient_id BIGINT REFERENCES patients (patient_id), starts_at TIMESTAMPTZ, visit_type TEXT ); CREATE TABLE medical_records ( record_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, patient_national_id TEXT REFERENCES patients (national_id), diagnosis TEXT, recorded_at DATE ); A few of its rows: patient_id national_id phone full_name health_fund --- --- --- --- --- 1 123456782 +972-50-0000001 Dana Cohen Clalit 2 234567893 +972-50-0000002 Yossi Levi Maccabi Who uses it? Six programs connect to this database. Each has its own database role, and each needs something different: Consumer Role What it needs to do --- --- --- Reception application reception_app Find a patient by the ID number they present, and show today's appointments Doctors' application doctors_app Find the patient in the room, and show their diagnoses Nightly reminder job reminder_job Send an SMS to every patient with an appointment tomorrow Billing job billing_job Report visits and diagnosis claims to the patients' health funds BI dashboard bi_dashboard Show visits per day and type, and diagnoses per health fund Scheduling assistant scheduling_agent An AI agent that suggests scheduling improvements from appointment patterns Dana Cohen, the first patient, appears throughout: she arrives at reception, sees a doctor, receives a reminder, and appears in the report to her health fund. Using a value and reading it What is the difference? Two words carry the whole argument of this document: - Using a value means letting the database apply it in an operation: comparing it in a WHERE clause, joining two tables through it, or checking it against a constraint. The value decides which rows the database works with. - Reading a value means receiving the value itself: seeing it in a query result, an error message, a log, or an export. Example. Dana presents her ID card at reception. - Reception needs to use her ID number, because that is how it finds her record. - Reception never needs to read it back from the database: Dana just handed it over. Key point: most of what applications do with sensitive identifiers is using them. Very little of it requires reading them. What goes wrong in an ordinary database Why is this a problem? In PostgreSQL, referencing a column in a WHERE clause requires SELECT privilege on that column, and the same privilege lets the column be returned in a result. Column privilege works as a single switch: a role may touch the value for any purpose, or not at all. Three failures follow from that. Failure 1: wholesale extraction. The clinic has just connected an AI agent directly to the database. The agent writes its own SQL, and it knows nothing about the privacy policy encoded in other applications. Asked for help, it runs: sql SELECT full_name, national_id, phone FROM patients; Output text full_name national_id phone -------------+-------------+----------------- Dana Cohen 123456782 +972-50-0000001 Yossi Levi 234567893 +972-50-0000002 ... 49,998 more rows Explanation: no one broke in, and every permission worked exactly as configured. Because the agent may search by ID number, it may also read every ID number. The entire register left the database in one query. Failure 2: invisible linking. A query can produce the most sensitive dataset without returning any identifier: sql SELECT p.full_name, m.diagnosis FROM patients AS p JOIN medical_records AS m ON m.patient_national_id = p.national_id; Output text full_name diagnosis ------------+------------------ Dana Cohen Asthma Dana Cohen Seasonal allergy Yossi Levi Diabetes ... Explanation: no ID number appears in the result, so hiding ID numbers would not help. Yet the query produced the name and diagnosis of every patient. Nothing in an ordinary database marks this join as different from looking up a single appointment. Failure 3: unknown exits. Ask the clinic: "which code paths can export our patients' ID numbers?" Answering means interviewing teams and reading code, because any role with SELECT on the column is a possible exit. Regulators increasingly expect organizations to answer that question on demand. Why existing controls are not enough What do databases offer today? Several controls, each addressing part of the problem: Control What it does What it leaves open --- --- --- Views Hide columns or rows A view that lets callers search by a column generally has to expose it, or something derived from it Row-level security Restricts which rows a role sees Does not distinguish using a value from reading it Dynamic masking and projection policies Change what a query returns The column can still be used in predicates and joins to single out one person or link two datasets, as the vendors' documentation acknowledges Application-side encryption Protects stored data The application holds the keys, so anything running with its credentials can decrypt Privacy as Code tools Check policy in code review and CI Do not see the query an agent composes at run time Explanation: none of these separates using from reading. So in practice privacy lives in the applications: developers must remember not to write SELECT , to strip columns before exports, and to scrub logs. Every new consumer, whether a report, an integration, or an AI agent, starts with none of those safeguards. Chapter 7 looks at Privacy as Code more closely, and Roadmap and Release compares DEP with existing products and research in detail. Key points - One privilege decides both using and reading a column. - That allows wholesale extraction, invisible linking, and exits nobody can list. - Existing controls each solve part of the problem, outside the place every query passes through. --- The idea In one sentence: separate the four things a client may do with a sensitive value (match, link, return, disclose), allow the everyday one freely, and require the other three to be declared in the schema. The principle What is the principle? > The ability to use a value for an operation does not require the ability to read it. Where does it come from? From passwords. A well-built login system verifies that a password is correct without storing it in readable form, and without ever showing it back to anyone. Verification is an operation; the password itself is never output. What does DEP add? Two things: 1. Connecting records. Protected values can connect records across tables, not only verify a single input. 2. Enforcement by the server. The rules are enforced inside the database server, across the whole execution of every query, not by a helper function a developer must remember to call. The change in the schema What changes? One qualifier on one column: sql national_id TEXT PROTECTED MATCH DOMAIN person_id UNIQUE, Explanation: - TEXT stays: PROTECTED is a qualifier added to an existing type, not a new type. The column is still text. - PROTECTED defines what the engine may do with the value: use it for matching, never return it in an ordinary query. - MATCH DOMAIN person_id says what kind of value this is, so it can be compared only with values of the same kind. The full syntax is in Declaring a protected column. The schema, connection path and declared exceptions are three separate parts of DEP. Four decisions instead of one What are the four decisions? With direct SELECT access to the underlying column, an application can use or return Dana's ID. DEP makes these value-use decisions explicit in the schema and query rules: Decision What it means In the clinic Ordinary SQL: direct SELECT In DEP --- --- --- --- --- Match Use a protected value to find, update, or connect the records of one value Reception finds Dana by the ID she presents Allowed with SELECT Authorized equality lookups on the operational path; protected joins need a single-value anchor Link Connect whole datasets through a protected value Diagnosis statistics per health fund Allowed with SELECT Allowed only inside a function declared LINKS Return Send a protected value back to a client Nothing in the clinic needs this Allowed with SELECT Never in an ordinary query; the value comes back as NULL Disclose Release a protected value deliberately The monthly report to the health funds Allowed with SELECT Allowed only inside a function declared DISCLOSES Why does the split fall there? Matching is the everyday work of an operational system: a receptionist finds the patient in front of her. DEP allows it and records it. The other three are where privacy is actually lost, at scale or by releasing the value itself, so DEP requires each of them to be declared in the schema, where it can be reviewed. What this protects, and what it does not What does DEP not prevent? When reception looks Dana up, it already holds her ID number, and DEP does not hide it from reception. The lookup also tells reception something: that Dana is a patient, and whatever ordinary fields come back with her record. A receptionist who types a stranger's ID number learns whether that person is a patient. What does DEP prevent? Wholesale extraction and unreviewed processing. The AI agent cannot run SELECT national_id FROM patients and walk away with the register, and a compromised reception application cannot join every patient to every diagnosis. > Ordinary queries never return protected plaintext. Permitted matching can still reveal record existence and associations with returned data. Explanation: releasing protected identifiers or linking protected datasets becomes an explicit, reviewable operation. Ordinary fields can still be returned according to their grants; they are not automatically anonymous. Ordinary SQL and DEP, side by side Four situations in the clinic, first in an ordinary database and then in DEP. Situation 1: Dana arrives at reception Without DEP, her ID number comes back with the answer: mermaid sequenceDiagram participant App as Reception application participant DB as Ordinary database App->>DB: SELECT full_name, national_id ... WHERE national_id = '123456782' DB->>DB: Compare plaintext values DB-->>App: Dana Cohen 123456782 Note over App: The database sent the ID back, and every layer that handles the response now holds it With DEP, the ID number is used and stays inside: mermaid sequenceDiagram participant App as Reception application participant DEP as DEP server App->>DEP: SELECT full_name, national_id ... WHERE national_id = $1 DEP->>DEP: Match on the keyed index DEP->>DEP: Suppress national_id at the output boundary DEP-->>App: Dana Cohen NULL Note over App: The database returned no identifier the application did not send Explanation: the query is the same. The difference is that DEP used the ID number to find Dana, and then sent NULL in place of the ID number. Situation 2: The AI agent tries to take everything Without DEP, one query is enough: mermaid sequenceDiagram participant A as Scheduling assistant participant DB as Ordinary database A->>DB: SELECT full_name, national_id, phone FROM patients DB-->>A: 50,000 rows with ID numbers and phones Note over A: The whole register has left With DEP, nothing protected leaves, whether through the agent on the masked path or through a compromised application on the operational path: mermaid sequenceDiagram participant X as Compromised reception app participant OP as DEP operational endpoint participant M as DEP masked endpoint participant A as Scheduling assistant X->>OP: SELECT full_name, national_id FROM patients OP-->>X: Names only, national_id is NULL A->>M: SELECT full_name FROM patients WHERE national_id = $1 M-->>A: ERROR DEP_ENDPOINT_OPERATION A->>M: SELECT CAST(national_id AS TEXT) FROM patients M-->>A: ERROR DEP_PROTECTED_OPERATION Explanation: names still reach the compromised application, which is why ordinary permissions still matter. The identifiers, the values that link a person across systems, do not. Situation 3: Linking patients to diagnoses Without DEP, the query from What goes wrong in an ordinary database is just another join: mermaid sequenceDiagram participant X as Compromised app participant DB as Ordinary database X->>DB: SELECT full_name, diagnosis FROM patients JOIN medical_records ON national_id DB-->>X: 50,000 rows of names with diagnoses Note over X: No ID left the database, and the clinic's records left anyway With DEP, the same join is allowed for one patient at a time, and only declared code may link everyone: mermaid sequenceDiagram participant D as Doctors' application participant OP as DEP operational endpoint participant B as BI dashboard participant M as DEP masked endpoint D->>OP: Same join, WHERE national_id = $1 for Dana OP-->>D: Dana's diagnoses D->>OP: Same join, no anchor OP-->>D: ERROR DEP_UNANCHORED_MATCH B->>M: SELECT FROM diagnoses_per_fund() M-->>B: Counts per health fund, from a declared LINKS function Explanation: the doctor's join names one patient, so it is allowed. The same join for everyone is rejected. The dashboard still gets its statistics, from a function the clinic declared and reviewed. Situation 4: Where ID numbers can leave the database Without DEP, every role with SELECT on the column is a potential exit, and finding them all means reading code: mermaid flowchart LR DB[(Ordinary database national_id TEXT)] --> R[Billing script] DB --> B[Dashboard export] DB --> S[Reception app logs] DB --> Q[Ad-hoc query] DB --> AI[AI agent] DB --> U[Something nobody remembers] With DEP, the exits are declared functions, and the catalog lists them: mermaid flowchart LR subgraph SRV["DEP server"] T[(patients national_id TEXT PROTECTED)] F["monthly_fund_report() DISCLOSES person_id"] T --> F end F --> HF[Report to the health funds] T -.->NULL or error O[Every other query] Explanation: the only way an ID number leaves is through monthly_fund_report, and anyone can find it in the catalog. Summary of the four situations Ordinary SQL DEP --- --- --- Finding Dana by her ID number The ID comes back with the answer The ID is matched internally and never returned Taking the whole register One SELECT ID numbers are NULL; matching on the masked path is rejected Linking patients to diagnoses One JOIN One patient at a time; everyone only in declared LINKS functions Where ID numbers can leave Wherever someone has SELECT Only through declared DISCLOSES functions, listed in the catalog Who enforces the policy Every client, separately The server, for every client Why it is a language feature Why not just a permission? Because a permission can be granted quietly, somewhere, by someone. DEP changes how developers write queries, in the way Rust changed how systems programmers write code. Rust is stricter than C, and the strictness is built into the language rather than left to discipline. Its exceptions are explicit: an unsafe block is allowed, but it is marked, local, and easy to find. How does DEP follow that pattern? By default, protected values cannot be read, and datasets cannot be linked through them. When they must be, the exception is a language construct (a function declared DISCLOSES or LINKS), not a permission granted out of sight. The additional effort is intentional: it is what makes every exception reviewable. Why it is a server Why can't the rules run in the application? Every guarantee depends on a trust boundary: the client sends SQL, and the enforcement, the keys, and the data live in a separate process the client does not control. A privacy rule checked inside the client's own process would be a simulation, not a protection, because whoever runs the process can bypass it. DEP is therefore always a server, and clients reach it only through the network protocol. The trust boundary explains the boundary in detail. Key points - The principle: using a value does not require reading it. - Matching is allowed and recorded; linking, returning, and disclosing are declared or impossible. - DEP does not hide what a client already knows; it stops wholesale extraction and unreviewed linkage. - Exceptions are language constructs, enforced by a server the client cannot bypass. --- Core concepts In one sentence: this chapter defines every DEP term once, in plain words, with an example from the clinic and a link to where it is explained in full. Values Protected field (PROTECTED) - What is it? A column whose value is never returned by an ordinary query, and on which only the operations DEP defines are allowed. In the first version, the only such operation is full-value equality. - In the clinic. patients.national_id, patients.phone, and medical_records.patient_national_id. - Note. A protected field is not necessarily a personal identifier: phone numbers, addresses, card numbers, or any other sensitive value can be protected. - See Declaring a protected column. Ordinary field - What is it? Any column that is not protected. It behaves exactly as in ordinary SQL, governed by ordinary permissions. - In the clinic. full_name, health_fund, diagnosis, and the internal key patient_id. Match domain (MATCH DOMAIN) - What is it? A named group of protected fields that hold the same kind of value, and may therefore be compared with one another. - In the clinic. person_id (national ID numbers) and phone_number. - See What a match domain decides. Protected input - What is it? A value the client sends in a protected position: compared with a protected column, or inserted into one. It is either a protected parameter (sent separately, as $1) or a protected literal (written in the query, as '123456782'). The engine treats both the same way. - See Parameters and literals. Index entry - What is it? A keyed hash of a protected value, stored next to it and used for all matching. It lets the database compare values without looking at them. Ordinary SQL cannot reach it. - See Matching with a keyed index. Operations Matching - What is it? Comparing protected values for equality, done by the engine on index entries, without making the values available to the rest of the query. Anchored matching - What is it? Matching tied to one value the client sent. A join between protected columns needs this anchor unless it runs inside a LINKS function. Simple equality lookups can also use IN lists; a list does not anchor a broader protected join. - Example. Finding Dana by her ID number, or showing Dana's diagnoses. - See Joining on protected columns. Anchor - What is it? The condition that limits a query to one value: an equality between a protected column and one protected input, at the top level of the query. - Example. WHERE p.national_id = $1. Linking - What is it? Matching that connects whole datasets through a protected value, rather than one value at a time. Allowed only inside a linking function. - Example. Counting diagnoses per health fund, which connects every patient to every diagnosis. Returning and suppression - What is it? Returning is sending a value to the client. When an ordinary query selects a protected value, it is suppressed: replaced with a real SQL NULL before the result is sent. - See Selecting a protected column. Disclosing - What is it? Deliberately turning a protected value into an ordinary one, so it can leave the database. Possible only through REVEAL inside a disclosing function. Connections Access path - What is it? A property of a connection, fixed when it logs in, that sets the most it may do with protected values. There are two paths. - See Two access paths. Operational path (OPERATIONAL) - What is it? The path for applications that find and update records. It allows reads, writes, anchored matching, and calls to declared functions the role may execute. - In the clinic. Reception, the doctors' application, the reminder job, and billing. Masked read path (MASKED_READ) - What is it? A read-only path on which protected values cannot be used for matching at all. It may call linking functions that take no protected input, but never disclosing functions. - In the clinic. The dashboard and the AI scheduling assistant. Endpoint - What is it? A server address that clients connect to, bound to one access path. - See CREATE ENDPOINT. Compare the operations needed by reception, doctors, analytics and billing. Declared code Declared function - What is it? A function whose signature says it does something an ordinary query may not: disclose protected values (DISCLOSES), link datasets through them (LINKS), or both. - See Declared functions. Disclosing function (DISCLOSES d) - What is it? A declared function that may reveal values of match domain d. The only place where REVEAL is legal. - In the clinic. monthly_fund_report, appointment_reminders. Linking function (LINKS d) - What is it? A declared function that may match values of domain d without an anchor. - In the clinic. diagnoses_per_fund. REVEAL - What is it? The only operation that turns a protected value into an ordinary one. - See REVEAL. Disclosed value - What is it? A value produced by REVEAL. It may be returned to the client, but not used to filter, join, group, store, or call a function. - See Disclosed values and the terminal rule. Linking region - What is it? The part of a query plan that came from the body of a linking function. Unanchored matching is accepted only inside it. - See Tracking disclosed values and linking regions. Enforcement Protected foreign key - What is it? A foreign key from a protected column to a protected column of the same match domain. Its integrity is checked inside the engine, and each check counts as a protected lookup. - See Protected foreign keys. Output boundary - What is it? The last stage before anything is sent to a client. It suppresses protected values, lets disclosed values through, and cleans every message. - See Components. Audit log - What is it? A record, kept by the server, of every protected match on the operational path and every call to a declared function, with the identity that made it. It never contains protected or disclosed values. - See Recording and auditing. Rate limit - What is it? A limit, per identity, on protected lookups. It stops one-value-at-a-time matching from becoming guessing every value. Policy rejection and execution failure - What is it? A policy rejection is an error because a statement is not allowed. It depends only on the statement, the path, the role, and the schema, and happens before any row is read. An execution failure happens while an allowed statement runs, and may depend on the data. - See 19.1. Fail closed - What is it? Any case the rules do not explicitly support is rejected, never silently allowed. What a match domain decides What is it? A match domain is more than a label. It decides four things: What it decides Meaning In the clinic --- --- --- Meaning Two equal values in the same domain refer to the same entity. "123456782" as a national ID and "123456782" as an internal record number are not the same thing, even though the digits match. Input representation Choose and enforce a consistent representation before writing and matching. The current Engine does not expose a configurable domain-normalization policy. Decide how the application handles leading zeros or spaces; do not assume DEP cleans them up. The matching key Each domain has its own secret key for its index entries. The same string in two domains produces unrelated entries, so values from different domains cannot be compared, even in storage. person_id and phone_number have separate keys. The scope of declarations DISCLOSES d and LINKS d apply only to values of domain d, and the privilege to declare them is granted per domain. A function declared DISCLOSES phone_number cannot reveal ID numbers. What a shared domain is not. A shared domain makes matching and linking technically possible. It is not consent, not legal approval to combine datasets, and not proof that a linked result is safe to disclose. Key points - Protected values are used through index entries and never returned by ordinary queries. - Equality lookups may use one value or a list; joins between protected columns need a single-value anchor or a LINKS function. Disclosing requires DISCLOSES. - The path sets the ceiling; column privileges decide who may match on what. --- Read the comparison correctly The ordinary SQL examples assume direct SELECT access to the base columns. Conventional databases can also constrain access with views, permissions and stored procedures. DEP makes its value-use rules explicit in the schema and analyzer. A MATCH DOMAIN is a matching and key boundary, not a GDPR legal purpose.

title: Write DEP SQL
text: Two access paths In one sentence: every connection is fixed, when it logs in, to one of two paths, and the path sets the most the connection can ever do with protected values. What an access path is What is it? An access path is a property of a connection that decides which operations on protected values are available to it. DEP has two paths: OPERATIONAL and MASKED_READ. Why is it needed? Permissions decide what a role may do, and roles can be granted by mistake, inherited, and switched. The path adds a ceiling that does not depend on any of that: whatever privileges a masked connection holds, it cannot match on protected values. Example. The same query, sent by two consumers: sql SELECT full_name FROM patients WHERE national_id = $1; -- $1 = '123456782' Output on the operational path (reception) full_name --- Dana Cohen Output on the masked path (the AI assistant) text ERROR: DEP_ENDPOINT_OPERATION DETAIL: Matching PROTECTED values is unavailable on a MASKED_READ connection. Explanation: reception's connection was fixed to the operational path when it logged in, so the lookup runs. The assistant's connection was fixed to the masked path, so matching on national_id is not available to it at all, whatever privileges its role holds. Rules in detail 1. The server decides the path when the connection authenticates, from the endpoint the client connected to and its identity. 2. The path cannot be changed for the rest of the session, by any statement, setting, or role switch (The path cannot change). 3. The path is an upper bound. Ordinary column privileges decide what a role may do beneath it (Who may match on what). 4. On both paths, an ordinary query never returns a protected value. CREATE ENDPOINT What is it? CREATE ENDPOINT defines a server address that clients connect to, and binds it to one access path. Syntax sql CREATE ENDPOINT endpoint_name MODE { OPERATIONAL MASKED_READ }; Parameters Parameter Meaning --- --- endpoint_name A name for the endpoint, unique in the server. MODE OPERATIONAL Connections through this endpoint receive the operational path. MODE MASKED_READ Connections through this endpoint receive the masked read path. Example. The clinic defines one endpoint per path: sql CREATE ENDPOINT operational MODE OPERATIONAL; CREATE ENDPOINT analytics MODE MASKED_READ; Explanation: reception, the doctors' application, the reminder job, and billing connect to operational. The dashboard and the scheduling assistant connect to analytics. Choosing an endpoint is the only way a client "chooses" a path, and only if its identity is allowed to connect there. Rules in detail 1. CREATE ENDPOINT is a server-level administrative command, not something an application runs. 2. DEP Engine 0.5.2 controls endpoint access with GRANT CONNECT ON ENDPOINT operational TO role_name. The endpoint is selected as the database name at login; two endpoints do not require two TCP ports. The connection path sets which operations are available; privileges still decide which objects a role may use. The operational path What is it? The path for applications that must find, create, and update records. --- --- Allows Reads and writes within ordinary permissions; inserting protected values; finding, updating, and connecting records by one protected value; calling declared functions the role may execute Does not allow Returning protected values from an ordinary query; unanchored matching outside a LINKS function; processing protected values (casts, substrings, ordering) Typical consumers Reception, the doctors' application, the reminder job, the billing job The masked read path What is it? A read-only path on which protected values cannot be used for matching at all. --- --- Allows Reading ordinary fields; joining on ordinary keys; aggregates; calling linking functions that take no protected input Does not allow Any matching on protected values, even for one value; any write; calling disclosing functions; calling linking functions that take a protected input Typical consumers Analysts, BI tools, and AI agents. The masked path is the default for any new consumer. Example. The assistant studies appointment patterns: sql SELECT visit_type, extract(hour FROM starts_at) AS hour, COUNT() FROM appointments GROUP BY visit_type, hour ORDER BY COUNT() DESC; Output visit_type hour count --- --- --- Follow-up 10 214 First visit 9 187 Explanation: the query uses only ordinary fields, so it runs exactly as in ordinary SQL. The masked path does not get in the way of the assistant's real work; it only removes access to identifiers. Capabilities of each path Capability OPERATIONAL MASKED_READ --- --- --- Read ordinary fields Allowed within ordinary permissions Allowed within ordinary permissions Join on ordinary fields Allowed Allowed Insert or update data Allowed within ordinary permissions Rejected Supply a value for a protected field on insert Allowed Rejected Find or update a record by one protected value Allowed, for columns the role may use; recorded Rejected Join on protected fields, anchored to one protected value Allowed, for columns the role may use; recorded Rejected Join on protected fields across whole datasets Rejected outside a LINKS function Rejected Return a protected field directly Suppressed (NULL) Suppressed (NULL) Call a LINKS function that takes no protected input Allowed with EXECUTE Allowed with EXECUTE Call a LINKS function that takes a protected input Allowed with EXECUTE Rejected Call a DISCLOSES function Allowed with EXECUTE Rejected Use REVEAL in an ordinary query Rejected Rejected Extract parts of, cast, or pass a protected field to a general function Rejected Rejected Who may match on what What is it? On the operational path, a role may match on a protected column if, and only if, it holds ordinary SQL privilege on that column. Why is it needed? It lets DEP reuse the privileges SQL already has, instead of inventing a new permission system. DEP only changes what a privilege can reveal: because a protected value is never returned by an ordinary query, privilege on a protected column means only "may use this column for matching." Example 1: Reception may search by ID number sql GRANT SELECT (patient_id, national_id, full_name, health_fund) ON patients TO reception_app; -- as reception_app SELECT full_name FROM patients WHERE national_id = $1; Output full_name --- Dana Cohen Explanation: reception holds privilege on national_id, so it may use it to find Dana. It still never receives the ID number itself. Example 2: Reception may not search by phone number sql -- as reception_app SELECT full_name FROM patients WHERE phone = $1; Output text ERROR: permission denied for column phone Explanation: reception holds no privilege on phone, so it cannot perform a reverse lookup by phone number, which would let a receptionist identify an unknown caller. This is an ordinary SQL permission error, not a DEP error. Three layers. Every decision about a protected column is made by exactly one of three layers: Layer Decides In the clinic --- --- --- The path Whether matching is possible at all The assistant, on the masked path, cannot match on anything Column privileges Who may match on which column Reception may match on national_id, but not on phone PROTECTED What a match can ever reveal No ordinary query returns either column Key point: every protected match on the operational path is written to the audit log with the identity that made it, and protected lookups are rate-limited per identity (Recording and auditing). The path cannot change What is it? A rule: once a connection has logged in, its path stays the same until it disconnects. Example. The assistant, connected to analytics, tries to promote itself: sql SET dep.path = 'OPERATIONAL'; Output text ERROR: DEP_PATH_IMMUTABLE DETAIL: The access path of this connection is MASKED_READ and cannot be changed. HINT: The path is fixed at authentication. Connect through the operational endpoint instead. Explanation: the path belongs to the connection as it logged in, not to anything the client can set afterwards. The same applies to SET ROLE, SET SESSION AUTHORIZATION, and pooled connections. Errors. DEP_PATH_IMMUTABLE. Choosing a path for a consumer How is a path chosen? From what the consumer must do with protected values: 1. A consumer that must match on a protected value connects on the operational path. 2. A consumer that must disclose values does so through a disclosing function, on the operational path. 3. A consumer whose only protected access is through linking functions that take no protected input connects on the masked path. 4. A consumer with no use for protected values connects on the masked path. 5. Any new consumer starts on the masked path, and moves only when someone decides, with a written reason, that it needs to match. In the clinic Consumer Path Why --- --- --- reception_app OPERATIONAL Matches on national_id doctors_app OPERATIONAL Matches on national_id and medical_records.patient_national_id reminder_job OPERATIONAL Calls a disclosing function billing_job OPERATIONAL Calls disclosing functions bi_dashboard MASKED_READ Only calls a linking function without protected input scheduling_agent MASKED_READ Has no use for protected values Chapter 4 derives these assignments from the clinic's privacy matrix. Key points - Two paths: operational for applications that find and update records; masked for analysts, dashboards, and agents. - The path is fixed at login and cannot be changed by any statement. - Column privileges decide who may match on which column, beneath the path. - New consumers start on the masked path. --- Writing DEP SQL In one sentence: this chapter shows every DEP construct used in ordinary statements, one at a time, turning the clinic's database into a DEP database. Before you start. Parameters written as $1, $2 are values sent separately from the query text, through the PostgreSQL protocol. Writing a value directly in the query works the same way (Parameters and literals). All examples run on the operational path unless stated otherwise. Declaring a protected column sql CREATE [TEMPORARY] TABLE name ( column type [PROTECTED MATCH DOMAIN domain] [constraints], column type PROTECTED REFERENCES other (column), ... ); PROTECTED MATCH DOMAIN d declares a protected column and names its match domain. A domain is created by its first use. A column that references a protected column is itself protected and takes the same domain: write PROTECTED REFERENCES t (c), without repeating the domain. Constraints (PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, REFERENCES) work on protected columns too; the engine checks them through the blind index, and the error never shows the value. text admin@operational=> CREATE TABLE patients ( patient_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, national_id TEXT PROTECTED MATCH DOMAIN person_id UNIQUE, full_name TEXT ); CREATE TABLE admin@operational=> CREATE TABLE records ( record_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, patient_national_id TEXT PROTECTED REFERENCES patients (national_id), diagnosis TEXT ); CREATE TABLE admin@operational=> SHOW COLUMNS FROM records; column type match_domain primary_key references not_null unique ---------------------+--------+--------------+-------------+------------------------+----------+-------- record_id BIGINT NULL yes NULL yes yes patient_national_id TEXT person_id patients (national_id) diagnosis TEXT NULL NULL (3 rows) The reference and the column it references must agree, and the engine checks it: text admin@operational=> CREATE TABLE bad1 (id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, nid TEXT PROTECTED); ERROR: PROTECTED column nid needs a match domain HINT: Write TEXT PROTECTED MATCH DOMAIN name, or PROTECTED REFERENCES a protected column. A protected value is never stored in an ordinary column; the next section shows the error. Inserting and updating protected values What is it? Protected values are written with ordinary INSERT and UPDATE statements. The server converts them to their protected form immediately. Example 1: Registering a patient sql INSERT INTO patients (patient_id, national_id, full_name, health_fund) VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4); Output text INSERT 0 1 Explanation: the ID number in $2 is normalized, turned into an index entry and a ciphertext, and stored. It never appears in the server's logs. Example 2: Updating a record found by its ID number Dana has changed her family name. Reception updates it, and uses the ID number only to locate the record: sql UPDATE patients SET full_name = $2 WHERE national_id = $1; Output text UPDATE 1 Explanation: WHERE national_id = $1 is an anchored lookup (Finding a record by a protected value): it finds one patient by one value. Example 3: The same update from the masked path Output text ERROR: DEP_ENDPOINT_OPERATION DETAIL: Writes are unavailable on a MASKED_READ connection. Explanation: the masked path is read-only. Compare with a string. Checking whether a protected value is present A missing value and a hidden value are different. A protected column comes back as NULL in ordinary query output even when the database stores a value. That output does not tell you whether the stored value is missing. Three SQL forms answer different questions: - IS NULL / IS NOT NULL checks whether the stored value in one row is missing or present. - COUNT(national_id) counts the rows whose stored national_id is not NULL. - COUNT() counts rows, without checking whether national_id has a value. Assume patients.national_id is protected and the role has the required ordinary SELECT privileges. The DEP rules distinguish these operations: Operation Operational Masked read --------- Filter rows with WHERE national_id IS NOT NULL (or IS NULL) Allowed Refused: ZD102 Return the test with SELECT national_id IS NULL (or IS NOT NULL) Refused: ZD101 Refused: ZD102 Count stored values with COUNT(national_id) Refused: ZD101 Refused: ZD102 Count rows with COUNT() Allowed Allowed Filter rows: allowed on the operational path. The application can select rows that have an identifier without returning the identifier or a separate presence flag. sql SELECT patient_id FROM patients WHERE national_id IS NOT NULL; Count rows: allowed on either path. This counts the rows the query selects, including rows whose identifier is missing. Adding a protected-value filter is a separate operation, and follows the rule in the first row of the table. sql SELECT COUNT() AS patient_count FROM patients; Return a presence flag or count stored identifiers: refused on either path. These reveal information about the protected column rather than simply counting rows. sql -- Refused: return whether an identifier is missing. SELECT national_id IS NULL AS identifier_missing FROM patients; -- Refused: count non-NULL identifiers. SELECT COUNT(national_id) AS identifiers_present FROM patients; Allowing a presence test in a filter does not allow COUNT(national_id) inside a condition such as HAVING. Use the distinct rules above rather than treating every presence-related expression as interchangeable. Selecting a protected column What is it? When an ordinary query selects a protected column, the value is replaced with a real SQL NULL before the result is sent. This is called suppression. Why is it needed? Existing applications, ORMs, and reports that select every column should keep working, without receiving identifiers. Example 1: Asking for the ID number with the name sql SELECT full_name, national_id FROM patients WHERE national_id = $1; Output full_name national_id --- --- Dana Cohen NULL Explanation: the match still works: Dana was found. But a protected value never leaves the database in an ordinary query, so national_id comes back as NULL. Example 2: SELECT sql SELECT FROM patients WHERE national_id = $1; Output patient_id national_id phone full_name health_fund --- --- --- --- --- 1 NULL NULL Dana Cohen Clalit Explanation: both protected columns are suppressed. An application that always selects every column keeps working; it simply never receives the identifiers. Rules in detail 1. Suppression happens at the output boundary, on both paths, in every result format. 2. The value is a real SQL NULL: not the string "NULL", not the stored ciphertext, and not a reusable token. 3. The column keeps its declared type in the result description. Notes - Why not a token? Returning stable "gibberish" in place of the ID would let clients track Dana across results. - Why not an error? Because selecting is harmless once the value is suppressed. Processing a protected value, as opposed to selecting it, is an error (Operations that are not allowed). - Telling suppression from absence. Whether a client can tell a suppressed value from a missing one is an open question (Roadmap and Release). Protected status is always visible in the schema. Queries on the masked path What is it? On the masked path, queries over ordinary fields run exactly as in ordinary SQL, and any matching on protected values is rejected. Example 1: Statistics the dashboard needs sql SELECT p.health_fund, COUNT() FROM appointments AS a JOIN patients AS p USING (patient_id) GROUP BY p.health_fund; Output health_fund count --- --- Clalit 1,284 Maccabi 903 Explanation: the query joins through the ordinary key patient_id and touches no protected column, so it runs as usual. Example 2: The assistant tries to look Dana up sql SELECT full_name FROM patients WHERE national_id = $1; Output text ERROR: DEP_ENDPOINT_OPERATION DETAIL: Matching PROTECTED values is unavailable on a MASKED_READ connection. HINT: This operation requires an OPERATIONAL connection. Explanation: the response is an error, not zero rows. An unsupported operation is a different outcome from an unsuccessful lookup, so the assistant cannot even learn whether Dana is a patient. Errors. DEP_ENDPOINT_OPERATION. A protected input is a value the client sends in a protected position. It can arrive in two forms, and both are allowed: - a protected parameter, sent separately from the query text, as $1; - a protected literal, written in the query text, as '123456782'. Why is it needed? DEP is SQL, and a query that searches for Dana has to send her ID number to the server. What counts as a protected position? A value compared with a protected column, joined against one, or inserted into one. Example 1: The same lookup, both ways sql -- As a parameter: the value travels separately from the query text SELECT full_name FROM patients WHERE national_id = $1; -- As a literal: the value is written in the query text SELECT full_name FROM patients WHERE national_id = '123456782'; Output (both) full_name --- Dana Cohen Explanation: both are anchored lookups, follow the same rules, and are recorded the same way. Example 2: Literals in an insert and an update sql INSERT INTO patients (patient_id, national_id, full_name, phone) VALUES (3, '345678904', 'Noa Mizrahi', '+972-50-0000003'); -- both stored protected UPDATE patients SET full_name = 'Dana Cohen-Levi' WHERE national_id = '123456782'; -- used for matching Explanation: '345678904' and '+972-50-0000003' go into protected columns, so they are protected literals. 'Noa Mizrahi' goes into an ordinary column, so it is ordinary. Example 3: What the server's log records text LOG: statement: UPDATE patients SET full_name = 'Dana Cohen-Levi' WHERE national_id = Explanation: the protected literal is redacted wherever the server records the statement. The ordinary literal is not. Rules in detail. From the moment the statement is parsed, a protected input is: 1. normalized and converted to an index entry with the match domain's key, and used only for matching or storage; 2. unavailable to the rest of the query, which cannot read, transform, or return it; 3. redacted from the statement text wherever the server records or echoes it: logs, query statistics, audit records, and error messages. Notes - Protection is positional. DEP recognizes a value as protected because of where it is used, not because of what it looks like. A value written elsewhere (SELECT '123456782', for instance) is ordinary text, and the server has no way to know it is an ID number. - Parameters are still recommended. They keep the value out of the query text entirely, and they are the standard defense against SQL injection. - Client-side substitution. Some drivers substitute values into the query text before sending it. To the server, that is a literal, and it is handled as one. Protected foreign keys What is it? A protected foreign key is a foreign key from a protected column to a protected column of the same match domain. Why is it needed? A foreign key promises that every value in one column also appears in another. When the referenced column is protected, the protected value now lives in two places; these rules keep the second place as protected as the first. Syntax sql column_name base_type PROTECTED REFERENCES table_name ( protected_column ) Example 1: Linking diagnoses through the protected ID number sql CREATE TABLE medical_records ( record_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, patient_national_id TEXT PROTECTED REFERENCES patients (national_id), -- inherits person_id diagnosis TEXT, recorded_at DATE ); Output text CREATE TABLE Explanation: the clinic links diagnoses to patients through the protected ID number, not through patient_id, because a list of patients next to their diagnoses is exactly the kind of link that must be guarded. The match domain person_id is inherited from patients.national_id. Example 2: Forgetting PROTECTED sql CREATE TABLE medical_records ( record_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, patient_national_id TEXT REFERENCES patients (national_id), diagnosis TEXT ); Output text ERROR: DEP_REFERENCE_MISMATCH DETAIL: medical_records.patient_national_id references patients.national_id, which is PROTECTED. HINT: Declare the column TEXT PROTECTED REFERENCES patients (national_id). Explanation: without PROTECTED, the second table would hold an ordinary copy of every ID number, and a plain SELECT on it would return them all. Example 3: Recording a diagnosis for a patient who does not exist sql INSERT INTO medical_records (record_id, patient_national_id, diagnosis) VALUES (104, $1, 'Migraine'); -- $1 is not any patient's ID number Output text ERROR: insert or update on table "medical_records" violates foreign key constraint "medical_records_patient_national_id_fkey" Explanation: the check happened inside the engine, on index entries. The error names only the constraint, never the value. But the failure itself reveals that no patient has that ID number, so the check is counted as a protected lookup, audited and rate-limited. Requiring qualified access > Future design, not supported in DEP Engine 0.5.2. This section records an idea from the proposal. The ALTER TABLE option below is not runnable on the current Engine; ZD105 is reserved. Current protected-join anchoring does not prohibit every unfiltered ordinary read or write. What is it? A table can require qualified access: every operational read or write on it must be anchored to one protected value or to its primary key. Why is it needed? For tables where every legitimate access is targeted, it turns an accidental UPDATE without a WHERE, or a full scan, into an explicit error. Syntax. The exact form is not yet fixed. One possibility is a table option: sql ALTER TABLE patients SET (qualified_access = true); Example 1: An update that names one patient sql UPDATE patients SET full_name = $2 WHERE national_id = $1; Output text UPDATE 1 Example 2: An update that names nobody sql UPDATE patients SET full_name = $1; Output text ERROR: DEP_UNQUALIFIED_ACCESS DETAIL: UPDATE on patients requires a qualifying lookup predicate. HINT: Locate the record by a single PROTECTED value or by its primary key. Explanation: without qualified access, the second statement would have renamed all 50,000 patients. Notes. Which tables should require qualified access, and whether it should be the default for tables with protected columns, is an open question (Roadmap and Release). Errors. CONNECT ENDPOINT e Log in through an endpoint, and so on its access path A role can connect only through endpoints it was granted, and an endpoint is bound to one path, so the grant decides the path. Only superusers create roles, endpoints and tables. The GRANT SELECT (columns) form is what makes the privacy matrix. Here support may match on email and marketing may not, because it connects through the masked read path: text admin@operational=> CREATE TABLE accounts (id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT PROTECTED MATCH DOMAIN email, name TEXT); CREATE TABLE admin@operational=> CREATE ROLE support LOGIN PASSWORD 'x'; CREATE ROLE admin@operational=> CREATE ROLE marketing LOGIN PASSWORD 'x'; CREATE ROLE admin@operational=> GRANT CONNECT ON ENDPOINT operational TO support; GRANT admin@operational=> GRANT CONNECT ON ENDPOINT analytics TO marketing; GRANT admin@operational=> GRANT SELECT (id, email, name) ON accounts TO support; GRANT admin@operational=> GRANT SELECT (id, name) ON accounts TO marketing; GRANT admin@operational=> SHOW PRIVACY MATRIX; match_domain column role paths may_match discloses_via links_via --------------+----------------+-----------+----------------------------------------------------+-----------+---------------+----------- email accounts.email admin analytics (MASKED_READ), operational (OPERATIONAL) yes email accounts.email marketing analytics (MASKED_READ) no email accounts.email support operational (OPERATIONAL) yes (3 rows) SHOW PRIVACY MATRIX lists, for every protected column and every role, whether the role may match on it, through which paths, and which declared functions it may use to disclose or link it. It is computed from the grants, so it cannot drift. SET ROLE A superuser can act as another role without reconnecting. It is the way to test what a role sees. text admin@operational=> SET ROLE reception_app; SET reception_app@operational=> SHOW ROLE; role --------------- reception_app (1 row) reception_app@operational=> SELECT phone FROM patients; ERROR: permission denied for column phone of table patients HINT: In DEP, the privilege on a PROTECTED column is the privilege to match on it. GRANT SELECT (phone) ON patients TO reception_app would allow it. SQLSTATE: 42501 reception_app@operational=> RESET ROLE; SET admin@operational=> SHOW ROLE; role ------- admin (1 row) SET ROLE changes the privileges that apply. It does not change the access path of the connection, which is fixed at login. Match limits A lookup on a protected column is a question, "is this value in the table?", and a program that can ask it without limit can guess every value. A match limit caps how many protected matches a role can make in a period. It is set per role, with a server default for roles that are not superusers (--match-limit). sql ALTER ROLE reception_app MATCH LIMIT 600 PER HOUR; -- units: SECOND, MINUTE, HOUR, DAY ALTER ROLE reception_app MATCH LIMIT NONE; -- no limit for this role ALTER ROLE reception_app MATCH LIMIT DEFAULT; -- the server default text admin@operational=> ALTER ROLE reception_app MATCH LIMIT 2 PER MINUTE; ALTER ROLE admin@operational=> \c operational reception_app You are now connected as "reception_app" through endpoint "operational" (OPERATIONAL). reception_app@operational=> SELECT full_name FROM patients WHERE national_id IN ('123456782', '234567893'); DEP: PROTECTED column patients.national_id is matched against a list of values through the blind index of MATCH DOMAIN person_id. full_name ------------ Dana Cohen Yossi Levi (2 rows) reception_app@operational=> SELECT full_name FROM patients WHERE national_id = '345678904'; ERROR: Role reception_app has made 2 protected matches of the 2 PER MINUTE it is allowed; this statement would make 1 more. HINT: Wait for the period to pass, or ask a superuser to change the limit (ALTER ROLE ... MATCH LIMIT n PER MINUTE). SQLSTATE: ZD109 (DEP_MATCH_RATE_LIMITED) A statement over the limit fails with ZD109 DEP_MATCH_RATE_LIMITED before it reads anything, and the refusal is audited. Every value in an IN list counts. Clinic schema mermaid flowchart LR P["patients identity"] ---"patient_id · ordinary key · open" A["appointments"] P -.-"national_id · protected key · guarded" M["medical_records diagnoses"] linkStyle 0 stroke:16a34a,stroke-width:2px linkStyle 1 stroke:d97706,stroke-width:2px,stroke-dasharray:6 4 The complete executable setup, including roles, grants, data and functions, is clinic.sql. Load it once using the clinic setup instructions. The clinic uses ordinary keys for appointments and protected keys for diagnoses; this is a modeling decision for this example, not a claim that appointment data is always non-sensitive.

title: Declared functions
text: In one sentence: a declared function is a SQL function whose signature states that it discloses protected values, links datasets through them, or both, and it is the only place where either can happen. Why declared functions are needed What problem do they solve? Most of the clinic's work is pull work: someone arrives with a value and asks for the matching record. Reception and the doctors work this way, with anchored matching, and never need the value back. Two kinds of legitimate work do not fit that pattern: Kind of work In the clinic Why ordinary queries cannot do it --- --- --- Releasing the values themselves The monthly report to the health funds; appointment reminders by SMS; diagnosis claims The database is the only party that knows the values at that moment, and ordinary queries never return them Linking whole datasets Diagnoses per health fund, for the dashboard Ordinary queries may match only one value at a time Why not a permission? A general "read permission" or "link permission" would collapse back into the column privileges DEP was meant to improve on. DEP instead forbids both by default and makes each exception an explicit construct of the language, as Rust does with unsafe. There are two such constructs: DISCLOSES and LINKS. Disclosure and linkage are separate declarations, each with domain privileges and explicit callers. REVEAL What is it? REVEAL is the only operation that turns a protected value into an ordinary one. Syntax sql REVEAL ( protected_column ) Parameters Parameter Meaning --- --- protected_column A protected column of match domain d. Return value. The value, with the base type of the column: REVEAL of a TEXT PROTECTED column returns TEXT. The result is a disclosed value (Disclosed values and the terminal rule). Example 1: REVEAL inside a disclosing function sql CREATE FUNCTION monthly_fund_report(report_month DATE) RETURNS TABLE (national_id TEXT, visit_date DATE, visit_type TEXT, health_fund TEXT) LANGUAGE sql DISCLOSES person_id AS $$ SELECT REVEAL(p.national_id), a.starts_at::date, a.visit_type, p.health_fund FROM appointments AS a JOIN patients AS p USING (patient_id) WHERE date_trunc('month', a.starts_at) = date_trunc('month', CAST(report_month AS TIMESTAMP)); $$; Output text CREATE FUNCTION Explanation: REVEAL(p.national_id) is allowed, because the function declares DISCLOSES person_id and national_id belongs to person_id. Example 2: REVEAL in an ordinary query sql SELECT REVEAL(national_id) FROM patients; Output text ERROR: DEP_REVEAL_OUTSIDE_DISCLOSURE DETAIL: REVEAL() of patients.national_id (match domain person_id) appears outside a disclosing function. HINT: Move the disclosure into a function declared DISCLOSES person_id. Explanation: outside a disclosing function, REVEAL does not exist as far as the client is concerned. Example 3: REVEAL of the wrong domain sql CREATE FUNCTION phones_and_ids() RETURNS TABLE (phone TEXT, national_id TEXT) LANGUAGE sql DISCLOSES phone_number AS $$ SELECT REVEAL(phone), REVEAL(national_id) FROM patients; $$; Output text ERROR: DEP_REVEAL_OUTSIDE_DISCLOSURE DETAIL: REVEAL() of patients.national_id (match domain person_id) appears outside a disclosing function. Explanation: the function may reveal phone numbers, but not ID numbers. Each domain must be declared separately. The check runs when the function is created, not only when it runs. Errors. DEP_REVEAL_OUTSIDE_DISCLOSURE. CREATE FUNCTION ... DISCLOSES What is it? A disclosing function is a function declared DISCLOSES d. Inside its body, values of match domain d may be revealed. Why is it needed? For any workflow that needs protected values to leave the database: a report, a file for an external system, a message to a person. Syntax sql CREATE FUNCTION function_name ( [ parameter_name type [, ...] ] ) RETURNS TABLE ( column_name type [, ...] ) LANGUAGE sql DISCLOSES domain_name [, ...] [ LINKS domain_name [, ...] ] AS $$ query $$; Parameters Clause Meaning --- --- function_name, parameters As in any PostgreSQL function. RETURNS TABLE (...) The columns the caller receives. A disclosed column has the base type of the protected column it comes from. LANGUAGE sql Required, so the engine can analyze the body when the function is created. DISCLOSES domain_name The match domains whose values the body may REVEAL. LINKS domain_name Optional; also allows unanchored matching in that domain (Declaring both). AS $$ ... $$ The function body, in ordinary PostgreSQL syntax. Working with the loaded clinic. Its functions already exist. Use SHOW FUNCTIONS to inspect them. The definitions below explain their construction; an administrator can use CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION to update one, or choose a new function name when experimenting. Example 1: Calling the monthly report The billing job calls the function from REVEAL with ordinary SQL: sql SELECT FROM monthly_fund_report('2026-10-01'); Output national_id visit_date visit_type health_fund --- --- --- --- 123456782 2026-10-14 Follow-up Clalit Explanation: the billing job receives a real ID number, as ordinary TEXT, because that is what the signature promises. This is one of only two places in the clinic where ID numbers can leave the database. Example 2: Reminders, in the other domain sql CREATE FUNCTION appointment_reminders(day DATE) RETURNS TABLE (phone TEXT, starts_at TIMESTAMPTZ) LANGUAGE sql DISCLOSES phone_number AS $$ SELECT REVEAL(p.phone), a.starts_at FROM appointments AS a JOIN patients AS p USING (patient_id) WHERE CAST(a.starts_at AS DATE) = day; $$; SELECT FROM appointment_reminders(DATE '2026-10-21'); -- as reminder_job Output phone starts_at --- --- +972-50-0000001 2026-10-21 10:30 Explanation: the function returns the phone number and the time, and nothing else. A reminder SMS does not need to say what the visit is for, so the visit type never leaves with the phone number. A declared function should return only what its purpose requires. Example 3: Calling a disclosing function from the masked path sql SELECT FROM monthly_fund_report('2026-10-01'); -- as bi_dashboard Output text ERROR: DEP_ENDPOINT_OPERATION DETAIL: Disclosing functions are unavailable on a MASKED_READ connection. Explanation: disclosure happens only on the operational path, even for a role that somehow holds EXECUTE. Rules in detail. The creator needs DISCLOSE ON MATCH DOMAIN d (GRANT DISCLOSE and GRANT LINK); the function is never executable by PUBLIC (GRANT EXECUTE on declared functions); it runs only on the operational path; and its disclosed output columns are terminal (Disclosed values and the terminal rule). The full list is in The rules for declared functions. Errors. DEP_DECLARATION_PRIVILEGE, DEP_DECLARED_LANGUAGE, DEP_DECLARED_CALL, DEP_REVEAL_OUTSIDE_DISCLOSURE, DEP_ENDPOINT_OPERATION. CREATE FUNCTION ... LINKS What is it? A linking function is a function declared LINKS d. Inside its body, protected values of domain d may be matched without an anchor, linking whole datasets. Why is it needed? For a workflow that must connect whole datasets through a protected value, typically to compute statistics, without releasing the values. Syntax sql CREATE FUNCTION function_name ( [ parameter_name type [, ...] ] ) RETURNS TABLE ( column_name type [, ...] ) LANGUAGE sql LINKS domain_name [, ...] AS $$ query $$; Example 1: Diagnoses per health fund sql CREATE FUNCTION diagnoses_per_fund() RETURNS TABLE (health_fund TEXT, diagnosis TEXT, patients BIGINT) LANGUAGE sql LINKS person_id AS $$ SELECT p.health_fund, m.diagnosis, COUNT() FROM patients AS p JOIN medical_records AS m ON m.patient_national_id = p.national_id GROUP BY p.health_fund, m.diagnosis; $$; GRANT EXECUTE ON FUNCTION diagnoses_per_fund() TO bi_dashboard; Output text CREATE FUNCTION GRANT Explanation: the join inside the body has no anchor; it links every patient to every diagnosis. That is allowed only because the function declares LINKS person_id. Example 2: The dashboard calls it from the masked path sql SELECT FROM diagnoses_per_fund(); Output health_fund diagnosis patients --- --- --- Clalit Diabetes 412 Maccabi Asthma 187 Explanation: the function returns only counts, so it discloses nothing. The dashboard receives the result of a linkage the clinic approved, without gaining any ability to link anything itself. It sends no protected value, so it cannot use the function to probe for one, which is why a linking function without protected input may run on the masked path. Example 3: The dashboard tries the same join itself sql SELECT p.health_fund, m.diagnosis, COUNT() FROM patients AS p JOIN medical_records AS m ON m.patient_national_id = p.national_id GROUP BY p.health_fund, m.diagnosis; Output text ERROR: DEP_ENDPOINT_OPERATION DETAIL: Matching PROTECTED values is unavailable on a MASKED_READ connection. Explanation: the permission belongs to the reviewed function, not to the caller. The same SQL, written outside the function, is rejected. Rules in detail 1. The creator needs LINK ON MATCH DOMAIN d. 2. LINKS alone does not permit REVEAL. 3. A linking function that takes no protected input may be called on both paths. 4. A linking function that takes a protected value as a parameter may be called only on the operational path, because calling it is itself a form of matching. Errors. DEP_DECLARATION_PRIVILEGE, DEP_ENDPOINT_OPERATION. Declaring both What is it? A function may declare both DISCLOSES d and LINKS d when it must link datasets and release values. Example: The diagnosis claims sql CREATE FUNCTION fund_claims_report(report_month DATE) RETURNS TABLE (national_id TEXT, diagnosis TEXT, recorded_at DATE) LANGUAGE sql DISCLOSES person_id LINKS person_id AS $$ SELECT REVEAL(p.national_id), m.diagnosis, m.recorded_at FROM medical_records AS m JOIN patients AS p ON p.national_id = m.patient_national_id WHERE date_trunc('month', CAST(m.recorded_at AS TIMESTAMP)) = date_trunc('month', CAST(report_month AS TIMESTAMP)); $$; GRANT EXECUTE ON FUNCTION fund_claims_report(DATE) TO billing_job; Explanation: - The join links every diagnosis of the month to its patient, which requires LINKS person_id. - The output includes the ID number, which requires DISCLOSES person_id. - "Returns ID numbers" and "links patients to diagnoses" are two different privacy decisions, and a reviewer should see both in the signature. DISCLOSES alone does not permit linking, and LINKS alone does not permit REVEAL. The working idiom: match first, reveal last. The join happens through internal matching on protected fields, and REVEAL appears only in the final projection, on the column the value is disclosed from. GRANT DISCLOSE and GRANT LINK What is it? GRANT DISCLOSE and GRANT LINK give a role the privilege to create disclosing and linking functions for one match domain. Why is it needed? Declaring a function is adding "unsafe code" to the database. Only designated roles should be able to do it, domain by domain. Syntax sql GRANT { DISCLOSE LINK } ON MATCH DOMAIN domain_name TO role_name [, ...]; REVOKE { DISCLOSE LINK } ON MATCH DOMAIN domain_name FROM role_name [, ...]; Parameters Parameter Meaning --- --- DISCLOSE Allows creating or altering functions declared DISCLOSES domain_name. LINK Allows creating or altering functions declared LINKS domain_name. domain_name The match domain the privilege applies to. role_name The role receiving the privilege. Example 1: The clinic's privacy administrator sql GRANT DISCLOSE ON MATCH DOMAIN person_id TO privacy_admin; GRANT LINK ON MATCH DOMAIN person_id TO privacy_admin; GRANT DISCLOSE ON MATCH DOMAIN phone_number TO privacy_admin; Explanation: every declared function in the clinic is created by privacy_admin. Note what is missing: nobody may declare LINKS phone_number, so phone numbers can never be used to link datasets. Example 2: A developer tries to declare a linking function sql -- as app_developer CREATE FUNCTION all_diagnoses() RETURNS TABLE (diagnosis TEXT) LANGUAGE sql LINKS person_id AS $$ ... $$; Output text ERROR: DEP_DECLARATION_PRIVILEGE DETAIL: Role app_developer may not declare functions LINKS person_id. HINT: This function must be created by a role holding LINK ON MATCH DOMAIN person_id. Explanation: the developer may write the function, but it must be reviewed and created by a role holding the privilege. Notes. These are the only two privileges DEP adds. They decide who may write declared functions, not who may call them. GRANT EXECUTE on declared functions What is it? Who may call a declared function is decided by the ordinary GRANT EXECUTE, with one difference: declared functions are never executable by PUBLIC. Syntax sql GRANT EXECUTE ON FUNCTION function_name ( argument_types ) TO role_name [, ...]; Example 1: Granting the reports to their jobs sql GRANT EXECUTE ON FUNCTION monthly_fund_report(DATE) TO billing_job; GRANT EXECUTE ON FUNCTION appointment_reminders(DATE) TO reminder_job; Explanation: each consumer appears in the grants by name, so the list of who may receive disclosed values is explicit. Example 2: Opening a disclosing function to everyone sql GRANT EXECUTE ON FUNCTION monthly_fund_report(DATE) TO PUBLIC; Output text ERROR: DEP_PUBLIC_EXECUTE DETAIL: monthly_fund_report is declared DISCLOSES person_id and cannot be executable by PUBLIC. HINT: Grant EXECUTE to the specific roles that need it. Explanation: in PostgreSQL, new functions are executable by PUBLIC by default. For declared functions that default would make every disclosure available to everyone, so DEP removes it. Rules in detail 1. Declared functions are created with no EXECUTE privilege for anyone but their owner. 2. Granting EXECUTE on a declared function to PUBLIC is rejected. 3. A caller needs only EXECUTE, not privilege on the protected columns the function matches on internally (The rules for declared functions, rule 8). Errors. DEP_PUBLIC_EXECUTE. The rules for declared functions Rule What it means --- --- --- 1 Location of REVEAL If x has type T PROTECTED in domain d, then REVEAL(x) has type T and is valid only in the body of a function declared DISCLOSES d. Checked at creation. 2 Location of unanchored matching Unanchored matching on values of domain d is valid only in the body of a function declared LINKS d. 3 Analyzable bodies Declared functions must be LANGUAGE sql. They may call user-defined functions only if those are declared for the same purpose and domain; otherwise a protected or revealed value could reach code that was never reviewed. 4 Disclosed values are terminal Values produced by REVEAL may be returned to the client, renamed or cast, but not used in a predicate, join condition, grouping, DISTINCT, aggregate, sort key, insert, or as the argument of a function or operator (Disclosed values and the terminal rule). 5 Paths Disclosing functions run only on the operational path. Linking functions run on the operational path, and on the masked path when they take no protected input. 6 Declaring is privileged DISCLOSES d requires DISCLOSE ON MATCH DOMAIN d; LINKS d requires LINK ON MATCH DOMAIN d (GRANT DISCLOSE and GRANT LINK). 7 No public execution Declared functions are never executable by PUBLIC (GRANT EXECUTE on declared functions). 8 Matching runs under the declaration The matches inside a declared function were reviewed as part of the function, so a caller needs only EXECUTE, much like SECURITY DEFINER in PostgreSQL. That is why the dashboard, which has no privilege on any protected column, can call diagnoses_per_fund. Disclosed values and the terminal rule What is it? A disclosed value is a value produced by REVEAL. The terminal rule says that a disclosed value may only be returned to the client: it is the end of the line inside the database. Implementation status: DEP.js applies the whole rule. DEP Engine 0.5.2 accepts three uses it forbids: a disclosed value as a sort key, as the argument of a function or operator, and as a DISTINCT key. See the known differences before relying on the rule in a released Engine. Why is it needed? Without it, the report approved for the health funds could be turned into a tool for linking patients to diagnoses inside the database. Example 1: Returning a disclosed value (allowed) sql SELECT national_id, visit_date FROM monthly_fund_report('2026-10-01'); Output national_id visit_date --- --- 123456782 2026-10-14 Explanation: returning the value is exactly what the function is for. Example 2: Joining a disclosed value back to diagnoses (rejected) sql SELECT r.national_id, m.diagnosis FROM monthly_fund_report('2026-10-01') AS r JOIN medical_records AS m ON m.patient_national_id = r.national_id; Output text ERROR: DEP_DISCLOSED_VALUE_USE DETAIL: Column national_id of monthly_fund_report() is a disclosed value and cannot be used in a join condition. HINT: Disclosed values can only be returned. Perform the match on PROTECTED fields inside a declared function, before REVEAL. Explanation: the signature says TEXT, and the developer sees an ordinary column. But the engine recorded that this column comes from REVEAL, so it may not be used as a join key. The report cannot become a linking tool. Example 3: Filtering a disclosed value (rejected) sql SELECT r.national_id FROM monthly_fund_report('2026-10-01') AS r WHERE r.national_id LIKE '1%'; Output text ERROR: DEP_DISCLOSED_VALUE_USE Explanation: filtering is a use, not a return. If the billing job needs only some rows, the filter belongs inside the declared function. Rules in detail 1. The engine records which output columns of a declared function come from REVEAL. 2. Those columns may be returned to the client, renamed (AS) or cast, and nothing else: no predicate, join condition, grouping, DISTINCT, aggregate, sort key, insert, or argument of a function or operator (upper(national_id), national_id '', CASE). Nothing is computed from a disclosed value inside the database. 3. A disclosed value keeps its base type. A revealed DATE remains a DATE; the terminal rule already prevents further processing, so converting everything to text would add no protection. What the rule does not prevent - Use after release. The rule governs what happens inside the database. Once a value is returned, DEP cannot control its use. The billing job can send the ID numbers back as parameters to later queries, but each is then an anchored lookup, audited and rate-limited. - Linkage through ordinary keys. The rule stops the marked value from being used as a key. If monthly_fund_report also returned patient_id, its output could be joined freely to every table that holds patient_id: sql -- Would be allowed, if the function returned patient_id: the join uses an ordinary key. SELECT r.national_id, a.visit_type FROM monthly_fund_report('2026-10-01') AS r JOIN appointments AS a USING (patient_id); Two design rules follow, and Designing with DEP applies both: a declared function returns only what its purpose requires (none of the clinic's functions returns patient_id), and a key that links sensitive datasets should itself be protected. Errors. DEP_DISCLOSED_VALUE_USE. Documenting purpose: COMMENT ON FUNCTION What is it? The purpose of a declared function is recorded with the standard COMMENT ON FUNCTION, which keeps it in the catalog without new syntax. Syntax sql COMMENT ON FUNCTION function_name ( argument_types ) IS 'text'; Example sql COMMENT ON FUNCTION monthly_fund_report(DATE) IS 'Purpose: monthly visit report to health funds. Owner: billing.'; COMMENT ON FUNCTION appointment_reminders(DATE) IS 'Purpose: SMS appointment reminders. Owner: operations.'; COMMENT ON FUNCTION diagnoses_per_fund() IS 'Purpose: diagnosis statistics per health fund. Owner: management.'; COMMENT ON FUNCTION fund_claims_report(DATE) IS 'Purpose: monthly diagnosis claims to health funds. Owner: billing.'; Explanation: the comment appears in the comment column of SHOW FUNCTIONS (Inspect declared functions), next to the declaration it explains. Notes. Whether purpose should become a first-class, machine-checked part of a declaration is an open question (Roadmap and Release). Inspect declared functions Use the implemented SHOW FUNCTIONS command to list signatures, discloses and links domains, owner, masked-path availability, comments, callers and SQL bodies. sql SHOW FUNCTIONS; SHOW GRANTS; SHOW PRIVACY MATRIX; The earlier dep.declared_functions SQL catalog view remains a design idea, not an implemented query interface. Use SHOW commands for exact columns and examples. The mapping to Rust Rust DEP --- --- An unsafe operation (dereferencing a raw pointer) REVEAL, or unanchored matching on a protected value unsafe fn or an unsafe block A function body declared DISCLOSES d or LINKS d A safe wrapper that exposes an ordinary API A declared function whose signature returns ordinary types A Safety comment documenting the contract COMMENT ON FUNCTION describing the purpose cargo geiger, which counts every unsafe in a project The SHOW FUNCTIONS command Future extension: partial disclosure > Future design. Suffix disclosure syntax is not supported in DEP Engine 0.5.2. What is the idea? Some recipients need less than the full value. A letter to Dana might show only the last four digits of her ID number, to confirm it reached the right person. A later version could make the form of disclosure part of the declaration, so that data minimization becomes a check at creation time: sql DISCLOSES person_id AS SUFFIX(4) Explanation: in such a body only REVEAL_SUFFIX(x, 4) would be legal; writing the full REVEAL(x) would be an error. This is intentionally outside the first version. Key points - REVEAL exists only inside DISCLOSES functions; unanchored matching only inside LINKS functions. - Declaring needs a per-domain privilege; calling needs EXECUTE, never PUBLIC. - Disclosed values can only be returned, never reused inside the database. - The catalog lists every declared function, so it is the complete answer to "where can values leave?" --- A permitted disclosure is shown as declared output in the client.
