title: Design with DEP
text: Design principles In one sentence: ten rules that every other part of DEP follows. Each is stated, illustrated with the clinic, and followed by what it means in practice. 1. Protection is declared in the schema. Marking a field as protected changes its behavior everywhere in the engine. There is no separate policy file that can drift out of sync with the table, and no application code that must agree to honor it. - Example. Declaring national_id TEXT PROTECTED protects it for all six consumers, including the AI agent connected last week. - In practice: reading the schema is enough to know what is protected. 2. Defined capabilities instead of general access. The rules are an allow-list. Anchored equality matching on the operational path is permitted; everything else (substrings, casts, ordering, ranges, arbitrary functions) is rejected until it is explicitly designed and added. - Example. WHERE RIGHT(national_id, 4) = '6782' is rejected, because "last four digits" was never designed as an operation. - In practice: a new SQL feature never weakens protection by accident. 3. Single values are operational work; bulk processing is declared. Finding, updating, or connecting the records of one protected value is everyday work, and DEP allows it to anyone who may use the column. Linking whole datasets, or releasing the values themselves, is an organizational decision, and DEP allows it only in declared code. - Example. The doctor sees Dana's diagnoses; listing every patient's diagnoses requires a declared function. - In practice: applications keep working; exports and linkages become reviewable objects. 4. Permit and attribute. DEP does not decide whether a particular person may look up a particular record; ordinary permissions and the organization's own rules do that. DEP guarantees that every protected match is recorded, attributed to an identity, and rate-limited. - Example. Reception may look anyone up, and every lookup is in the audit log under reception_app. - In practice: a single action is allowed and visible; misuse can be detected and traced. 5. Protection travels with the value. Aliases, subqueries, common table expressions, views, temporary tables, and planner transformations must not turn a protected value into an ordinary one. - Example. Wrapping national_id in a common table expression and calling length() on it is still rejected. - In practice: there is no way to launder a value through query structure. 6. Exceptions are explicit and local. The only way to reveal a protected value is REVEAL inside a function declared DISCLOSES, and the only way to link whole datasets through protected values is a function declared LINKS. - Example. monthly_fund_report is visible in the schema as the place ID numbers leave. - In practice: every exception is visible in the code, not hidden in a grant. 7. Reject rather than silently weaken. When a query asks for something forbidden, DEP returns an explicit error. It never "fixes" the query by removing a condition, because that would change its meaning and could return far more data than intended. - Example. The assistant's lookup returns DEP_ENDPOINT_OPERATION, not zero rows. - In practice: an error never looks like an empty result, and an empty result never hides an error. 8. The path belongs to the connection, not to the query. Whether a client is operational or masked is decided by the server at login. No statement, session variable, role switch, or pooled connection can change it. - Example. SET dep.path = 'OPERATIONAL' on the assistant's connection is rejected. - In practice: a misbehaving client cannot promote itself. 9. Familiar SQL wherever possible. DEP adds a few constructs to PostgreSQL-style syntax and reuses everything else: CREATE FUNCTION, LANGUAGE sql, $$ bodies, GRANT, COMMENT ON. It adds no permission system of its own beyond two privileges for declaring functions. - Example. The monthly report is an ordinary CREATE FUNCTION with one extra word, DISCLOSES. - In practice: a PostgreSQL developer can read DEP code without learning a new language. 10. A precise promise rather than a grand one. DEP prevents direct disclosure, unreviewed linkage, and arbitrary processing of protected fields. It does not promise anonymity, and it says so. - Example. DEP states plainly that a successful lookup reveals that a patient exists. - In practice: every claim in this document can be tested. --- DEP and Privacy as Code In one sentence: with DEP, the privacy policy is enforced by the engine that runs every query, and the evidence of that enforcement is produced in the same place. Chapter 7 compares DEP with Privacy as Code tools and with privacy frameworks. This chapter shows what Privacy as Code looks like in day-to-day work with DEP. What changes in practice What is different? Four things, each explained below with an example: Without DEP With DEP --- --- --- Where values may leave Wherever a role has SELECT Only in declared functions, listed in the catalog (A complete inventory by construction) Who looked up what Unknown, unless every application logs it Every protected match is recorded by the server (Everyday work is attributed) Review of privacy-relevant changes Depends on reviewers noticing Declared functions are syntax that CI can find (Review happens in code) Who decides Whoever holds a permission People decide; the engine enforces exactly what they approved (The engine enforces, people decide) A complete inventory by construction What is it? Because REVEAL is legal only inside disclosing functions, and unanchored matching only inside linking functions, the set of places where protected values can leave the database, or link whole datasets, is exactly the set of declared functions. Example sql SHOW FUNCTIONS; Selected output fields (SHOW FUNCTIONS also returns owner, callers, masked-path availability and the body): function discloses links comment --- --- --- --- diagnoses_per_fund() person_id Diagnosis statistics per health fund fund_claims_report(DATE) person_id person_id Monthly diagnosis claims to health funds monthly_fund_report(DATE) person_id Monthly visit report to health funds appointment_reminders(DATE) phone_number SMS appointment reminders Explanation: these four rows are the clinic's complete answer to "where can identifiers leave, and where are datasets linked through them?" The answer is complete because of how the system is built, not because someone remembered to document every export. Everyday work is attributed What is it? Anchored matching is allowed without any declaration, but every protected match on the operational path is recorded in the audit log with the identity that made it, and without the value itself. Example. An administrator reviewing yesterday's activity might see entries like these: time identity operation protected columns rows --- --- --- --- --- 2026-10-19 09:12 reception_app lookup patients.national_id 1 2026-10-19 09:31 doctors_app anchored join patients.national_id, medical_records.patient_national_id 2 2026-10-19 23:00 reminder_job call appointment_reminders() patients.phone 64 Explanation: the clinic can show who looked up what, and when, without the log itself containing a single ID number. An audit log that held every identifier ever searched for would become the most sensitive table in the system. This table summarizes operations rather than reproducing the native audit format; use SHOW AUDIT for the implemented columns. Review happens in code What is it? Declared functions live in migration files like any other schema change. Because DISCLOSES and LINKS are syntax, a CI pipeline can find every addition or change and require approval from the organization's privacy officer before it merges. Example. A developer adds a new disclosing function in a migration. The pipeline reports: text privacy check: 1 change requires approval + CREATE FUNCTION marketing_contacts() ... DISCLOSES phone_number no matching cell in privacy/matrix.md (phone x Marketing) approval required: privacy-officer Explanation: the engine adds the guarantee that makes this review meaningful. Code that is not declared cannot reveal values or link datasets, so the review cannot be bypassed by writing the same logic somewhere else. The checks themselves are described in Step 7: Keep the matrix and the database in sync. The engine enforces, people decide What is the division of work? DEP does not run approval workflows, judge lawful bases, or decide what is legitimate. Those decisions belong to the privacy officer, legal counsel, and management. DEP ensures that their decisions are implemented exactly as approved, and that the organization can demonstrate it. Key points - The catalog is a complete list of exits and linkages. - The audit log attributes every lookup, without holding values. - Privacy-relevant changes are syntax, so CI can require their review. - People decide; DEP enforces and produces the evidence. --- Designing with DEP In one sentence: with DEP, privacy decisions are schema decisions, so they are made first, recorded as reviewed artifacts, and turned into grants, declared functions, and tests. Why the order of design changes What changes? In a conventional project the schema comes first, the application is built on it, and privacy is reviewed afterwards, usually by asking which columns should be hidden from whom. With DEP that order no longer works, because privacy decisions are schema decisions: whether a field is PROTECTED, which match domain it belongs to, which consumer connects on which path, which roles may use which protected column, and which declared functions exist at all. How does the method work? It has eight steps. Each produces an artifact that lives in the repository next to the code, is reviewed like code, and is checked automatically. That is what makes it Privacy as Code rather than a checklist. mermaid flowchart LR W[1. Workflows] --> C[2. Classification] C --> M[3. Privacy matrix] M --> P[4. Paths] M --> S[5. Schema] M --> T[6. Tests] S --> V[7. Review and sync] T --> V V --> X[8. Change the matrix first] X --> M Step 1: Start from the workflows Question. What must the system do, and who or what does it? Why first? A value is sensitive only in relation to what is done with it, so workflows, not data, are the starting point. In the clinic Workflow Consumer What it needs to do --- --- --- Check-in reception_app Find a patient by the ID number they present and show today's appointments Consultation doctors_app Find the patient in the room by ID number and show their diagnoses Reminders reminder_job Send an SMS to each patient with an appointment tomorrow Visit report billing_job Report each visit to the patient's health fund, identified by ID number Claims billing_job Submit each month's diagnoses to the health funds, identified by ID number Statistics bi_dashboard Show how many patients of each health fund have each diagnosis Scheduling scheduling_agent Suggest scheduling improvements from appointment patterns Artifact: privacy/workflows.md. Step 2: Classify the fields Question. Which fields are protected, in which match domain, and which keys link sensitive data? How? Ask two questions about every field the workflows touch: 1. Is the value sensitive, and is it mostly used rather than read? Protect it when the system needs to use it (to find, deduplicate, or connect records) but most consumers have no need to see it. Fields that people must see to do their work, such as a name at reception or a diagnosis in the consultation room, stay ordinary in the first version, governed by ordinary permissions. 2. Does the field link datasets whose linkage is sensitive? DEP enforces anchoring and LINKS only on protected columns, so a key that connects two tables is a privacy decision in its own right. In the clinic Field Protected Match domain Reason --- --- --- --- patients.national_id Yes person_id Used to find patients and in the health-fund reports; nobody needs to browse it patients.phone Yes phone_number Needed only to send reminders medical_records.patient_national_id Yes person_id Links patients to diagnoses, and that linkage is sensitive patients.patient_id No None Internal key linking patients to appointments; that linkage is not sensitive patients.full_name No None Reception and doctors must see it medical_records.diagnosis No None Sensitive, but doctors must read it; governed by ordinary permissions Explanation: note what the design avoids: medical_records has no patient_id. Its only connection to patients is the protected ID number, so there is no ordinary path around the linkage rules. Choosing how tables are connected What are the options? - An ordinary key is an open road: anyone with privilege on both tables can join them, on both paths, without anchoring or declaration. - A protected key is a road with a barrier: joins through it are anchored on the operational path, declared in LINKS everywhere else, and impossible on the masked path. The clinic's map: mermaid flowchart LR P["patients identity"] ---"patient_id · ordinary key · open" A["appointments"] P -.-"national_id · protected key · guarded" M["medical_records diagnoses"] linkStyle 0 stroke:16a34a,stroke-width:2px linkStyle 1 stroke:d97706,stroke-width:2px,stroke-dasharray:6 4 Rule 1: the default is an ordinary internal key. Most links are not sensitive. If appointments referenced patients through the protected ID number, the simplest dashboard figure, visits per health fund, would fail on the masked path, and every such report would need a reviewed LINKS function. Rule 2: a protected foreign key is for links that are themselves sensitive. A list of names next to diagnoses is the clinic's most sensitive dataset even without a single ID number. Rule 3: a sensitive pair must not also be connected by an open road. Example: an open road around the barrier. A designer adds a visits table with a diagnosis code, connected to patients through patient_id: mermaid flowchart LR P["patients identity"] ---"patient_id · open" A["appointments"] P -.-"national_id · guarded" M["medical_records diagnoses"] P ---"patient_id · open" V["visits diagnosis_code"] linkStyle 0 stroke:16a34a,stroke-width:2px linkStyle 1 stroke:d97706,stroke-width:2px,stroke-dasharray:6 4 linkStyle 2 stroke:dc2626,stroke-width:3px sql SELECT p.full_name, v.diagnosis_code FROM patients AS p JOIN visits AS v USING (patient_id); Output text full_name diagnosis_code ------------+---------------- Dana Cohen J45 ... Explanation: the query returns every patient's diagnoses, on both paths, without anchoring, without LINKS, and without touching a protected column. DEP cannot detect this by itself: to the engine, patient_id is an ordinary column like any other. Hence the rule: > Between a table that holds identities and a table that holds sensitive data, there must be no path made only of ordinary keys, of any length. Three questions decide each connection mermaid flowchart TD Q1{"If someone received every row of this join, would that harm privacy?"} Q1 -- No --> K1["Use an ordinary internal key"] Q1 -- Yes --> K2["Use a protected foreign key"] K2 --> Q2{"Is there another path between the same data made only of ordinary keys?"} Q2 -- Yes --> F["Close it: protect a key on that path, or move the sensitive column"] Q2 -- No --> Q3 F --> Q3 K1 --> Q3{"Does any declared function return this key without its recipient needing it?"} Q3 -- Yes --> R["Remove it from the output"] Q3 -- No --> D["Done"] The first question is a business decision. The other two can be checked from the schema itself, which makes them a natural CI check (Step 7: Keep the matrix and the database in sync). Artifact: privacy/classification.md. Step 3: Build the privacy matrix What is it? The privacy matrix has one row per protected field and one column per workflow. Every cell holds one of four decisions: Decision Meaning --- --- MATCH The workflow uses the value to find, update, or connect the records of one value at a time, and never sees it. LINK The workflow connects whole datasets through the value. DISCLOSE The workflow needs the value itself to leave the database. NONE The workflow has no use for the value. Rules. The default is NONE. Every MATCH, LINK, and DISCLOSE carries a written reason. A cell may hold two decisions when a workflow both links and discloses. In the clinic Check-in Consultation Reminders Visit report Claims Statistics Scheduling --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- patients.national_id MATCH MATCH NONE DISCLOSE DISCLOSE + LINK LINK NONE patients.phone NONE NONE DISCLOSE NONE NONE NONE NONE medical_records.patient_national_id NONE MATCH NONE NONE LINK LINK NONE Explanation: reading by column tells you what each consumer may do. Reception finds patients by ID number, but cannot look anyone up by phone and never reaches diagnoses. Doctors reach diagnoses one patient at a time: MATCH, not LINK. The reminder job releases phone numbers and touches no ID number. The dashboard links without matching anything itself, by calling a declared function. The scheduling assistant touches no protected value at all. Explanation: reading by row tells you where each value goes. The ID number is used in two workflows, leaves the database in two, and links datasets in two. The phone number is never used for search and leaves only for reminders. The copy of the ID number in medical_records is used only by doctors, one patient at a time, and otherwise only in declared linkage; it never leaves. The matrix covers only protected columns. Ordinary fields are governed by ordinary permissions. Artifact: privacy/matrix.md, or an equivalent machine-readable file, with a reason next to every MATCH, LINK, and DISCLOSE. Step 4: Assign consumers to paths Question. Which consumer connects on which path? How? Apply the rules of Choosing a path for a consumer to the matrix: Consumer Path Declared functions it may call --- --- --- reception_app OPERATIONAL None doctors_app OPERATIONAL None reminder_job OPERATIONAL appointment_reminders billing_job OPERATIONAL monthly_fund_report, fund_claims_report bi_dashboard MASKED_READ diagnoses_per_fund scheduling_agent MASKED_READ None Artifact: endpoint and role configuration. Step 5: Translate the decisions into schema Question. How does each decision become code? Matrix decision Schema construct In the clinic --- --- --- MATCH Privilege on that protected column for the consumer's role, and the operational endpoint GRANT SELECT (patient_id, national_id, full_name, health_fund) ON patients TO reception_app LINK A function declared LINKS, with GRANT EXECUTE diagnoses_per_fund for bi_dashboard DISCLOSE A function declared DISCLOSES, with GRANT EXECUTE appointment_reminders for reminder_job NONE No privilege on that column for that role Reception has no privilege on phone Explanation: declared functions are created with no public EXECUTE, so every consumer appears in the grants by name. The complete schema, functions, and grants are in Appendix A. Three details in them come straight from the method: - The reminder function returns the phone number and the appointment time, but not the visit type. A reminder SMS does not need to say what the visit is for. - No declared function returns patient_id. Each returns only what its recipient needs, so its output cannot be joined back to other tables through an ordinary key. - Nobody has privilege on patients.phone. The only route to phone numbers is appointment_reminders, and the NONE cells in the phone row are enforced by the absence of a grant. Artifact: migration files. Step 6: Write the tests before the implementation Question. How do we prove each decision holds? How? Every cell of the matrix becomes a test. Each test states a statement, a role, a path, and the expected result or error. The NONE cells produce negative tests, and they are the most important ones: they prove what must not happen. In the clinic sql -- national_id x Check-in = MATCH -- role: reception_app path: OPERATIONAL expect: Dana's appointments; no national_id in output SELECT p.full_name, a.starts_at FROM patients AS p JOIN appointments AS a USING (patient_id) WHERE p.national_id = '123456782'; -- phone x Check-in = NONE -- role: reception_app path: OPERATIONAL expect: permission denied for column phone SELECT full_name FROM patients WHERE phone = '+972-50-0000001'; -- medical_records x Consultation = MATCH (anchored) -- role: doctors_app path: OPERATIONAL expect: Dana's diagnoses SELECT m.diagnosis FROM patients AS p JOIN medical_records AS m ON m.patient_national_id = p.national_id WHERE p.national_id = '123456782'; -- medical_records x Consultation: linking everyone is not MATCH -- role: doctors_app path: OPERATIONAL expect: DEP_UNANCHORED_MATCH SELECT p.full_name, m.diagnosis FROM patients AS p JOIN medical_records AS m ON m.patient_national_id = p.national_id; -- national_id x Statistics = LINK -- role: bi_dashboard path: MASKED_READ expect: rows of counts SELECT FROM diagnoses_per_fund(); -- national_id x Scheduling = NONE -- role: scheduling_agent path: MASKED_READ expect: DEP_ENDPOINT_OPERATION SELECT a.starts_at FROM patients AS p JOIN appointments AS a USING (patient_id) WHERE p.national_id = '123456782'; -- phone x Visit report = NONE -- role: billing_job path: OPERATIONAL expect: permission denied for function SELECT FROM appointment_reminders(DATE '2026-10-21'); -- Disclosed values are terminal -- role: billing_job path: OPERATIONAL expect: DEP_DISCLOSED_VALUE_USE SELECT r.national_id, m.diagnosis FROM monthly_fund_report('2026-10-01') AS r JOIN medical_records AS m ON m.patient_national_id = r.national_id; Explanation: these tests use the same format a DEP conformance suite would. If any of them stops behaving as expected, a privacy decision has been broken, and the build fails. Artifact: the matrix-derived test suite. Step 7: Keep the matrix and the database in sync Question. Does what runs match what was decided? How? The matrix and the schema live in the same repository and are reviewed together. A CI pipeline can enforce that: 1. every declared function in the migrations corresponds to a DISCLOSE or LINK cell, and every such cell has a function; 2. every privilege on a protected column corresponds to a MATCH cell for that role; 3. every new declared function, every GRANT EXECUTE on one, and every new privilege on a protected column is approved by the clinic's privacy officer; 4. every MATCH, LINK, and DISCLOSE cell carries a written reason; 5. the map of foreign keys contains no path made only of ordinary keys between a table that holds identities and a table that holds sensitive data; 6. the matrix-derived tests pass. After deployment. The same comparison runs against the live database: SHOW FUNCTIONS and the privileges on protected columns are checked against the matrix. Example: a drift report text drift: 1 object in the database is not in the matrix GRANT EXECUTE ON FUNCTION monthly_fund_report(DATE) TO bi_dashboard matrix: national_id x Statistics = LINK (not DISCLOSE) Explanation: someone granted the dashboard access to a disclosing function by hand. The grant would be useless on the masked path, but it contradicts what was decided, so it is reported. Artifact: CI checks and a drift report. Step 8: Change the matrix first What is the rule? When a new need arrives, the first change is to the matrix, not to the code. Example. The marketing team asks to send patients a promotional SMS. That is a new column in the matrix, and a new question in one cell: phone x Marketing = DISCLOSE? Explanation: the question "may we?" is now asked explicitly, with the reason written down and reviewed, and perhaps answered no. Without the matrix, it would have been answered by whoever happened to have permission to run a query. Summary of the method Step Question it answers Artifact --- --- --- 1. Workflows What must the system do, and who does it? privacy/workflows.md 2. Classification Which fields are protected, in which match domain, and which keys link sensitive data? privacy/classification.md 3. Privacy matrix For each field and workflow: match, link, disclose, or nothing? privacy/matrix.md 4. Paths Which consumer connects on which path? Endpoint and role configuration 5. Schema How do the decisions become code? Migrations: tables, declared functions, grants 6. Tests How do we prove each decision holds? Matrix-derived test suite 7. Review and sync Does what runs match what was decided? CI checks and drift report 8. Change How does the system evolve? Matrix first, code second Notes. The method does not replace legal review or a data protection impact assessment. It gives them precise inputs (the matrix and its reasons) and verifiable outputs: the schema, the tests, and the catalog. Key points - Decide privacy first: workflows, then fields, then the matrix. - Every matrix cell becomes a grant or a declared function, and a test. - CI and the drift report keep the database equal to what was decided. --- Use cases In one sentence: the same three patterns (match one value, link through declared code, disclose through declared code) appear wherever an organization holds identifiers it uses more than it reads. In the clinic Workflow What DEP allows What DEP prevents --- --- --- Reception Finding a patient by the ID number she presents, and showing her appointments Downloading the register; reaching diagnoses; reverse lookup by phone Consultation room Seeing the diagnoses of the patient in the room, through an anchored join Listing the diagnoses of every patient Statistics Diagnoses per health fund, through the declared diagnoses_per_fund Any linkage the dashboard writes itself Reports to the health funds The visit report and the claims, through declared disclosing functions Any other route by which ID numbers leave The AI agent Exploring, aggregating, and joining appointments and patients through ordinary keys Looking a patient up by ID number, or extracting identifiers, whatever SQL it generates Explanation: in every case, the legitimate work keeps running. What changes is that a compromised application, or an agent following the wrong instructions, cannot turn its access into a full export or a full linkage. Privacy is enforced by the server, not by the agent's prompt. Beyond the clinic Setting Matching Linking Disclosing --- --- --- --- Customer service in a bank or a telecom company Agents find a caller by the identifier they give Complaint statistics per product A regulatory report identified by customer number Human resources and payroll HR finds an employee by ID number Salary statistics per department The annual salary report to the tax authority Development and support access None None None: engineers query realistic data through the masked path without ever seeing identifiers --- Automating the review The matrix-to-schema checks and drift report above describe a review workflow to implement in your own project. DEP Engine exposes SHOW FUNCTIONS, SHOW GRANTS and SHOW PRIVACY MATRIX; it does not ship the illustrated CI policy or an automatic privacy-officer approval service. Compare the computed privacy matrix with the workflows and permissions you approved.

title: Build an application
text: This chapter builds the downloadable starter, a smaller clinic with a records table. Earlier book examples use the full clinic with medical_records. These are separate databases; the section Run the full clinic below prepares the earlier examples. Create a small patient lookup application with a protected identifier. You will set up an isolated local server, create a schema and roles, connect from Python or Node.js, and verify both permitted and refused operations. Target: DEP Engine 0.5.2. Time: about 15 minutes after installing the tools. This walkthrough builds an application for the example clinic. Download the complete starter: schema, Python and Node.js examples, environment files and a verification script. The website's SQL examples are checked against DEP.js; verify them against your installed Engine before relying on an integration. 1. Prepare the tools Install DEP Engine and DEP CLI from the Install page, then extract the starter and open a terminal in its dep-starter folder. The walkthrough uses 127.0.0.1:5543 to avoid the service port 5433 that an installer may already use. It creates a separate database in ./data. You do not need to stop an existing service. You also need either Python 3.10+ with a virtual environment, or Node.js 22+. For a browser-only introduction, use the playground. 2. Start an isolated server Terminal A: keep this running: sh dep-engine --listen 127.0.0.1:5543 --data-dir ./data \ --admin-password local-dev-only --init ./schema.sql The initialization script runs only when this database is new. It creates patients, a related records table, a lookup role demo_app, and a separate disclosure role export_job. The passwords in the starter are deliberately local demonstration values. The server binds to loopback. For a shared server, use your own credentials and TLS; follow Administration. The server reports its listeners and storage configuration at startup. The server reports its listeners and storage configuration at startup. 3. Inspect the schema and grants The starter's schema.sql runs as admin. These are the core declarations already executed by schema.sql. Read them here; do not execute them a second time in the initialized database: sql CREATE TABLE patients ( patient_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, national_id TEXT PROTECTED MATCH DOMAIN person_id UNIQUE, full_name TEXT ); CREATE TABLE records ( record_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, patient_national_id TEXT PROTECTED REFERENCES patients (national_id), diagnosis TEXT ); INSERT INTO patients VALUES (1, '123456782', 'Dana Cohen'); INSERT INTO records VALUES (1, '123456782', 'Synthetic example'); CREATE ROLE demo_app LOGIN PASSWORD 'demo-local'; GRANT CONNECT ON ENDPOINT operational TO demo_app; GRANT SELECT (patient_id, full_name, national_id) ON patients TO demo_app; GRANT SELECT ON records TO demo_app; ALTER ROLE demo_app MATCH LIMIT 600 PER HOUR; Both protected columns belong to person_id; the protected reference inherits its domain. A SELECT grant on the protected column allows matching, not plaintext output. Terminal B: connect as the application: sh DEP_PASSWORD=demo-local dep-cli -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5543 -U demo_app -d operational Here the database name operational chooses the endpoint and fixes the access path for the session. Use a separate connection or pool for another role or endpoint. 4. Find a patient without receiving their ID sql SELECT full_name, national_id FROM patients WHERE national_id = '123456782'; Expected result: text full_name national_id ------------+------------ Dana Cohen NULL The identifier matched by equality. The NULL is protected output, not proof that the stored identifier is missing. DEP notes explain the operation. This query must be refused with ZD101: sql SELECT full_name FROM patients WHERE national_id LIKE '123%'; 5. Connect from your application Exit the shell with \q before running these terminal commands. Choose one language; you do not need both. Python Node.js Python / psycopg The starter includes requirements for psycopg 3.3 and loads connection settings from the environment. sh python3 -m venv .venv . .venv/bin/activate pip install -r python/requirements.txt export DEP_DSN='host=127.0.0.1 port=5543 user=demo_app password=demo-local dbname=operational sslmode=disable' python python/app.py The essential query uses a bound parameter: python import os import psycopg with psycopg.connect(os.environ['DEP_DSN'], autocommit=True) as conn: row = conn.execute( 'SELECT full_name, national_id FROM patients WHERE national_id = %s', ('123456782',) ).fetchone() print(row) ('Dana Cohen', None) Node.js / node-postgres sh cd node npm install cp .env.example .env node --env-file=.env app.js The essential query uses the same PostgreSQL parameter convention: javascript const { Client } = require('pg'); async function main() { const client = new Client({ connectionString: process.env.DEP_DSN }); await client.connect(); try { const result = await client.query( 'SELECT full_name, national_id FROM patients WHERE national_id = $1', ['123456782'] ); console.log(result.rows); // national_id: null } finally { await client.end(); } } main().catch(error => { console.error(error.code error.message); process.exitCode = 1; }); Run this as the application role demo_app, using the connection string in .env. The full starter also demonstrates handling a refused partial match. sslmode=disable is appropriate only for this loopback demonstration. Use verified TLS when connecting over a network. Handle DEP errors by SQLSTATE and avoid logging parameter values. 6. Connect related records This join is tied to one supplied protected value: sql SELECT p.full_name, r.diagnosis FROM patients AS p JOIN records AS r ON r.patient_national_id = p.national_id WHERE p.national_id = '123456782'; Removing the WHERE anchor must produce ZD107, because the join would match whole datasets. A justified dataset-wide match belongs inside a function declared LINKS person_id. 7. Declare a narrow disclosure The complete starter also creates privacy_owner (a NOLOGIN role) and export_job. As admin, it grants the owner the operational endpoint, SELECT and DISCLOSE, switches to that owner to declare the function, then resets the role. The following explains the existing schema.sql setup; it is not an additional initialization step: sql GRANT CONNECT ON ENDPOINT operational TO privacy_owner; GRANT SELECT ON patients TO privacy_owner; GRANT DISCLOSE ON MATCH DOMAIN person_id TO privacy_owner; SET ROLE privacy_owner; CREATE FUNCTION patient_identifier(id BIGINT) RETURNS TABLE (national_id TEXT) LANGUAGE sql DISCLOSES person_id AS $$ SELECT REVEAL(p.national_id) FROM patients AS p WHERE p.patient_id = id $$; COMMENT ON FUNCTION patient_identifier(BIGINT) IS 'Purpose: approved single-patient identifier export for this local demo.'; GRANT EXECUTE ON FUNCTION patient_identifier(BIGINT) TO export_job; RESET ROLE; To call it yourself, open a new connection as export_job. This role was created by schema.sql and has EXECUTE on this function, but no direct table-read grant. Terminal command: sh DEP_PASSWORD=export-local dep-cli -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5543 -U export_job -d operational SQL in that connection: sql SELECT FROM patient_identifier(1); Expected output: text national_id ----------- 123456782 The synthetic ID is returned. demo_app has no EXECUTE grant and cannot call this function. Under the specification, the disclosed ID may only be returned: do not sort, filter or join on it. Match inside the function before REVEAL. See the known native sorting difference for implementation status. 8. Verify the boundaries and inspect the audit The starter's checks connect with separate application identities. Use the version for the language you installed: Python: from the starter root, with the virtual environment activated: sh python python/verify.py Node.js: from the starter's node folder: sh npm run verify Both print PASS when the required boundaries hold. They fail if the connected Engine behaves differently from the documented rules. Both also require disclosed sorting to fail with ZD104. A review reports that native 0.5.1 accepts it, so an affected Engine will fail this check. Keep that failure visible until native enforcement is fixed; it does not indicate an application setup error. Native 0.5.2 has not been retested here for this issue. They verify that lookup output is NULL, a partial match fails with ZD101, an unanchored join fails with ZD107, disclosure fails for demo_app, and export_job can call its approved function. This requires the running DEP Engine and the dependency for your chosen language from step 5. Connect as admin to inspect governance: sh DEP_PASSWORD=local-dev-only dep-cli -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5543 -U admin -d operational sql SHOW PRIVACY MATRIX; SHOW AUDIT 20; Audit records attribute protected operations to roles without recording the protected values. Inspect notes and errors, match limits, and the server guide before expanding the application. Restarting and changing your schema Stop Terminal A with Ctrl+C, then run the same server command to reopen ./data. The initialization script will not run again. DEP Engine 0.5.2 has no ALTER TABLE support: for a different tutorial schema, choose a new directory such as ./data-v2, or plan an explicit migration. Do not assume an ORM's migration commands will work. If something does not work Symptom What to check Next step --------- dep-engine or dep-cli: command not found The binary was not installed, or your shell PATH has not refreshed Follow the Install page for your OS; open a new terminal after installation Address already in use Another server is listening on the selected port This tutorial uses 5543; choose another local port and update every client connection consistently patients already exists The schema was imported into a database that already contains it Connect without importing again, or start a new isolated data directory The changed schema.sql seems ignored --init runs only for a new database Use a new directory such as ./data-v2 when testing a new tutorial schema SQLSTATE ZD102 on a lookup The connection is on the MASKED_READ path Open a new authorized operational connection; SET cannot change the path SQLSTATE 42501 on the disclosure The connection is demo_app, or an EXECUTE/owner privilege is missing Use export_job for the approved export; inspect grants as admin national_id is NULL The selected output is protected This is expected. Match on the input value or call an explicitly approved disclosure function An integration check fails Installed Engine behavior or the loaded schema differs from this guide Keep the SQLSTATE and compare the exact version and schema; the website build verifies DEP.js, not a native Engine process For a slower explanation of each operation and result, read Understand the examples. Connection settings Setting Value ------ Host, port The server's --listen address (default 127.0.0.1:5433) User The role, for example reception_app Database The endpoint, for example operational or analytics. It fixes the access path. Password The role's password SSL mode require or verify-full for any server that is not on the same machine; see the administration guide The role is a database role, not a person, in most deployments: one role per application or job, each granted the endpoint, columns and functions it needs and nothing more. Connect an analytics tool through analytics and it cannot match, write, or disclose, whatever its role is granted. A connection keeps its role and path for its whole life. The path is fixed when it logs in, and cannot be changed by SET. If an application needs two access paths, it opens two connections, ideally with two roles. Parameters Use parameters, as with any database. DEP treats a protected parameter ($1 compared with a protected column, or inserted into one) exactly as it treats a protected literal. In the extended protocol the engine infers the types of parameters for queries and for INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE. An error message never carries the value of a bound parameter. Notes and errors - Notes. Each rule that applies produces a DEP note, sent as a PostgreSQL NOTICE whose text starts with DEP: . Drivers deliver notices through a handler (add_notice_handler in psycopg, the notice event in node-postgres). They need no handling: ignore them in production and read them while developing. - Errors. A DEP error has a ZDnnn SQLSTATE and a message and a hint. Branch on the SQLSTATE. The DEP_... name is not sent over the PostgreSQL protocol; the error reference maps one to the other. Constraint violations use PostgreSQL's SQLSTATEs (23505, 23502, 23503), and 40001 means the transaction should be retried. - Protected columns come back as NULL. SELECT national_id returns a row with NULL, never an error. An application that needs the value must call a declared function, and the role must have EXECUTE on it. Pools, roles and sessions - One pool per role and endpoint. A connection's identity is its role and path, so do not share a pool between applications. The audit log attributes every protected match to the role that made it. - Do not rely on SET ROLE. Only a superuser may use it, and it changes the privileges that apply without changing the path. Use separate connections. - Keep transactions short. One transaction writes at a time, and a transaction left idle for --idle-in-transaction-timeout is rolled back. See Transactions. - Retry on 40001. It means another transaction changed a table this one wanted to write. - Mind the match limit. An application that looks up many protected values in a short time can reach its role's limit (ZD109). The limit counts every value of an IN list. HTTP clients Clients without a PostgreSQL driver can use POST /v1/query. It uses role authentication and the same endpoint and grants. Open transactions must finish in one HTTP request; see the API reference for request and result formats. Run the full clinic 1. Choose a local environment This setup loads the full clinic used in chapters 1 to 4, instead of the smaller starter database above. Install DEP Engine and DEP CLI from Install. Studio can also run an embedded database: choose New Local Database and load the clinic there, without starting another server. Download clinic.sql into your current folder. The commands below use ./clinic.sql, not a repository-relative examples path. 2. Start the clinic, or use your running service Choose one option. An installer may already have started a persistent service on port 5433. Option A: isolated manual server (recommended for this tour) Use port 5543 so the tour can run beside an installed service. Keep Terminal A running: sh dep-engine --listen 127.0.0.1:5543 --init ./clinic.sql --admin-password local-dev-only --http-listen 127.0.0.1:8543 This instance is in memory: its data disappears when it stops. Every connection below uses port 5543 and the HTTP examples use 8543. The clinic's application-role passwords are demo. Option B: the installed background service Use the service on 5433 instead of starting another process. Import ./clinic.sql only into a fresh evaluation database. --init only runs when a database is new. On Linux, read the package-generated admin password and import the clinic: sh export DEP_PASSWORD=$(sudo cat /etc/dep-engine/admin-password) dep-cli -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5433 -U admin -d operational -f ./clinic.sql On macOS: sh export DEP_PASSWORD=$(cat "$HOME/Library/Application Support/Project Hoopeo/admin-password") dep-cli -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5433 -U admin -d operational -f ./clinic.sql If you choose this option, replace 5543 with 5433 in the connection examples below. The service's HTTP API is optional: do not assume port 8543 exists. Use CLI or psql, or configure the HTTP listener explicitly through Administration. Already loaded the clinic? Connect to it without importing again. Existing table errors mean that this is not an empty database. For an isolated first try, use Option A. The clinic has three tables, eight roles and two endpoints. The database name is the endpoint: operational permits authorized matching and writes; analytics is MASKED_READ. The access path is fixed at login. 3. Connect The user name is the role, and the database name is the endpoint. There are three ways in. DEP CLI sh dep-cli -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5543 -U reception_app -d operational The password comes from DEP_PASSWORD, PGPASSWORD or a prompt. For a first try without a server, DEP CLI can hold the clinic itself, in memory: sh dep-cli --memory --init ./clinic.sql -U reception_app Type \dt to list the tables, and any statement to run it. DEP notes are printed before each result: DEP CLI: the tables, a lookup with its DEP notes, and a refused partial match psql, or any PostgreSQL driver DEP Engine speaks the PostgreSQL wire protocol, so psql works as it is. The DEP notes of each statement arrive as ordinary NOTICE messages. sh export PGPASSWORD=demo psql "host=127.0.0.1 port=5543 user=reception_app dbname=operational sslmode=disable" \ -c "SELECT full_name, national_id FROM patients WHERE national_id = '123456782'" psql connected to DEP Engine, with the DEP notes as notices sslmode=disable is for this local try. See the administration guide for TLS. The HTTP API sh curl -s -u reception_app:demo "http://127.0.0.1:8543/v1/query?endpoint=operational" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"sql": "SELECT full_name, national_id FROM patients WHERE national_id = $1", "params": ["123456782"]}' text {"endpoint":"operational","open_transaction_rolled_back":false,"path":"OPERATIONAL","results":[{"columns":["full_name","national_id"],"elapsed_ms":3.13,"notes":["PROTECTED column patients.national_id is matched by equality through the blind index of MATCH DOMAIN person_id.","Output column national_id is PROTECTED column patients.national_id (MATCH DOMAIN person_id) and is returned as NULL."],"row_count":1,"rows":[["Dana Cohen",null]],"statement":"SELECT full_name, national_id FROM patients WHERE national_id = $1"}],"role":"reception_app"} The HTTP API reference describes the request and the response. title: Run the server
text: Know the supported forms and version differences before deploying a server or choosing an integration. Compatibility Know what DEP Engine 0.5.2 supports before choosing it for an application. This is an experimental reference server for evaluation and non-production testing. What you are running DEP Engine is built on Apache DataFusion. It accepts DEP SQL and speaks the PostgreSQL wire protocol. It is a separate database server: these additions cannot be installed by running CREATE EXTENSION in an existing PostgreSQL database. PostgreSQL drivers can connect, but PostgreSQL wire compatibility does not mean that PostgreSQL SQL, extensions, catalogs or ORM migrations are all supported. Support at a glance Capability Current behavior ------ Ordinary queries SELECT, joins, CTEs, subqueries, aggregates and window functions, within the analyzer's supported forms Writing INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE Protected matching Whole-value equality and lists of values; appropriate privileges and OPERATIONAL path required Protected output NULL in ordinary query output; explicit DISCLOSES functions may release values Protected joins A single-value anchor, or a declared LINKS function, is required Transactions Transactions and savepoints; one writer at a time Constraints PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE, NOT NULL and REFERENCES, including protected columns Schema migration ALTER TABLE is not supported Defaults and validation DEFAULT and CHECK are not supported Bulk statements COPY and MERGE are not supported Referential actions NO ACTION only; no ON DELETE CASCADE Declared functions LANGUAGE sql and RETURNS TABLE; no PL/pgSQL Protected transformations No LIKE, range, sort, cast, substring or arbitrary function calls on protected values. The design allows presence tests in operational filters, but refuses returning the test or COUNT(col) on either path. See the presence-test table and the native differences below. Disclosed values The specification permits output only (renamed or cast); filtering, joining, grouping, DISTINCT, sorting, storing and function arguments are forbidden. DEP Engine 0.5.2 does not apply all of it: see the known differences below. The language guide defines the rules and their error codes. Transactions and constraints covers concurrency, indexes and EXPLAIN. Clients tested by the project The examples of chapter 5 are documented as tested against DEP Engine 0.5.2 with: Client Documented version Status --------- psql 16 Connection and query examples Python psycopg 3.3 Application examples node-postgres 8.23 Application examples Other PostgreSQL drivers Not verified Expected to connect; not individually verified by that guide ORMs and migration frameworks Not verified No general compatibility claim; test generated SQL and catalog access Use explicit SQL for the first application. Before introducing an ORM, check its connection probes, schema introspection, transaction behavior and migrations against the supported forms. The simulator and the server DEP.js runs in your browser on sql.js / SQLite, using the synthetic clinic. It demonstrates DEP SQL rules; enforcement for connected applications is provided by DEP Engine on the server. DEP Engine enforces the rules on the server for connected clients. The server, operating system and administrator are trusted. Identifiers are stored as a blind index and ciphertext; authorized matches still reveal that a record exists. Ordinary names, dates and ordinary join keys remain governed by ordinary permissions. Aggregates can identify people in small groups. Values released to a client are outside DEP's control. Read DEP and GDPR for the implications. Known difference: sorting disclosed values The terminal rule in chapter 3 forbids using a disclosed value as a sort key. DEP.js follows this rule and returns ZD104 (DEP_DISCLOSED_VALUE_USE) for each query below: sql -- Sort by the disclosed column's name. SELECT national_id FROM monthly_fund_report(DATE '2026-10-01') ORDER BY national_id; -- Sort by an alias of the disclosed column. SELECT national_id AS exposed_id FROM monthly_fund_report(DATE '2026-10-01') ORDER BY exposed_id; -- Sort by the disclosed column's position in the result. SELECT national_id FROM monthly_fund_report(DATE '2026-10-01') ORDER BY 1; Native testing of DEP Engine 0.5.1 confirmed that it accepts all three forms, contrary to the specification. Version 0.5.2 changed licensing and distribution only, and its query behavior is the same, so assume that 0.5.2 accepts them too. Sort reports by an ordinary output column, such as visit_date or visit_type. This keeps examples within the specified rules; it does not repair enforcement in an affected Engine. The compatibility suite includes name, alias and ordinal cases without suppressing differences. Other known differences in DEP Engine 0.5.2 The same testing found three more places where the native analyzer checks less than the specification. DEP.js follows the specification in all three. Rule DEP.js and the specification DEP Engine 0.5.2 --------- Presence of a protected value A filter such as WHERE national_id IS NOT NULL is allowed only on the operational path. Returning the test or using COUNT(national_id) is refused on either path (ZD101 operational; ZD102 masked). COUNT() counts rows and is allowed on either. Examples and permission table. Accepts IS NULL, IS NOT NULL and COUNT(col) on both paths, so a masked connection can learn whether a person has a value on record Computing on a disclosed value upper(national_id), concat(national_id, ''), CASE over a disclosed value and SELECT DISTINCT national_id are refused (ZD104); renaming and casting are allowed Accepts functions, operators and DISTINCT over a disclosed value in the output Rows of a VALUES list Checked like any projection, including scalar subqueries Not checked. A DataFusion limitation currently stops a scalar subquery inside VALUES from running, so no value leaks today, but the analyzer does not enforce the rules there Fixes for all four differences, with regression tests, exist in the development source of DEP Engine and are not yet in a release. Until a release includes them, test these cases against the Engine you run, and do not rely on the specification's guarantees for them. Version, licensing and readiness - Current documented engine: 0.5.2. The release is available as binary packages. - Readiness: experimental evaluation software, not a production-readiness assurance. - Open material: specification and documentation under CC BY 4.0; DEP.js, the playground and examples under Apache 2.0. - Binary licensing: evaluation terms apply to Engine, CLI and Studio. A commercial license is a licensing arrangement, not evidence of production readiness. - Future plans: the design roadmap discusses possible future work, including PostgreSQL. It is not the current feature list. See licensing and the current releases. Server administration This guide is for the person who runs DEP Engine as a server for other people or programs: configuration, TLS, the data directory and its key, resources, the audit log, key rotation, upgrades and metrics. Experimental Project Hoopeo is an experimental, conceptual project. See the terms of use . Running the server sh dep-engine --listen 127.0.0.1:5433 --data-dir /var/lib/dep-engine/data --http-listen 127.0.0.1:8433 Every option has an environment variable too, which is how the packages configure the server. The server options reference lists them all. Installed as Configuration Data Notes ------------ Linux .deb /etc/dep-engine/dep-engine.env, then sudo systemctl restart dep-engine /var/lib/dep-engine/data A systemd service as the dep-engine user. The admin password of a new database is in /etc/dep-engine/admin-password Linux tarball sudo ./install.sh installs the same service the same sudo ./install.sh --uninstall removes it and keeps the data macOS service A launch agent, started at login ~/Library/Application Support/Project Hoopeo/data Listens on 127.0.0.1:5433 Docker Environment variables (DEP_ADMIN_PASSWORD, ...) the volume at /var/lib/dep-engine Self-signed TLS by default Logs: journalctl -u dep-engine on Linux, /tmp/dep-engine.log for the macOS service, and docker logs in a container. The admin password admin is the superuser of a new database. Set its password with --admin-password (at every start) or --init-admin-password-file (for a new database only, read from a file). With neither, a random password is printed once, when the database is created: sh dep-engine --listen 127.0.0.1:5433 --data-dir /var/lib/dep-engine/data text DEP Engine 0.5.2 listening on 127.0.0.1:5433 data directory: /var/lib/dep-engine/data (new) TLS: off (use --tls-cert and --tls-key, or --tls-self-signed) query memory: 6144 MB (beyond it, encrypted spill files); data file cache: 3072 MB; idle transactions end after 300 s; at most 200 connections password for admin: d251f045a4d6029dddcc681f dep-cli -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5433 -U admin -d operational (OPERATIONAL) dep-cli -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5433 -U admin -d analytics (MASKED_READ) Create a role for each application, grant it only the endpoint and the columns it needs, and keep admin for administration. See chapter 2. TLS Without TLS, passwords and results cross the network in clear text. A server that accepts connections from other machines should use it. - --tls-cert FILE --tls-key FILE use your own PEM certificate chain and private key. - --tls-self-signed creates a self-signed certificate in DATA_DIR/tls, valid for localhost and each --tls-host NAME. - --tls-required refuses connections without TLS. The same certificate serves the HTTP API, which then runs over HTTPS. Clients choose the mode: --sslmode require encrypts, and verify-full also checks the certificate against a CA file (--sslrootcert; for a self-signed certificate, the certificate itself). sh dep-engine --listen 127.0.0.1:5433 --data-dir /var/lib/dep-engine/data --tls-self-signed --tls-required --admin-password admin export DEP_PASSWORD=admin Without TLS dep-cli -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5433 -U admin -d operational --sslmode disable -c "SELECT 1;" 2>&1 Verified TLS, with the server's own certificate as the CA dep-cli -h localhost -p 5433 -U admin -d operational --sslmode verify-full \ --sslrootcert /var/lib/dep-engine/data/tls/server.crt -c '\conninfo' text ERROR: this DEP Engine server accepts only TLS connections HINT: Connect with sslmode=require (dep-cli --sslmode require). SQLSTATE: 28000 Role "admin", endpoint "operational", access path OPERATIONAL, server localhost:5433. Keep the private key readable only by the server's user. The packages do this for the files they create. The data directory and the master key The data directory holds the database (data.redb), the audit log (audit.redb), a lock file and, with --tls-self-signed, the certificate. The master key (master.key) is the secret from which every protected value's index key and encryption key derive. Without it the protected values cannot be read or matched, and with it anyone with the data can read them. - By default the key is in the data directory. Keep it apart: --key-file /etc/dep-engine/master.key on another volume, with its own permissions and its own backup. A stolen backup of the data alone then holds only ciphertext and index entries. - Neither file is useful without the other, so back up both, and test the restore. - Back up while the server is stopped, or from a filesystem snapshot. Copying data.redb while the server writes can produce a file that does not open. - The key file and the data directory should be readable only by the server's user. sh dep-engine --data-dir /var/lib/dep-engine/data --key-file /etc/dep-engine/master.key --admin-password admin find /var/lib/dep-engine /etc/dep-engine -type f sort text /etc/dep-engine/master.key /var/lib/dep-engine/data/.lock /var/lib/dep-engine/data/audit.redb /var/lib/dep-engine/data/data.redb Data persists across restarts when --data-dir is set. Without it the database lives in memory and is lost when the server stops. Resources and limits Option Default Effect --------- --memory-limit a quarter of RAM Memory for running queries. Beyond it, sorts and aggregations spill to encrypted temporary files, since they can hold values a disclosing function released. A hash join whose smaller side exceeds it fails with 53200. --cache-size an eighth of RAM, at most 4 GB Page cache of the data file --max-connections 200 Client connections served at once (0: no limit) --idle-in-transaction-timeout 300 s A transaction left idle is rolled back (0: never) --lock-timeout 30 s How long a writer waits for the write lock before 55P03 --match-limit none Default limit on protected matches for roles that are not superusers, for example 1000/minute In a container the defaults follow the container's memory limit, not the host's. One transaction writes at a time; readers never wait. Match limits A lookup on a protected column answers the question "is this value here?", and a client that can ask without limit can guess every value. Set a default for all roles that are not superusers with --match-limit, and a specific limit per role with ALTER ROLE r MATCH LIMIT 600 PER HOUR. A statement over the limit is refused with ZD109 and recorded. See chapter 2. The audit log The audit log is audit.redb, written with group commit: a statement returns only after its records are on disk. It records: The audit log in Hoopeo Studio kind When ------ match A protected match, with the number of values matched disclose, link A call of a function declared DISCLOSES or LINKS denied A refused statement, with the error code rate_limited A statement over a match limit key_rotated A master key rotation Each record has a sequence number, a time, the session user and the current role, the endpoint and path, the object and match domain, and the count. It never holds a protected value, a disclosed value, or the text of a statement. Superusers read it with SHOW AUDIT [n] (the latest n records, default 100; DEP CLI's \audit shows 50). The log is not rotated or truncated by the server. text reception_app@operational=> SELECT full_name FROM patients WHERE national_id IN ('123456782', '234567893'); DEP: PROTECTED column patients.national_id is matched against a list of values through the blind index of MATCH DOMAIN person_id. full_name ------------ Dana Cohen Yossi Levi (2 rows) reception_app@operational=> SELECT full_name FROM patients WHERE national_id LIKE '1%'; ERROR: LIKE is not supported for PROTECTED values (patients.national_id). HINT: PROTECTED values support only full-value equality matching. To release a value, use a disclosing function. SQLSTATE: ZD101 (DEP_PROTECTED_OPERATION) reception_app@operational=> \c operational billing_job You are now connected as "billing_job" through endpoint "operational" (OPERATIONAL). billing_job@operational=> SELECT count() FROM monthly_fund_report(DATE '2026-10-01'); DEP: monthly_fund_report() is declared DISCLOSES person_id: the columns it declares are returned in plaintext. count() ---------- 10 (1 row) billing_job@operational=> \c operational admin You are now connected as "admin" through endpoint "operational" (OPERATIONAL). admin@operational=> SHOW AUDIT 10; seq at session_user role endpoint path kind object domain count detail -----+--------------------------+---------------+---------------+-------------+-------------+----------+-----------------------+-----------+-------+------------------------- 3 2026-10-23T12:27:12.903Z billing_job billing_job operational OPERATIONAL disclose monthly_fund_report() person_id NULL NULL 2 2026-10-23T12:27:12.900Z reception_app reception_app operational OPERATIONAL denied SELECT NULL NULL DEP_PROTECTED_OPERATION 1 2026-10-23T12:27:12.899Z reception_app reception_app operational OPERATIONAL match patients.national_id person_id 2 NULL (3 rows) Key rotation ALTER SYSTEM ROTATE MASTER KEY replaces the master key. Every protected value is decrypted with the old key and re-indexed and re-encrypted with a new one, and every index is rebuilt, in a single commit. A crash at any point leaves either the old key and data or the new ones. It needs a superuser, and it cannot run in a transaction block. Take a backup of the key file and the data first; the old key stops working. text admin@operational=> ALTER SYSTEM ROTATE MASTER KEY; DEP: The master key was replaced: 18 protected values were indexed and encrypted again with the new key, and the indexes were rebuilt. The old key no longer opens this data. ALTER SYSTEM admin@operational=> SELECT full_name FROM patients WHERE national_id = '123456782'; DEP: PROTECTED column patients.national_id is matched by equality through the blind index of MATCH DOMAIN person_id. full_name ------------ Dana Cohen (1 row) With --key-file, the new key is written to the key file. The rotation is recorded in the audit log. Upgrading and migrating Replace the binary or the package and restart. Older data directories are converted the first time they are opened: - a 0.4 directory is converted in place (rows are re-encoded, indexes are built, the audit log moves to audit.redb); - a 0.3 directory is converted into a new data.redb, and its old files are kept in legacy-0.3/; - a primary or unique key whose existing rows have duplicates (0.4 did not enforce keys) is kept, but not enforced. The server says so when it starts, and SHOW INDEXES shows enforced empty. Remove the duplicates, then run REINDEX TABLE t. Back up the data directory and the key before upgrading. A directory converted by a newer version is not guaranteed to open in an older one, so do not move back. Metrics GET /metrics on the HTTP port (no authentication, no data) returns counters in the Prometheus text format, and GET /v1/health returns {"status":"ok", ...}. Both are meant for a local monitor or a firewall-protected port. Metric Meaning ------ dep_statements_total, dep_commits_total, dep_rollbacks_total Statements and transactions dep_protected_matches_total, dep_disclosures_total, dep_links_total Protected matches, and calls of DISCLOSES and LINKS functions dep_rate_limited_total Statements refused by a match limit dep_index_lookups_total, dep_full_scans_total, dep_rows_read_total How tables were read dep_idle_transactions_ended_total Transactions ended by the idle timeout dep_wire_connections_total, dep_wire_connections_active, dep_http_requests_total Connections and requests dep_tables, dep_rows, dep_persistent Size of the database, and whether it is kept on disk dep_query_memory_limit_bytes, dep_spilled_bytes_total Query memory and the bytes spilled to encrypted files dep_errors_total{code="..."} Failed statements, by SQLSTATE or DEP code sh curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8433/metrics grep -v '^' head -12 text dep_statements_total 40 dep_protected_matches_total 0 dep_disclosures_total 0 dep_links_total 0 dep_rate_limited_total 0 dep_commits_total 38 dep_rollbacks_total 0 dep_wire_connections_total 1 dep_wire_connections_active 0 dep_http_requests_total 0 dep_index_lookups_total 0 dep_full_scans_total 0 A checklist for an evaluation server Experimental software calls for caution, so treat this as the minimum for a shared evaluation server, and not as a statement that anything is production-ready. 1. Remember that the project is experimental: read the terms of use. 2. TLS on, and --tls-required if clients are remote. 3. A strong admin password, and one role per application. 4. The master key on a separate volume, with its own permissions. 5. A match limit as the default. 6. Memory and connection limits sized for the machine. 7. The HTTP port bound to 127.0.0.1 or behind a firewall. 8. Backups of the data and the key, tested by a restore. 9. Someone reads SHOW AUDIT and /metrics. This guide covers the parts of DEP Engine that behave like an ordinary SQL database: transactions and savepoints, transactional schema changes, constraints, indexes and EXPLAIN. DEP's privacy rules apply inside all of them. Examples run against the demo clinic, and the output is real. Transactions Every statement runs in a transaction: its own, or one you open. sql BEGIN; -- or START TRANSACTION ... COMMIT; -- or END ROLLBACK; -- or ABORT A transaction sees a consistent snapshot of the data and its own writes. Nobody else sees them until COMMIT, which is one durable write. SHOW TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL reports repeatable read. DEP CLI marks the prompt: => inside a transaction, =!> after an error. text admin@operational=> BEGIN; BEGIN admin@operational=> INSERT INTO patients (patient_id, national_id, phone, full_name, health_fund) VALUES (7, '789012348', '+972-50-0000007', 'Lior Katz', 'Clalit'); DEP: PROTECTED column patients.national_id (MATCH DOMAIN person_id) is stored as a blind index and ciphertext. DEP: PROTECTED column patients.phone (MATCH DOMAIN phone_number) is stored as a blind index and ciphertext. INSERT 0 1 admin@operational=> SELECT full_name FROM patients WHERE national_id = '789012348'; DEP: PROTECTED column patients.national_id is matched by equality through the blind index of MATCH DOMAIN person_id. full_name ----------- Lior Katz (1 row) admin@operational=> ROLLBACK; ROLLBACK admin@operational=> SELECT count() FROM patients; count() ---------- 6 (1 row) After an error An error inside a transaction aborts it. Every later statement fails with 25P02 until you run ROLLBACK, or ROLLBACK TO a savepoint. text admin@operational=> BEGIN; BEGIN admin@operational=> INSERT INTO patients (patient_id, national_id, phone, full_name, health_fund) VALUES (7, '789012348', '+972-50-0000007', 'Lior Katz', 'Clalit'); DEP: PROTECTED column patients.national_id (MATCH DOMAIN person_id) is stored as a blind index and ciphertext. DEP: PROTECTED column patients.phone (MATCH DOMAIN phone_number) is stored as a blind index and ciphertext. INSERT 0 1 admin@operational=> INSERT INTO patients (patient_id, national_id, phone, full_name, health_fund) VALUES (8, '789012348', '+972-50-0000008', 'Second', 'Clalit'); ERROR: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "patients_national_id_key": Key (national_id) already exists. SQLSTATE: 23505 admin@operational=!> SELECT 1; ERROR: current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block HINT: ROLLBACK (or ROLLBACK TO a savepoint), then run the statements again. SQLSTATE: 25P02 admin@operational=!> ROLLBACK; ROLLBACK The second insert reuses an ID number, and the unique constraint refuses it without showing the value. A DEP rule violation, such as an unanchored join, aborts a transaction in the same way. Savepoints SAVEPOINT name, ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT name and RELEASE SAVEPOINT name work as in PostgreSQL. Rolling back to a savepoint also ends the aborted state. A transaction with a savepoint in DEP CLI, and the prompts of an open and a failed transaction text admin@operational=> BEGIN; BEGIN admin@operational=> SAVEPOINT before_change; SAVEPOINT admin@operational=> UPDATE patients SET health_fund = 'Leumit' WHERE patient_id = 1; UPDATE 1 admin@operational=> SELECT health_fund FROM patients WHERE patient_id = 1; health_fund ------------- Leumit (1 row) admin@operational=> ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT before_change; ROLLBACK admin@operational=> SELECT health_fund FROM patients WHERE patient_id = 1; health_fund ------------- Clalit (1 row) admin@operational=> COMMIT; COMMIT Schema changes are transactional CREATE and DROP of tables, indexes, functions, roles, grants and endpoints happen on the transaction's own copy of the catalog. Other connections see them after COMMIT, and ROLLBACK undoes them. text admin@operational=> BEGIN; BEGIN admin@operational=> CREATE TABLE visitors (visitor_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT); CREATE TABLE admin@operational=> INSERT INTO visitors VALUES (1, 'Guest'); INSERT 0 1 admin@operational=> SHOW TABLES; table protected_columns rows temporary -----------------+---------------------+------+----------- appointments 10 medical_records patient_national_id 6 patients national_id, phone 6 visitors 1 (4 rows) admin@operational=> ROLLBACK; ROLLBACK admin@operational=> SHOW TABLES; table protected_columns rows temporary -----------------+---------------------+------+----------- appointments 10 medical_records patient_national_id 6 patients national_id, phone 6 (3 rows) ALTER SYSTEM ROTATE MASTER KEY is the exception: it cannot run inside a transaction block (25001). Concurrent transactions Readers never wait for writers, and never see uncommitted data. One transaction writes at a time. A second writer waits up to --lock-timeout (30 seconds by default) and then fails with 55P03. A transaction that writes a table which another transaction changed after it began fails with 40001; roll back and run it again. This script starts the server with --lock-timeout 2 and shows both: python import psycopg dsn = "host=127.0.0.1 port=5433 user=admin password=admin dbname=operational sslmode=disable" a = psycopg.connect(dsn, autocommit=True) b = psycopg.connect(dsn, autocommit=True) a.execute("BEGIN") a.execute("UPDATE patients SET health_fund = 'Maccabi' WHERE patient_id = 1") print("a sees:", a.execute("SELECT health_fund FROM patients WHERE patient_id = 1").fetchall()) print("b sees:", b.execute("SELECT health_fund FROM patients WHERE patient_id = 1").fetchall()) try: b.execute("UPDATE patients SET health_fund = 'Leumit' WHERE patient_id = 2") except psycopg.Error as e: print("b write:", e.sqlstate, str(e).strip()) a.execute("COMMIT") print("b now sees:", b.execute("SELECT health_fund FROM patients WHERE patient_id = 1").fetchall()) b takes a snapshot, then a commits a change to patients; b may no longer write that table b.execute("BEGIN") b.execute("SELECT count() FROM patients") a.execute("UPDATE patients SET health_fund = 'Clalit' WHERE patient_id = 1") try: b.execute("UPDATE patients SET health_fund = 'Leumit' WHERE patient_id = 2") except psycopg.Error as e: print("b write after a committed:", e.sqlstate, str(e).strip()) b.execute("ROLLBACK") text a sees: [('Maccabi',)] b sees: [('Clalit',)] b write: 55P03 could not obtain the write lock within 2 s: another transaction is writing HINT: Commit or roll back the other transaction, or retry. b now sees: [('Maccabi',)] b write after a committed: 40001 could not serialize access due to a concurrent update of patients HINT: Another transaction committed a change to this table after this transaction began. Roll back and run it again. A transaction left idle holds the write lock, so the server ends it. After --idle-in-transaction-timeout (300 seconds by default; 0 never) the transaction is rolled back and the next statement on the connection fails with 25P03. SQLSTATE Meaning What to do --------- 25P02 The transaction is aborted ROLLBACK, or ROLLBACK TO a savepoint 40001 Another transaction changed a table you want to write Roll back and retry 55P03 The write lock was not free within --lock-timeout Retry, or find the long transaction 25P03 The transaction was idle too long and was rolled back Start again, and keep transactions short 25001 ALTER SYSTEM ROTATE MASTER KEY inside a transaction Run it on its own Constraints PRIMARY KEY (single or composite), UNIQUE, NOT NULL and REFERENCES (NO ACTION) are enforced, with PostgreSQL's SQLSTATEs. DEFAULT, CHECK and ON DELETE CASCADE are not supported. text admin@operational=> INSERT INTO patients (patient_id, national_id) VALUES (1, '999999990'); ERROR: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "patients_pkey": Key (patient_id)=(1) already exists. SQLSTATE: 23505 admin@operational=> INSERT INTO patients (patient_id, national_id) VALUES (NULL, '999999990'); ERROR: null value in column "patient_id" of relation "patients" violates not-null constraint SQLSTATE: 23502 admin@operational=> INSERT INTO appointments VALUES (999, 77, '2026-10-30 10:00:00', 'Follow-up'); ERROR: insert or update on table "appointments" violates foreign key constraint "appointments_patient_id_fkey": Key (patient_id)=(77) is not present in table "patients". SQLSTATE: 23503 admin@operational=> DELETE FROM patients WHERE patient_id = 1; ERROR: update or delete on table "patients" violates foreign key constraint "appointments_patient_id_fkey" on table "appointments": Key (patient_id)=(1) is still referenced from table "appointments". SQLSTATE: 23503 SQLSTATE Constraint ------ 23505 A primary or unique key already exists 23502 A NOT NULL column received NULL 23503 A reference points at nothing, or a referenced row is changed or deleted A constraint on an ordinary column shows its key in the message. A constraint on a protected column never does: the unique key on national_id is checked through blind index entries, and the error names the column only. text admin@operational=> INSERT INTO patients (patient_id, national_id, phone, full_name, health_fund) VALUES (9, '123456782', '+972-50-0000009', 'Copy', 'Clalit'); ERROR: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "patients_national_id_key": Key (national_id) already exists. SQLSTATE: 23505 admin@operational=> INSERT INTO medical_records VALUES (300, '000000000', 'Asthma', DATE '2026-10-01'); ERROR: insert or update on table "medical_records" violates foreign key constraint "medical_records_patient_national_id_fkey": Key (patient_national_id) is not present in table "patients". SQLSTATE: 23503 Indexes The engine keeps an index for every primary key, unique key, reference and protected column. On a protected column the key is the blind index entry, so a lookup never needs a plaintext value. CREATE [UNIQUE] INDEX adds more, and DROP INDEX removes only those you made. The indexes of patients, and EXPLAIN reading two keys of the blind index text admin@operational=> CREATE INDEX appointments_by_type ON appointments (visit_type); CREATE INDEX admin@operational=> CREATE UNIQUE INDEX appointments_by_time ON appointments (starts_at); CREATE INDEX admin@operational=> CREATE UNIQUE INDEX appointments_by_type_u ON appointments (visit_type); ERROR: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "appointments_by_type_u": Key (visit_type)=(Follow-up) already exists. HINT: The table has rows with equal keys; remove the duplicates first. SQLSTATE: 23505 admin@operational=> SHOW INDEXES FROM appointments; table index columns kind enforced made_by keys --------------+-----------------------------+----------------+-------------+----------+--------------+-------- appointments appointments_pkey appointment_id primary key yes engine values appointments appointments_patient_id_idx patient_id engine values appointments appointments_by_type visit_type CREATE INDEX values appointments appointments_by_time starts_at unique yes CREATE INDEX values (4 rows) admin@operational=> DROP INDEX appointments_by_type; DROP INDEX admin@operational=> DROP INDEX appointments_pkey; ERROR: cannot drop index appointments_pkey: the engine keeps it for a key, a reference or a PROTECTED column of appointments SQLSTATE: 2BP01 An index on a protected column answers equality only: text admin@operational=> CREATE INDEX phones ON patients (phone); DEP: Index phones keys PROTECTED column(s) phone by their blind index entries: it answers equality only, and holds no plaintext. CREATE INDEX REINDEX TABLE t rebuilds the indexes of a table. After a data directory migration, it also makes a key enforced again once its duplicates are removed. EXPLAIN EXPLAIN shows the plan after the DEP rewrite, and below it a Read: section that says how each table is read: an index lookup, or every row. Reading by an index touches only the matching rows; reading every row is a scan. Explain Plan in Hoopeo Studio text admin@operational=> EXPLAIN SELECT FROM appointments WHERE appointment_id = 101; dep_plan --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Projection: appointments.appointment_id, appointments.patient_id, appointments.starts_at, appointments.visit_type Projection: appointments.appointment_id, appointments.patient_id, appointments.starts_at, appointments.visit_type Filter: appointments.appointment_id = Int64(101) TableScan: appointments Read: appointments: index appointments_pkey, 1 key(s) (6 rows) admin@operational=> EXPLAIN SELECT FROM appointments WHERE starts_at > '2026-10-01'; dep_plan --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Projection: appointments.appointment_id, appointments.patient_id, appointments.starts_at, appointments.visit_type Projection: appointments.appointment_id, appointments.patient_id, appointments.starts_at, appointments.visit_type Filter: appointments.starts_at > Utf8("2026-10-01") TableScan: appointments Read: appointments: every row (6 rows) admin@operational=> EXPLAIN SELECT full_name FROM patients WHERE national_id = '123456782'; DEP: PROTECTED column patients.national_id is matched by equality through the blind index of MATCH DOMAIN person_id. dep_plan -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Projection: patients.full_name Projection: patients.full_name Filter: patients.national_id = dep_index(Utf8("person_id"), CAST(Utf8("123456782") AS Utf8)) TableScan: patients Read: patients: index patients_national_id_key, 1 key(s) (6 rows) In the last plan the protected value has become a call of the internal function dep_index, which computes the blind index entry. The statement and its plan are shown to the role that sent them, and never recorded in the audit log. /metrics counts index lookups, full scans and rows read; see the administration guide.

title: Privacy as Code & GDPR
text: Privacy as Code, privacy by design, and the GDPR In one sentence: DEP takes three established ways of thinking about privacy (Privacy as Code, privacy by design, and the GDPR's data protection by design and by default) and turns each of them into something the database enforces on every query. This chapter explains each framework in plain terms, shows what it asks for, and shows how DEP applies it, and where it does not. It uses DEP's constructs before they are defined in detail; each is linked to the chapter that explains it. What is Privacy as Code? What is it? Privacy as Code is the practice of writing privacy policy as an executable artifact: kept in a repository, reviewed like code, tested, and checked automatically. How is it practiced today?
