Most tools in this space work around the database: Kind of tool Example What it does --- --- --- Policy evaluation in CI Fides Describes systems and datasets with a shared taxonomy of data categories, uses, and subjects, and rejects a change whose declared use violates a policy Code scanning Privado Scans application code to find which personal data is collected and where it flows Authorization as code Open Policy Agent, Cedar Evaluates access rules written as code, when an application or gateway asks What is missing? These tools check code that someone wrote and submitted. They do not see the query an AI agent composes at run time, or an ad-hoc query an analyst types. The database, the one component every query passes through, enforces none of the policy. Example: one policy, two ways. The clinic's policy is: patients' ID numbers may leave the database only for reporting to the health funds. Without DEP, the policy lives outside the database. A CI check can confirm that the billing code declares the right data use, and a scanner can flag code that reads national_id. But any role with SELECT on the column can still export it, and the new AI agent's query never passes through CI. With DEP, the policy is part of the schema: sql -- The only place ID numbers may leave CREATE FUNCTION monthly_fund_report(report_month DATE) RETURNS TABLE (national_id TEXT, visit_date DATE, visit_type TEXT, health_fund TEXT) LANGUAGE sql DISCLOSES person_id AS $$ ... $$; GRANT EXECUTE ON FUNCTION monthly_fund_report(DATE) TO billing_job; And it can be checked by a query: sql SHOW FUNCTIONS; Output function_name kind --- --- monthly_fund_report DISCLOSES fund_claims_report DISCLOSES, LINKS Explanation: in DEP, REVEAL is legal only inside functions declared DISCLOSES (REVEAL). So this list is not documentation that might be out of date: it is the complete set of places where ID numbers can leave, by construction. Any other query, including the agent's, gets NULL or an error. Comparison Privacy as Code around the database DEP --- --- --- Where the policy is written Policy files, annotations, CI configuration The schema: PROTECTED, declared functions, grants When it is checked Before deployment, on code that was submitted On every statement, at run time What it can see Code that passes through the pipeline Every query, from every client A new AI agent or ad-hoc query Depends on whether its access passes through the policy enforcement point The implemented DEP rules apply to its queries Evidence it produces Scan and CI reports Metadata and audit records; a project can implement drift reporting How the two fit together. DEP does not replace these tools; it gives them a point of enforcement. A Fides-style taxonomy can decide which columns should be PROTECTED, and a CI pipeline can check that every declared function matches an approved decision (Step 7: Keep the matrix and the database in sync). The development method in Designing with DEP is built on exactly that idea. What is privacy by design? What is it? Privacy by design is a framework developed by Ann Cavoukian, then Information and Privacy Commissioner of Ontario, which holds that privacy should be built into systems from the start rather than added afterwards. It was recognized by the International Conference of Data Protection and Privacy Commissioners in a 2010 resolution adopted in Jerusalem, and its idea is now part of the GDPR as data protection by design (What does the GDPR require?). Its seven foundational principles, and how DEP applies them Principle What it asks How DEP applies it Coverage --- --- --- --- 1. Proactive not reactive; preventative not remedial Prevent privacy-invasive events before they happen A forbidden query is rejected before any row is read; ordinary queries cannot export protected values or perform unanchored protected linkage; unsupported forms fail closed Applies 2. Privacy as the default Protect personal data without any action by the individual or the user Protected values are suppressed by default; a role must be granted its endpoint; analytics consumers can be assigned MASKED_READ; declared functions are never executable by PUBLIC; internal keys are ordinary by default Applies 3. Privacy embedded into design Make privacy part of the architecture, not an add-on Protection is part of the type system and the query semantics; the design method starts from a privacy matrix, before the first table Applies 4. Full functionality: positive-sum, not zero-sum Achieve privacy without giving up legitimate functionality Reception, doctors, reminders, reports, and statistics all keep working; SELECT keeps working, with NULL in place of protected values Applies 5. End-to-end security: lifecycle protection Secure data through its whole lifecycle Encrypted storage, keyed matching, redaction from logs, and audit inside the database Partly: DEP covers storage and use inside the database, not collection at the source, retention periods, or deletion schedules 6. Visibility and transparency Keep practices open and verifiable The catalog lists every disclosure and linkage; purposes are recorded; the audit log attributes every lookup; teams can compare metadata with their approved matrix Applies, to the organization and its reviewers 7. Respect for user privacy Keep the individual's interests central: strong defaults, notice, user-friendly controls Strong defaults, and a subject-access export can be a declared function Limited: notice and consent are outside the database Explanation: DEP is strongest on the principles that a database can enforce by itself (1 to 4 and 6). It contributes to the lifecycle and the individual's rights, but those also depend on applications and on organizational processes. What does the GDPR require? Which parts are relevant? Three parts of the GDPR matter most for a database. Article 5: the principles. Personal data must be processed lawfully, fairly, and transparently; collected for specified purposes (purpose limitation); limited to what is necessary (data minimisation); kept accurate; kept no longer than necessary (storage limitation); and processed securely (integrity and confidentiality). The controller must be able to demonstrate all of this (accountability, Article 5(2)). Article 25(1): data protection by design. The controller must implement appropriate technical and organisational measures, such as pseudonymisation, designed to implement the data-protection principles effectively, both when deciding how processing will be done and during the processing itself, taking into account the state of the art, the cost, and the risks. Article 25(2): data protection by default. By default, only the personal data necessary for each specific purpose may be processed. The obligation applies to four dimensions: the amount of data collected, the extent of processing, the period of storage, and accessibility. In particular, personal data must not be made accessible, by default, to an indefinite number of people. The EDPB's guidance. The European Data Protection Board's Guidelines 4/2019 on Article 25 (version 2.0, adopted 20 October 2020) explain how these duties are applied. Among other things, they expect measures to be effective rather than formal, the state of the art to be assessed continuously, access to personal data to be limited to those who need it and to the types of access they need, and technical limitations on the reuse of data. Example: the four dimensions of Article 25(2) in the clinic Dimension What it means How DEP applies it --- --- --- Amount collected Collect only what is necessary Not addressed: DEP stores what is inserted Extent of processing Process only as much as each purpose needs Matching is limited to one value at a time; linking whole datasets requires a declared LINKS function; the only operation on a protected value is equality Period of storage Keep data only as long as necessary Not addressed: retention is set by the organization Accessibility Limit who can access the data Protected values are never returned by ordinary queries; column privileges decide who may match on what; disclosure goes only to roles granted EXECUTE by name, and never to PUBLIC Explanation: a receptionist who may look up a patient no longer has access, by default, to all 50,000 ID numbers. The extent of what each role can do is limited to what its purpose needs, and the only exceptions are named, reviewed functions. That is Article 25(2) expressed as database behavior. Mapping of DEP to GDPR principles and duties Principle or duty Supporting DEP construct --- --- Data minimisation, Art. 5(1)(c) Ordinary queries never return protected values; analytics and agents use the masked path (Two access paths). Purpose limitation, Art. 5(1)(b) Each linkage and disclosure is a named, described function with explicit EXECUTE grants; each matrix cell records its reason (Declared functions, Step 3: Build the privacy matrix). Data protection by design and by default, Art. 25 Protection is the default for a PROTECTED column; every exception must be declared; internal keys are ordinary by default. Security of processing, Art. 32 Engine-enforced typing, per-domain keyed matching, encrypted storage of protected values, audited and rate-limited lookups (Storage and matching). Accountability, Art. 5(2) The catalog lists every disclosure and linkage; the audit log attributes every lookup to an identity (DEP and Privacy as Code). Records of processing, Art. 30 The catalog supplies the technical part of the record: where identifiers leave, and for which described purpose. Access and erasure, Arts. 15 and 17 A subject-access export as a DISCLOSES function anchored to the requester's identifier; erasure as an anchored, audited DELETE. What does privacy engineering add? What is privacy engineering? The discipline of turning privacy goals into system properties. NIST's Introduction to Privacy Engineering and Risk Management in Federal Systems (NISTIR 8062, 2017) defines three privacy engineering objectives: Objective NIST's definition How DEP applies it --- --- --- Predictability Enabling reliable assumptions by individuals, owners, and operators about personal information and its processing by a system The rules are fixed in the schema, and the catalog states exactly where values may leave or be linked Manageability Providing the capability for granular administration of personal information, including alteration, deletion, and selective disclosure Anchored updates and deletes; disclosure only through declared functions that return only what their purpose requires Disassociability Enabling the processing of personal information or events without association to individuals or devices beyond the operational requirements of the system The core of DEP: values are used for matching without being returned, and records are associated one value at a time unless linkage is declared Explanation: disassociability is the closest existing term for DEP's principle. The NIST Privacy Framework (version 1.0) makes it concrete in its Disassociated Processing category, whose first subcategory (CT.DP-P1) is that data are processed to limit observability and linkability. Anchored matching is a direct way to limit linkability: a query can associate records only for the value it names. What DEP does not cover Where are the limits? DEP is a technical measure inside the database. It does not address: - the lawful basis for processing, or consent and its withdrawal; - notice to individuals and transparency toward them; - what is collected in the first place, and how long it is kept; - data protection impact assessments and organizational governance; - international transfers; - data that has already been disclosed and left the database. The mappings in this chapter describe technical contributions, not compliance. Any mapping to specific legal duties should be validated by privacy counsel. Key points - Privacy as Code checks policy around the database; DEP enforces it inside the database, on every query. - DEP applies most privacy-by-design principles directly, and the lifecycle and user-centric principles only in part. - For the GDPR, DEP's strongest contribution is to Article 25(2): it limits the extent of processing and the accessibility of protected values by default. - In privacy-engineering terms, DEP is a mechanism for disassociability: using values without associating them beyond what each operation needs. --- A practical implementation workflow 1. Classify: identify personal identifiers and ordinary fields that can identify people. 2. Specify: record the legitimate application tasks and the data each task requires. 3. Declare: map identifiers to PROTECTED columns and meaningful MATCH DOMAINs. 4. Grant: separate application roles and access paths. Set match limits for lookup roles. 5. Review exceptions: inspect each DISCLOSES or LINKS function, its owner, purpose and callers. 6. Test: check both permitted operations and attempts that must be refused. 7. Observe: inspect SHOW PRIVACY MATRIX and SHOW AUDIT; review access and function changes. 8. Operate: configure TLS, separate key custody, backups, retention and incident procedures. Build a small application with these controls → What remains outside DEP DEP does not decide the lawful basis for processing, collect consent, issue notices, set retention periods, perform impact assessments or govern international transfers. Rights of access, rectification, erasure and portability need complete workflows across all systems, including backups and recipients. Protected identifiers are not anonymous data. A successful lookup reveals that a record exists; ordinary names, dates and join keys may identify someone. Encrypted or pseudonymised data may still be personal data. Aggregates are not automatically anonymous, particularly for small groups. The server is trusted. DEP does not protect against an administrator who can read server memory or a compromised operating system. The simulator provides no server-side protection. The model's guarantees and limits should be part of any evaluation. From concept to implementation The Privacy as Code introduction is the short entry point for readers who do not need the whole book. Continue to Design with DEP for classification and the matrix, or Build an application to run the controls.

title: Inside the engine
text: This chapter explains the architecture and design contract. It is not a line-by-line implementation audit. Features explicitly marked as future design are not available in the current Engine; see current capabilities and native differences. Architecture In one sentence: a DEP server is an ordinary query pipeline with DEP's checks added at each stage, running in a process the client cannot reach. The trust boundary Definition. The trust boundary is the line between the client's process, which DEP does not trust, and the server's process, which it does. Every guarantee in DEP depends on one architectural fact: the client and the enforcement run in different processes, and the client controls only its own. What the client holds. A connection and the ability to send SQL. It never holds the data files, the matching keys, the server's memory, or the code that enforces the rules. Everything it learns arrives through the protocol, after the output boundary. Why DEP is a server and not a library. If the same rules ran inside the client's process (a query engine embedded in an application or a notebook), whoever runs that process could read the data directly, load the keys, or simply change the code. The rules would still describe correct behavior, but they would not enforce it. Such an embedded build can be useful as a playground for learning the syntax (Roadmap and Release), but it must be labeled clearly: it offers no protection, because whoever runs it holds all the data. Two consequences. 1. Keys never cross the boundary. Matching keys and encryption keys are loaded by the server from a location the client cannot reach: a key-management service, or at minimum a server-side file or environment variable. 2. The path is a property of the endpoint. Each access path is bound to a listening endpoint and to authenticated identities at connection time. Nothing a client sends afterwards can change it. Overview The figure shows the whole server, using the clinic's six consumers. Numbers give the order in which a statement passes through it. The DEP server architecture: clients outside the trust boundary connect to two endpoints; statements pass through the parser, the DEP analyzer, the planner, and the executor; the output boundary returns results and errors. Step What happens --- --- ① The client sends SQL over the PostgreSQL protocol to the endpoint of its path. ② The endpoint authenticates the client and fixes the path for the session. ③ The parser reads the statement, including DEP syntax, and marks protected literals. DDL that declares functions also goes to the declaration checker, which records declarations in the DEP catalog. ④ The DEP analyzer resolves names and types through the catalog, and checks typing, anchoring, and path rules. A forbidden statement is rejected here with an explicit DEP error, before any row is read. ⑤ The planner optimizes the statement and re-checks the final plan. ⑥ The executor runs the plan. ⑦ Protected matching compares keyed index entries in protected storage, using the domain's key; every protected match is audited and counted against the rate limit. ⑧ Results pass to the output boundary. ⑨ The output boundary suppresses protected values, passes disclosed values, scrubs errors, and sends the response. Components The same logical architecture applies whichever query engine sits underneath. Component Definition Role --- --- --- Endpoints Listening server addresses, one per access path Authenticate the client and fix the access path for the session. DEP catalog The server's record of DEP objects Holds protected columns, match domains, protected foreign keys, declared functions, disclosed output columns, linking regions, DISCLOSE and LINK privileges, and purposes. Parser The SQL parser, with DEP's additions to the grammar Understands PROTECTED, MATCH DOMAIN, DISCLOSES, LINKS, GRANT DISCLOSE, GRANT LINK, and CREATE ENDPOINT; identifies protected literals. DEP analyzer A checker over the resolved statement Checks every statement by its resolved meaning (which table, column, type, and operator), not by its spelling, including whether protected matching is anchored. Declaration checker A checker for declared functions Validates DISCLOSES and LINKS bodies at creation, and records disclosed columns and linking regions. Plan re-check A second check after optimization Ensures no transformation reintroduces a forbidden use. Matching component The part of execution that handles protected comparisons Performs lookups and joins on protected values through the internal matching index. Protected storage Internal columns that ordinary SQL cannot address Holds each protected value's index entry and ciphertext. Key management The server-side source of keys Supplies one versioned matching key per match domain, and encryption keys. Output boundary The last stage before the protocol Suppresses protected values, passes disclosed values, and scrubs every outgoing message. Audit and rate limiting A server-side recorder and limiter Records every protected match on the operational path and every call to a declared function, with the identity that made it; enforces per-identity limits; records withheld errors. Never records protected values. How the components fit together The path selects the execution rules; DEP enforces them inside the server. The path does not rewrite queries for the client. Some queries run with suppressed output, some are rejected because the requested operation is forbidden, and some return disclosed values or linked results because a declared function says they may. --- The life of a query In one sentence: DEP keeps the ordinary pipeline of a query engine (authenticate, analyze, plan, execute, return) and adds enforcement at every stage. The query Reception sends this query when Dana arrives, with 123456782 supplied as $1: sql SELECT full_name, national_id FROM patients WHERE national_id = $1; In an ordinary engine The query passes through four stages, and the protected column is treated like any other text: mermaid flowchart LR C[Client] --> A[Authentication] A --> P[Parse and semantic analysis] P --> PL[Planning and optimization] PL --> X[Execution plaintext comparison] X --> R[Result to client Dana Cohen, 123456782] In DEP The same pipeline, with DEP's additions highlighted: mermaid flowchart LR C[Client] --> A[Authentication path mode fixed] A --> P[Parse and semantic analysis] P --> D{DEP contract check} D -- forbidden --> E[Explicit DEP error] D -- allowed --> PL[Planning and plan re-check] PL --> X[Execution with internal matching] X --> O[Output boundary suppression] O --> R[Result to client Dana Cohen, NULL] classDef dep fill:bfdbfe,stroke:1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:0b1f4d class A,D,E,PL,X,O dep Stage Ordinary engine DEP --- --- --- Authentication Identifies the user Also fixes the access path for the whole session Analysis Resolves names and types Also checks every use of a protected or disclosed value against the rules, and rejects forbidden ones with an explicit error Planning Optimizes the query Also re-checks the final plan, so no optimization reintroduces a forbidden use Execution Compares stored values directly Compares keyed index entries; the value itself is never compared or exposed Output Sends whatever was selected Suppresses protected values, passes only declared disclosed values, and scrubs every message Follow a statement through parsing, privacy analysis, planning, execution and the output boundary. Step by step Step 1: The connection already carries its path. At authentication the server fixed the path, here OPERATIONAL, and the client cannot change it. The path accompanies the query through checking and execution. It is not a separate engine; it is the context in which the engine runs. Step 2: The engine resolves what the query means. DEP works on the engine's resolved internal representation: which table patients refers to, which column national_id refers to, what its type is and whether it is protected, which operator implements =, and which fields are meant to reach the client. At this point DEP sees two different uses of the same column: in WHERE national_id = $1 it is used for matching, and in SELECT national_id it is a request to return the value. Step 3: DEP checks the operations against the path. On the operational path, the match is allowed: the role holds privilege on national_id, and the match is anchored to the single value $1. Returning the value is not allowed, so the projection will be suppressed. On the masked path, the matching itself is forbidden, and the query is rejected before any search runs. The engine never deletes the WHERE clause to "legalize" a query; that would change its meaning and could return the whole table. Step 4: The engine plans execution. Conceptually, the plan is: find the matching record using the protected identifier; read the permitted full_name field; produce NULL for the protected output column; return the result. The predicate national_id = $1 is rewritten into a comparison between the column's internal index entries and the keyed hash of the normalized parameter. This is fundamentally different from replacing national_id with NULL everywhere, which would destroy the search. Because the optimizer can transform queries, DEP re-checks the final plan rather than trusting only the check before planning. Step 5: The engine performs the internal match. The matching component computes the index entry for the parameter with the match domain's key and locates the record (Matching with a keyed index). The same mechanism serves joins between protected fields of the same domain: a join on two person_id columns becomes an equi-join on their index entries. Step 6: The result crosses the output boundary. Before anything is sent, DEP enforces the output rules, in text and binary result formats and on every output path: full_name national_id --- --- Dana Cohen NULL Had the same value been produced by REVEAL inside a disclosing function, the output boundary would have let it through as a disclosed value, and Step 3 would have rejected any attempt to use it for anything but output. --- How declared functions and anchoring are enforced Chapter 3 defines the rules for REVEAL, DISCLOSES, LINKS, and anchored matching. Enforcing them takes five mechanisms. Validation at creation When. CREATE FUNCTION ... DISCLOSES d or CREATE FUNCTION ... LINKS d runs. What the server does, in order: 1. checks that the creating role holds DISCLOSE ON MATCH DOMAIN d or LINK ON MATCH DOMAIN d, respectively; 2. checks that the function is LANGUAGE sql, and parses and analyzes its body; 3. checks that every REVEAL in the body applies to a domain the function declares DISCLOSES, and that every unanchored match applies to a domain it declares LINKS; 4. checks that every user-defined function the body calls is itself declared for the same purpose and domain; 5. determines which output columns come from REVEAL, and records them in the DEP catalog as disclosed columns; 6. determines whether the function takes any parameter used for protected matching, and records whether it may be called on the masked path; 7. creates the function with no EXECUTE privilege for PUBLIC; 8. records the function, its kinds, its domains, its owner, and its comment in SHOW FUNCTIONS. On failure. Any failure rejects the whole statement. Later attempts to GRANT EXECUTE on a declared function to PUBLIC are rejected. Notes. The checks run unconditionally. If the underlying engine has a setting that skips function-body validation (as PostgreSQL does with check_function_bodies, which is turned off while restoring a dump), DEP's checks run regardless, and are repeated at execution time. Tracking disclosed values and linking regions The problem. A declared function is usually executed by expanding its body into the calling query, much as a view is. After expansion, the planner no longer sees a function boundary. Two things must survive this: the terminal rule, and the permission for unanchored matching. Implementation difference: DEP Engine 0.5.2 does not yet track disclosed values through sorting, functions and DISTINCT; the gaps are documented in chapter 6. The following describes the specified tracking rule. Marked expressions. DEP represents REVEAL(x) internally as a marked expression: ordinary for the purpose of output, but carrying a disclosed marker. The analyzer propagates the marker through aliases, subqueries, common table expressions, and projections, and rejects any plan in which a marked expression reaches a filter, a join key, an aggregate, a sort key, a function argument, or a write. The only legal destination of a marked expression is the output boundary. Linking regions. In the same way, the expanded body of a linking function is marked as a linking region. Unanchored matching is accepted inside that region and rejected anywhere else in the same plan, so a caller cannot extend the function's permission to its own joins. Symmetry. This is the same mechanism that keeps protected values protected, with the opposite permission: protected values may be matched but not output; disclosed values may be output but not matched. Deciding whether matching is anchored Scope. Outside a linking region, joins between protected columns require a single-value anchor. Plain equality lookups and IN lists are permitted on the operational path; they do not by themselves authorize a protected join. The analyzer decides this on each query block of the resolved query. Definitions. - A protected input is a parameter or a literal in a protected position (Parameters and literals). - A top-level conjunct of a query block is a condition joined by AND at the top of its WHERE clause or of an inner join condition. It therefore holds in every row the block produces. - The match graph of a query block has one vertex for each protected column, per table instance, that occurs in a matching comparison, and one edge for each equality between two protected columns. - A vertex is anchored if the block contains, as a top-level conjunct, an equality between that column and a single protected input. The rule. A query block is admissible if every connected component containing a protected-to-protected join edge contains an anchored vertex, or if the block lies inside a linking region for the component's domain. Anchored lookup sql WHERE p.national_id = $1 -- anchored WHERE p.national_id = '123456782' -- anchored Anchored join. One component, {p.national_id, m.patient_national_id}, anchored through p: sql FROM patients AS p JOIN medical_records AS m ON m.patient_national_id = p.national_id WHERE p.national_id = $1 Not anchored Form Why --- --- A join between protected columns with no anchored lookup on either side Links whole datasets IN with more than one value, or several equalities combined with OR Allowed for lookups, but not a single-value anchor for a protected join Comparison with the result of a subquery, IN (SELECT ...), EXISTS correlated on a protected column Asks about a whole dataset of values Comparison with a value computed inside the query Not a client-supplied value An anchor inside an OR or an outer join condition Does not hold in every row the block produces Design discussion. The following cases are retained from the proposal; use the supported-form examples in chapter 2 and test the installed Engine rather than assuming these proposals are implemented. Discussed further in the roadmap (Roadmap and Release), with a proposal for each: - Anchoring through a different protected column of the same table (a join on national_id restricted by WHERE p.phone = $1) counts as anchored, because it is still a single protected value. - Anchoring through an ordinary key (WHERE p.patient_id = 42) does not count, because it can be iterated over every key. At minimum, such queries count against the protected-lookup rate limit. Recording and auditing What is recorded. Every protected match on the operational path and every call to a declared function: which identity, when, which statement or function version, which protected columns were matched, and how many rows were returned. What is never recorded. Protected values and disclosed values. An audit log holding every identifier that was ever looked up or released would itself become the most sensitive table in the system. Rate limiting. The same component enforces the per-identity rate limit on protected lookups, and raises DEP_MATCH_RATE_LIMITED when it is exceeded. Foreign keys The rules for protected foreign keys (Protected foreign keys) are enforced in three places: When What the server does --- --- At definition CREATE TABLE and ALTER TABLE check that a foreign key and the column it references have the same protection and match domain, fill in the inherited domain, and record the reference in the DEP catalog. A mismatch is rejected with DEP_REFERENCE_MISMATCH. At write time Referential checks compare index entries, never plaintext. Because both columns use the same domain key, an index entry computed for the referencing value can be looked up directly in the unique index of the referenced column. Cascading updates recompute index entries in the referencing rows; cascading deletes and RESTRICT locate them through the index. Each check passes through the audit and rate-limit component as one protected lookup. On failure Violation messages are reduced to the constraint's name before they reach the output boundary. The underlying engine's own message, which in most engines quotes the offending key, is never sent. --- Layers of enforcement In one sentence: no single check is trusted to catch everything, so each stage of execution enforces the rules that apply to it. Layer What DEP does there --- --- Connection Fixes the access path from the endpoint and the authenticated identity; rejects any later attempt to change it. Function creation Validates every DISCLOSES and LINKS body, records disclosed columns and linking regions, and withholds public execution (Validation at creation). Parsing and analysis Detects every use of a protected field or disclosed value and checks it against what the path allows, including whether protected matching is anchored (Deciding whether matching is anchored). Identifies protected literals and records their positions so the statement text can be redacted wherever it is kept. Type checking Rejects casts, functions, and operators not defined for protected values. Because the protected type defines no conversion to plain types, many attacks fail here by construction. Planning Re-validates the final plan, so that view inlining, function inlining, subquery flattening, or other transformations cannot reintroduce a forbidden use. Execution Performs permitted matches through the matching component. Protected comparison operations themselves verify the path, so indirect calls cannot bypass the earlier checks. Intermediate results Copying into a temporary table or passing through a common table expression does not turn a protected value into an ordinary one. Forms that cannot yet guarantee this are rejected as unsupported. Output boundary Suppresses protected values, passes disclosed values, and scrubs errors and notices, in every result format. Why rewriting the query is not enough Editing the internal representation of a query is part of the implementation, but it is not sufficient on its own. If DEP only rewrote the outer query, a function, a view, or a subquery could route around it. Protection has to hold during execution, as the engine passes values between operations. That is why the protected type, the matching component, and the output boundary each enforce the rules independently, rather than relying on a single check at the start. --- Storage and matching In one sentence: each protected value is stored twice inside the engine, once as a keyed hash used for matching and once encrypted, and SQL sees neither. Internal columns Definition. A protected column is presented to SQL as one logical column, but stored as two internal columns that ordinary SQL cannot address. Internal column Contents Used for --- --- --- Index entry Keyed hash of the normalized value, with a key version Matching, joins, uniqueness, and foreign-key checks Ciphertext The value under authenticated encryption REVEAL, key rotation, and re-indexing Rules. 1. Every protected column is stored the same way. There are no storage options for the user to choose in the first version. 2. SELECT , the catalog's column listings, and every other introspection path show only the logical column. 3. The internal columns are reachable only by the matching component and by REVEAL. Encrypted storage Protected values are stored with an established authenticated-encryption scheme, with keys held outside ordinary tables. Plaintext inputs are excluded from logs and error messages. Role of encryption. Encryption is a complementary storage layer. DEP's query rules do not depend on a client being unable to decrypt a string it received, because clients never receive the stored representation in the first place. Matching uses the keyed index entry; authorized disclosure uses the ciphertext. Matching with a keyed index Definition. A keyed equality index (sometimes called a blind index) stores, alongside each protected value, a keyed hash of its normalized form. Lookups and joins compare these entries instead of the values. What its design must define. Aspect Meaning --- --- Normalization How leading zeros, whitespace, or check digits are treated, so that equal values always produce equal index entries. Domain separation Each match domain, and each tenant, uses its own key, so that index entries from different domains cannot be compared. Key versions Each entry records which key produced it, so keys can be rotated. Collision handling A matching index entry is confirmed against the ciphertext before it is treated as a match. What it reveals. Such an index reveals equality patterns to anyone who can inspect storage directly: equal values have equal entries. This is acceptable under the threat model in Guarantees and limits, but it is not evidence of anonymity, and the technique itself is not new. Foreign-key columns A column that references a protected column stores its own index entry and ciphertext, like any protected column. Because both columns use the same domain key, their index entries are directly comparable, which is what makes internal referential checks and joins possible. The encrypted value now exists in two tables, which is one more reason to prefer ordinary internal keys unless the link itself is sensitive (Step 2: Classify the fields). Rotation is three different things Mechanism What it changes --- --- Key rotation Which keys are in use Re-encryption The stored ciphertext Token rotation Identifiers visible to consumers (outside the first version) None of them can retract data that a client has already received. A possible later extension: match-only storage Idea. A protected column could, in principle, store only its index entry and discard the value itself. Matching, joins, uniqueness, and foreign-key checks would work unchanged; REVEAL would become impossible forever, and so would key rotation, re-normalization, migration, and correcting a mistyped value, unless the original values were re-supplied from elsewhere. Why it is not planned. Its benefit is smaller than it appears. Against clients, DEP already prevents disclosure outside declared functions. Against theft of the database together with its keys, it protects little for low-entropy identifiers: there are only about 100 million valid Israeli ID numbers, and anyone holding both the index entries and the index key can hash every one of them. It protects well only high-entropy values that are verified and never read, which is password hashing, a technique that already exists. --- Leakage channels In one sentence: suppressing values in an ordinary SELECT is the easy part; a credible implementation must account for every other way a value can leave the server. Rule. Each channel below must be either covered or rejected as unsupported. Channel Risk Treatment in the first version --- --- --- Text and binary result formats A value encoded before suppression Suppress before encoding, in both formats RETURNING INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE returning rows Suppress protected columns, or reject where unsupported COPY TO and bulk export Output that bypasses ordinary result handling Reject for tables with protected columns DEP's own errors A message that quotes a value Never include values (19.1) The underlying engine's errors An internal error that quotes a literal or a row Scrub; replace with DEP_ERROR_WITHHELD when in doubt Constraint violations A unique-key or foreign-key error that reports the conflicting value Report the constraint name only; the violation itself still reveals whether the value exists, a documented limitation Foreign-key checks Inserts used to test identifiers one by one, without any SELECT Each check counts as a protected lookup: audited and rate-limited (Foreign keys) Server logs Statement and parameter logging that records identifiers Never log protected parameters; redact protected literals from statement text Protected literals in statement text An identifier written in the query, recorded or echoed with it Redact at every place the text is kept: logs, query statistics, audit records, error messages (Parameters and literals) EXPLAIN Plans that show constants, parameters, or column statistics Reject for statements involving protected values Optimizer statistics Minimum, maximum, and most-common values of a column Never collect value statistics on internal protected columns; never expose them User-defined functions, triggers, notices User code that receives a value and emits it elsewhere Protected values cannot be passed to user code at all, except declared functions Views, temporary tables, CREATE TABLE AS Derived objects that shed protection Views inherit protection; materializing protected columns is rejected until designed Disclosed values Reuse of a revealed value after REVEAL The terminal rule (Tracking disclosed values and linking regions) Unanchored matching A join or lookup that links whole datasets without returning any identifier Rejected outside LINKS functions (Deciding whether matching is anchored) Linkage through ordinary keys Datasets joined through an ordinary column, bypassing every linkage rule Outside the engine's reach; a design responsibility (Linkage through ordinary keys) Timing Execution time that depends on whether a match exists Out of scope for the first version; documented as a known limitation Protection is incomplete if a value is hidden in the result but appears in a log. --- Guarantees and limits In one sentence: DEP makes four precise guarantees under stated assumptions, and is explicit about everything they do not cover. Who is trusted Trusted. The database server and its code, the operating system it runs on, the deployment administrator, the key-management service, and the roles granted DISCLOSE or LINK on a match domain. Not trusted. Clients: applications, analysts, BI tools, and AI agents, even when they are authenticated. Clients cannot install native code, disable DEP, replace type functions, declare functions without the corresponding privilege, or obtain administrative credentials. Out of scope. DEP does not protect against a compromised operating system or an administrator who can read the server's memory. If an administrator can modify the server itself, the rules of the query language cannot stop them. Encrypted backup and restore require a separate, controlled administrative design. DEP is therefore complementary to client-side encryption, which assumes the opposite trust model. What DEP guarantees Assumptions. The guarantees hold if: 1. the server is trusted, as described in Who is trusted; 2. the rules are applied to the final plan of every statement, after views, common table expressions, and declared functions are expanded, and after optimization; 3. declared functions are created only by roles holding the declaration privilege, and invoked only by roles granted EXECUTE; 4. error text, logs, statistics, and plan output carry no protected values. Two kinds of information flow. An explicit flow computes an output value from a protected value. An implicit flow lets a protected value decide which rows are produced, as a matching predicate does. The four guarantees Guarantee Statement --- --- No return In any statement, on either path, every output value computed from a protected value comes from REVEAL inside a declared disclosing function that the caller was explicitly allowed to execute. Every other protected value reaches the client as NULL. No statement can copy a protected value into an ordinary column, so a value cannot be laundered through storage. Anchored linkage On the operational path, an ordinary query combines records through a protected value only for the single value the client supplied. With a per-identity rate limit, this bounds how many people an operational client can link records for in a given period. Terminal disclosure A disclosed value never reaches a filter, join key, grouping, DISTINCT, sort key, aggregate, function argument, or write. A client can use disclosed values against protected data again only by sending them back one at a time, as anchored lookups. A disclosure therefore cannot be turned into bulk linkage inside the database. Masked-path confinement On the masked path, the result of a query does not depend on protected values at all, except through the outputs of approved linking functions. Two databases that differ only in their protected values give the same answer to any query on that path. Notes. These are properties of the design. An implementation has them only to the extent that it applies the rules faithfully. The accompanying paper states them formally, with proof sketches. The masked-path guarantee depends on the rule that a masked connection cannot test whether a protected value is present (IS NULL, or COUNT of the column); without it, whether a value is present would be an implicit flow. DEP.js applies that rule; DEP Engine 0.5.2 does not yet (see chapter 6). Matching reveals information The limit. Every permitted match is a question the database answers. A successful lookup confirms that a record with that value exists; a join associates it with an appointment or a diagnosis; a returned name can identify the person behind it, however well the identifier is hidden. Enumeration. Low-entropy identifiers make this concrete. An Israeli national ID has nine digits, the last of which is a check digit, so there are only about 100 million valid values. A client allowed 10,000 lookups per second could test every one of them in under three hours. Anchored matching without limits would be an enumeration oracle: one value at a time, but as many times as the client likes. DEP's answer: permit and attribute. On the operational path, a role may match on any protected column it is permitted to use, and DEP does not judge each individual lookup. Instead: - every protected match is audited, with the identity that made it, and without the value itself; - protected lookups are rate-limited per identity, so that one value at a time cannot become every value in an afternoon; - qualified access is a future proposal, not a current control: the proposed table option would require every operational read or write to be anchored (Requiring qualified access); - ordinary column privileges decide who may match on what (Who may match on what). Declared functions are trusted code A declared function is, by design, an opening in the wall. DEP guarantees that the opening is declared, located, limited by the rules, and listed in the catalog. It does not guarantee that the declared purpose is legitimate, nor that the recipient will use the data properly. The quality of these decisions depends on the people who hold the DISCLOSE and LINK privileges and on the review process around them. Released values are beyond DEP's reach > Disclosure tracking applies within database execution. Once a value is returned to a client, DEP cannot control its subsequent use. A client that received identifiers from a disclosing function can keep them, combine them with other data, or send them back as parameters in later queries, within whatever matching its permissions allow. Linkage through ordinary keys DEP enforces anchoring and LINKS only on protected columns. If two datasets are connected through an ordinary key, linkage through that key is governed by ordinary permissions alone, and every rule about linkage can be bypassed through it. The same is true of an ordinary key returned by a declared function. This is a design responsibility, not an engine guarantee: keys that link sensitive datasets must themselves be protected, there must be no path made only of ordinary keys between identities and sensitive data, and declared functions should not return keys their recipients do not need (Step 2: Classify the fields). Ordinary data is not anonymous data The masked path can run aggregate queries over ordinary fields and call linking functions that return aggregates, but that does not make results anonymous. Small groups and combinations of released attributes can still identify people. DEP is one control among several, not a replacement for anonymization or data-minimization practices. Known limitations of the first version - Timing differences between matching and non-matching lookups are not addressed. - Constraint violations on protected columns reveal whether a value exists, even though the error never contains the value: a duplicate in a UNIQUE column means it exists, and a failed foreign-key check means it does not. Both count as protected lookups. - Only full-value equality is supported on protected values. - SQL forms outside the published supported-forms list are rejected rather than supported. - Protection of ordinary fields is left to ordinary permissions. The precise promise > Ordinary queries never return protected plaintext, and never link whole datasets through protected values. Protected values leave the database only through explicitly declared disclosures, and datasets are linked through them only in explicitly declared linking functions. Permitted matching can still reveal record existence and associations with returned data, and DEP does not guarantee that nothing can be inferred from permitted information. --- Reading and sources The book develops the original DEP design by Reuven Mandelovich. Proposed extensions and comparisons are collected in Roadmap and release. How to cite This document is licensed under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License. title: Glossary
text: Every term of DEP, with what it means, why it exists, an example from the demo clinic, and where you will meet it. Each term has its own address (glossary/protected-column), so any page can link to it. For a first reading, DEP SQL in five minutes introduces the main terms in order. The terms: Access path · Anchor · Audit log · Blind index · Ciphertext · Declared function · DEP error · DEP note · Disclosure · Endpoint · Linking · Masked read path · Master key · Match domain · Match limit · Matching · Operational path · Privacy matrix · Protected column · REVEAL · Terminal rule The data Protected column A column whose values the database uses, but never returns. A column is protected when the schema says so: PROTECTED MATCH DOMAIN after its type. Its type does not change; national_id is still TEXT. The database can compare it with a whole value for equality, so the column can still find a row, carry a primary or unique key, and connect two tables. What it cannot do is come back: in any query, on any path, for any role, including the administrator, a protected column in the output is returned as NULL. Anything that would reveal part of a value, or its order, is refused: LIKE, substrings, casts, sorting, ranges, min and max, or passing the value to a function. On the operational path, WHERE col IS NULL or IS NOT NULL may filter rows. Returning the presence test and using COUNT(col) are refused on either path; COUNT() simply counts rows and is allowed on either. See the presence-test examples and permission table for the rules and implementation status. sql national_id TEXT PROTECTED MATCH DOMAIN person_id UNIQUE, patient_national_id TEXT PROTECTED REFERENCES patients (national_id), -- takes the domain of the column it references - Why: the application that finds a patient by ID number never needs to read ID numbers, and now it cannot. - You will meet it: in the DEP note "Output column national_id is PROTECTED ... and is returned as NULL", and in error ZD101 when an operation is refused. - More: Concepts: Protected columns, DEP SQL: Protected columns. Match domain A family of values that may be compared with each other, with its own keys. Every protected column belongs to one match domain, named in its declaration. Values can be compared only within a domain: every column that holds ID numbers is in person_id, every column of phone numbers in phone_number, and an ID number can never be compared with a phone number, even by mistake. Each domain has its own keys, so the stored form of a value in one domain says nothing about the same characters in another. Permissions to disclose and to link are also given per domain. sql GRANT DISCLOSE ON MATCH DOMAIN phone_number TO privacy_admin; -- may write functions that return phone numbers - Why: a domain is the unit of meaning ("a person's ID number") that the privacy rules talk about. - You will meet it: in every DEP note about a protected column, and in error ZD103 when two domains are mixed. - More: Concepts: Match domains. Blind index What the database stores instead of the value: a keyed fingerprint, the same for equal values. When a protected value is written, DEP Engine computes its index entry: a keyed hash (HMAC-SHA256) of the value with the key of its match domain, stored as ie1: and 32 hexadecimal digits. Equal values give equal entries, so the engine can find, join and check uniqueness by comparing entries, without the plain value. Without the key, an entry cannot be turned back into the value, and it says nothing about order or prefixes, which is why LIKE and ranges cannot work. One thing it does show, to someone who can read the stored data: which rows share a value. text '123456782' -> ie1:fed1451ad4eb22a68f74e52c2945fbd5 - Why: equality is all that finding and connecting records needs. - You will meet it: in the DEP note "matched by equality through the blind index of MATCH DOMAIN person_id", in EXPLAIN (Read: index patients_national_id_key), and in SHOW STORAGE. - More: Concepts: Blind indexes and ciphertexts. Ciphertext The encrypted copy of a protected value, stored next to its index entry. A protected value is also encrypted (XChaCha20-Poly1305, with the key of its domain) and stored as ct1:.... The database never decrypts it to answer a query; only REVEAL, inside a disclosing function, does. It exists so that a value can be disclosed when a declared purpose requires it, and so that keys can be rotated. - You will meet it: in SHOW STORAGE patients, which shows a table as it is kept: index entries and ciphertexts. Master key The one secret from which every other key is derived. Each database has a 256-bit master key, in master.key in the data directory, or elsewhere with --key-file. The keys of each match domain (one for index entries, one for encryption) are derived from it. Kept on another volume, it makes a copy of the data directory worthless on its own: only index entries and ciphertexts. ALTER SYSTEM ROTATE MASTER KEY replaces it, and re-encrypts every value and recomputes every index entry. - More: Administration: The data directory and the master key, Key rotation. The connections Endpoint The door a connection comes in by. It fixes the connection's access path. A client connects to an endpoint by name, where PostgreSQL clients name a database: -d operational. Each endpoint has an access path, and a role may use an endpoint only if it was granted to it. The demo clinic has two: operational and analytics. More can be made with CREATE ENDPOINT. sql GRANT CONNECT ON ENDPOINT analytics TO bi_dashboard; - Why: what a connection may do depends on what it is for, not only on who it is. A dashboard and a reception desk need different powers even with the same data. - More: Concepts: Endpoints and access paths. Access path What a connection may do with protected values: OPERATIONAL or MASKED_READ. The path is set by the endpoint at login and stays for the whole session: SET ROLE keeps it, and SET dep.path is refused (error ZD106). To work on another path, connect through another endpoint. It is the second question the engine asks about every statement, after the role's privileges. Operational path For applications that serve one person at a time. On OPERATIONAL a connection may match protected values, write, change the schema, and call declared functions. Protected outputs are still NULL. This is the path of reception, the doctors' application and the jobs that act on one person or send a report. Masked read path For dashboards, reports and analysis: read what is ordinary, match nothing. On MASKED_READ a connection reads ordinary columns, and protected columns come back as NULL. It may not match protected values, test whether one is present, write, change the schema, or call a disclosing function (error ZD102). It may call a function declared LINKS, which is how a dashboard gets statistics that need protected values. text bi_dashboard@analytics=> SELECT patient_id FROM patients WHERE national_id = '123456782'; ERROR: Matching PROTECTED values is unavailable on a MASKED_READ connection. The queries Matching Finding rows by a protected value, by equality only. A match compares a protected column with a whole value (national_id = '123456782', or a parameter $1), with a list (IN, NOT IN, OR), or with another protected column of the same domain (a join). The engine computes the index entry of the given value and compares entries. Matching needs the OPERATIONAL path and a column privilege: in DEP, SELECT on a protected column is the privilege to match on it. Every match is counted for the match limit and written to the audit log. - You will meet it: in the DEP note "is matched by equality through the blind index". - More: DEP SQL: Matching. Anchor The one value that a join on protected columns is tied to. A join between protected columns is allowed when the query also pins one side to a single value: then it connects the records of one person. Without that value, the same join would connect every person in one table to every person in the other, which is linking, and it is refused before a row is read (error ZD107). sql -- anchored: the records of one patient SELECT m.diagnosis FROM patients AS p JOIN medical_records AS m ON m.patient_national_id = p.national_id WHERE p.national_id = '123456782'; - You will meet it: in the DEP note "is anchored to a single protected value", and in error ZD107 with a hint that shows how to anchor. - More: DEP SQL: Joins and anchors. Linking Connecting protected values across whole tables, without an anchor. Only in a LINKS function. Statistics, deduplication and reports often need every record joined on a protected value. That is the most powerful thing a database can do with personal data, so DEP allows it only inside a declared function with LINKS for the domain. GROUP BY and DISTINCT on a protected column are also linking. sql CREATE FUNCTION diagnoses_per_fund() RETURNS TABLE (health_fund TEXT, diagnosis TEXT, patients BIGINT) LANGUAGE sql LINKS person_id AS $$ SELECT p.health_fund, m.diagnosis, COUNT() FROM patients AS p JOIN medical_records AS m ON m.patient_national_id = p.national_id GROUP BY p.health_fund, m.diagnosis $$; The exceptions Declared function A named function that may do what ordinary queries may not: disclose, or link. A declared function is written in SQL (LANGUAGE sql) and declares its purpose and domain: DISCLOSES person_id, LINKS person_id, or both. Only a role granted DISCLOSE or LINK on that match domain may create one; other roles get EXECUTE on it, never PUBLIC. It runs with its owner's privileges, so the caller needs no access to the tables. Every call is in the audit log. COMMENT ON FUNCTION records its purpose and owner, and the privacy matrix lists it. - Why: every exception has a name, an owner, a reviewer and a record, instead of being a privilege hidden in an application. - You will meet it: marked D and L in Hoopeo Studio's object browser, and in SHOW FUNCTIONS. - More: Concepts: Declared functions, DEP SQL: Declared functions. Disclosure Returning a protected value in plain text. Only in a DISCLOSES function, with REVEAL. When a value must leave the database for a declared purpose (the ID numbers on a report to the health funds, the phone numbers for appointment reminders), a disclosing function returns it. The columns it discloses are marked in its result, and each call is audited with the number of values disclosed. text billing_job@operational=> SELECT FROM monthly_fund_report(DATE '2026-10-01'); DEP: Output column national_id is disclosed: Column national_id of monthly_fund_report() (DISCLOSES person_id). REVEAL The one operation that decrypts a protected value. REVEAL(p.national_id) turns a protected value into plain text. It is accepted only inside a function declared DISCLOSES for that column's domain (error ZD001 anywhere else), and its result is a disclosed value. Terminal rule A disclosed value can be returned, and used for nothing else. Once a value has been disclosed, it is plain text, and the database could no longer protect it in a further match. So it may only leave, renamed or cast at most: the specification forbids filtering, joining, grouping, sorting, computing on it or matching it again (error ZD104). A query that needs to match should do so on the protected column inside the function, before REVEAL. See the known native differences before relying on enforcement in a released Engine. text ERROR: Column national_id of monthly_fund_report() is a disclosed value and cannot be used in a join condition. SQLSTATE: ZD104 (DEP_DISCLOSED_VALUE_USE) What the database tells you DEP note A line with a result that says how protected columns were handled. Every statement that touches a protected column comes back with DEP notes: which column was matched and how, which output was returned as NULL, which join was anchored, which value was disclosed. They are notices on the PostgreSQL protocol (NOTICE: DEP: ... in psql), a notes field in the HTTP API, DEP: lines in DEP CLI, and the Output pane of Hoopeo Studio. They explain; they never change the result. - More: The notes reference. DEP error A refusal, with a ZD code and a hint that says what would be allowed. A statement that breaks a rule is refused before it reads any data. The error has a message, a hint, a SQLSTATE of class ZD (ZD001 to ZD109) and a name such as DEP_UNANCHORED_MATCH. An error never contains a protected value or the value of a parameter. - More: The error reference. Audit log The record of every protected match, disclosure, linking and refusal, without values. DEP Engine writes an audit record for each protected match (with the number of values), each call of a declared function, each refused statement, each match limit reached and each key rotation, with the role, the endpoint, the path, the object and the domain. It never records a protected value or the text of a statement. SHOW AUDIT shows the latest records; Hoopeo Studio has Tools > Audit Log. - More: Administration: The audit log. Match limit How many protected matches a role may make per minute. A reception desk looks up a few patients an hour; a script that tries a million ID numbers is an attack. A match limit stops it: ALTER ROLE reception_app MATCH LIMIT 100 PER MINUTE, or --match-limit for every role that is not a superuser. A role over its limit gets error ZD109, and the audit log records it. - More: DEP SQL: Match limits. Privacy matrix Who may match, and who may disclose, each protected column, through which path. SHOW PRIVACY MATRIX (Tools > Privacy Matrix in Hoopeo Studio) lists every protected column against every role: the paths it can use, whether it may match, and the declared functions through which it may disclose. It is computed from the schema and the grants, so it is always the rules as the engine applies them, and it is the table a privacy officer reviews. - More: The SHOW reference.

title: Errors & notes
text: A DEP error is an ordinary PostgreSQL error with a SQLSTATE in class ZD, a message, and a hint. DEP CLI and Hoopeo Studio print the DEP code beside the SQLSTATE, as in SQLSTATE: ZD107 (DEP_UNANCHORED_MATCH). Over the PostgreSQL protocol only the SQLSTATE travels, so a program branches on ZD107; the HTTP API also returns the code. Errors that DataFusion or PostgreSQL would also raise keep their usual SQLSTATEs, listed in the second table. A DEP error in Hoopeo Studio: the message, the code and the hint A policy rejection depends only on the statement, the access path, the role and the schema, and happens before any row is read. An execution failure happens while an allowed statement runs and may depend on the data (a constraint, for example). An error message never contains a protected value or the value of a bound parameter. DEP errors SQLSTATE Code Raised when --------- ZD001 DEP_REVEAL_OUTSIDE_DISCLOSURE REVEAL is used outside a function that declares DISCLOSES for the column's match domain ZD002 DEP_DECLARATION_PRIVILEGE A role declares a DISCLOSES or LINKS function for a domain without GRANT DISCLOSE or GRANT LINK, or DISCLOSE or LINK is granted to PUBLIC ZD003 DEP_DECLARED_LANGUAGE A declared function is not LANGUAGE sql ZD004 DEP_DECLARED_CALL A declared function calls another declared function that is not declared for the same purpose and domain ZD005 DEP_PUBLIC_EXECUTE EXECUTE on a function declared DISCLOSES or LINKS is granted to PUBLIC ZD006 DEP_REFERENCE_MISMATCH A reference joins a protected column and an ordinary one ZD101 DEP_PROTECTED_OPERATION An operation other than full-value equality is applied to a protected value ZD102 DEP_ENDPOINT_OPERATION The operation is not allowed on the connection's access path: matching, testing whether a protected value is present, writing, schema changes, or disclosing on the MASKED_READ path ZD103 DEP_MATCH_DOMAIN_MISMATCH Two protected columns of different match domains are compared or referenced ZD104 DEP_DISCLOSED_VALUE_USE A disclosed value is used for anything but being returned: the terminal rule ZD105 DEP_UNQUALIFIED_ACCESS Reserved. Defined by the design, and not raised by DEP Engine 0.5 ZD106 DEP_PATH_IMMUTABLE A connection tries to change its access path ZD107 DEP_UNANCHORED_MATCH A match of protected values is not anchored to a single value, outside a function declared for linking (LINKS) ZD108 DEP_UNSUPPORTED_FORM A form DEP cannot analyze, rejected rather than run with uncertain protection ZD109 DEP_MATCH_RATE_LIMITED A role went over its match limit ZD901 An internal code with no SQLSTATE of its own. DEP Engine does not raise it Examples Each was run against the demo clinic. The role is in the prompt. text admin@operational=> SET ROLE privacy_admin; SET privacy_admin@operational=> SELECT full_name, REVEAL(national_id) FROM patients; ERROR: REVEAL() of patients.national_id (match domain person_id) appears outside a disclosing function. HINT: Move the disclosure into a function declared DISCLOSES person_id. SQLSTATE: ZD001 (DEP_REVEAL_OUTSIDE_DISCLOSURE) privacy_admin@operational=> CREATE FUNCTION no_sql(id TEXT) RETURNS TABLE (x TEXT) LANGUAGE plpgsql DISCLOSES person_id AS $$ SELECT 1 $$; ERROR: Function no_sql is written in LANGUAGE plpgsql. HINT: Declared functions must be LANGUAGE sql, so the engine can analyze their bodies. SQLSTATE: ZD003 (DEP_DECLARED_LANGUAGE) privacy_admin@operational=> CREATE FUNCTION wrap(d DATE) RETURNS TABLE (national_id TEXT) LANGUAGE sql LINKS person_id AS $$ SELECT r.national_id FROM monthly_fund_report(d) AS r $$; ERROR: Function wrap calls monthly_fund_report(), which is not declared for the same purpose and match domain. HINT: Inline the logic, or declare both functions for the same purpose. SQLSTATE: ZD004 (DEP_DECLARED_CALL) privacy_admin@operational=> GRANT EXECUTE ON FUNCTION monthly_fund_report(DATE) TO PUBLIC; ERROR: Function monthly_fund_report is declared DISCLOSES or LINKS, and cannot be executable by PUBLIC. HINT: Grant EXECUTE to the specific roles that need it. SQLSTATE: ZD005 (DEP_PUBLIC_EXECUTE) privacy_admin@operational=> RESET ROLE; SET admin@operational=> GRANT DISCLOSE ON MATCH DOMAIN person_id TO PUBLIC; ERROR: DISCLOSE and LINK cannot be granted to PUBLIC. HINT: Grant them to the roles that declare functions. SQLSTATE: ZD002 (DEP_DECLARATION_PRIVILEGE) admin@operational=> \c operational app_developer You are now connected as "app_developer" through endpoint "operational" (OPERATIONAL). app_developer@operational=> CREATE FUNCTION all_ids() RETURNS TABLE (national_id TEXT) LANGUAGE sql DISCLOSES person_id AS $$ SELECT REVEAL(national_id) FROM patients $$; ERROR: Role app_developer may not declare functions that DISCLOSES match domain person_id. HINT: A superuser can allow it: GRANT DISCLOSE ON MATCH DOMAIN person_id TO app_developer. SQLSTATE: ZD002 (DEP_DECLARATION_PRIVILEGE) app_developer@operational=> \c operational admin You are now connected as "admin" through endpoint "operational" (OPERATIONAL). admin@operational=> CREATE TABLE bad (id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, nid TEXT REFERENCES patients (national_id)); ERROR: Column bad.nid references PROTECTED column patients.national_id (match domain person_id) but is not PROTECTED. HINT: Declare it TEXT PROTECTED REFERENCES patients (national_id), so the reference is kept as an index entry. SQLSTATE: ZD006 (DEP_REFERENCE_MISMATCH) admin@operational=> SELECT full_name FROM patients WHERE national_id LIKE '1%'; ERROR: LIKE is not supported for PROTECTED values (patients.national_id). HINT: PROTECTED values support only full-value equality matching. To release a value, use a disclosing function. SQLSTATE: ZD101 (DEP_PROTECTED_OPERATION) text bi_dashboard@analytics=> SELECT health_fund FROM patients WHERE national_id = '123456782'; ERROR: Matching PROTECTED values is unavailable on a MASKED_READ connection. HINT: This operation requires an OPERATIONAL connection. SQLSTATE: ZD102 (DEP_ENDPOINT_OPERATION) bi_dashboard@analytics=> SET dep.path = 'OPERATIONAL'; ERROR: The access path of this connection is MASKED_READ and cannot be changed. HINT: The path is fixed at authentication. Connect through another endpoint instead. SQLSTATE: ZD106 (DEP_PATH_IMMUTABLE) text admin@operational=> CREATE TABLE a (id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, x TEXT PROTECTED MATCH DOMAIN d1); CREATE TABLE admin@operational=> CREATE TABLE b (id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, y TEXT PROTECTED MATCH DOMAIN d2); CREATE TABLE admin@operational=> SELECT 1 FROM a, b WHERE a.x = b.y; ERROR: a.x (match domain d1) cannot be compared with b.y (match domain d2). HINT: Values from different match domains are different kinds of value. SQLSTATE: ZD103 (DEP_MATCH_DOMAIN_MISMATCH) text doctors_app@operational=> SELECT p.full_name FROM patients AS p JOIN medical_records AS m ON m.patient_national_id = p.national_id; ERROR: Join on PROTECTED columns patients.national_id and medical_records.patient_national_id is not anchored to a single protected value. HINT: Anchor the join with a lookup such as WHERE patients.national_id = $1, or perform it inside a function declared LINKS person_id. SQLSTATE: ZD107 (DEP_UNANCHORED_MATCH) text billing_job@operational=> SELECT FROM monthly_fund_report(DATE '2026-10-01') AS r WHERE r.national_id = '123456782'; ERROR: Column national_id of monthly_fund_report() is a disclosed value and cannot be used in a filter. HINT: Disclosed values can only be returned. Perform the match on PROTECTED fields inside a declared function, before REVEAL. SQLSTATE: ZD104 (DEP_DISCLOSED_VALUE_USE) text admin@operational=> SELECT full_name FROM patients ORDER BY national_id; ERROR: ORDER BY is not supported for PROTECTED values (patients.national_id). HINT: PROTECTED values support only full-value equality matching. To release a value, use a disclosing function. SQLSTATE: ZD101 (DEP_PROTECTED_OPERATION) admin@operational=> MERGE INTO patients USING patients p2 ON patients.patient_id = p2.patient_id WHEN MATCHED THEN DELETE; ERROR: Statement not supported: MERGE INTO patients HINT: DEP rejects forms it cannot analyze rather than run them with uncertain protection. SQLSTATE: ZD108 (DEP_UNSUPPORTED_FORM) admin@operational=> ALTER ROLE reception_app MATCH LIMIT 1 PER MINUTE; ALTER ROLE admin@operational=> \c operational reception_app You are now connected as "reception_app" through endpoint "operational" (OPERATIONAL). reception_app@operational=> SELECT full_name FROM patients WHERE national_id = '123456782'; DEP: PROTECTED column patients.national_id is matched by equality through the blind index of MATCH DOMAIN person_id. full_name ------------ Dana Cohen (1 row) reception_app@operational=> SELECT full_name FROM patients WHERE national_id = '234567893'; ERROR: Role reception_app has made 1 protected matches of the 1 PER MINUTE it is allowed; this statement would make 1 more. HINT: Wait for the period to pass, or ask a superuser to change the limit (ALTER ROLE ... MATCH LIMIT n PER MINUTE). SQLSTATE: ZD109 (DEP_MATCH_RATE_LIMITED) PostgreSQL SQLSTATEs These are the SQLSTATEs DEP Engine itself raises, besides ZD. DataFusion may raise others for ordinary SQL, such as a type error. SQLSTATE Meaning In DEP Engine --------- 08000, 08001, 08006 Connection exception A TLS setup or handshake failure; an unknown endpoint at login; a client that could not connect 0LP01 Invalid grant operation A privilege that does not apply to the object (for example EXECUTE on a table) 22023 Invalid parameter value An unknown endpoint mode, role, match limit or period 22P02 Invalid text representation A malformed JSON body in the HTTP API 23502 Not-null violation NULL in a NOT NULL column 23503 Foreign-key violation A reference to nothing, or a referenced row changed or deleted 23505 Unique violation A primary or unique key already exists. For a protected column the message never shows the value 25000, 25001 Invalid transaction state The transaction has ended; ALTER SYSTEM ROTATE MASTER KEY inside a transaction block 25P01 No active transaction SAVEPOINT, ROLLBACK TO or RELEASE outside a transaction block 25P02 In failed transaction A statement after an error, until ROLLBACK or ROLLBACK TO 25P03 Idle-in-transaction timeout The transaction was idle longer than --idle-in-transaction-timeout and was rolled back 28000 Invalid authorization A role that does not exist, cannot log in, or may not use the endpoint; a plain connection to a server that requires TLS 28P01 Invalid password Wrong password (also 401 over HTTP) 2BP01 Dependent objects exist Dropping a table that others reference, or an index the engine keeps 3B001 Invalid savepoint ROLLBACK TO or RELEASE of a savepoint that does not exist 40001 Serialization failure A transaction wrote a table that another transaction changed after it began 42501 Insufficient privilege A missing privilege, for a table, column, function, or the right to create objects. For a protected column the hint names the grant that would allow matching 42601 Syntax error A malformed statement, and a PROTECTED column with no match domain 42703, 42P01 Undefined column, undefined table A name that does not exist 42704 Undefined object A role, index, endpoint, match domain or type that does not exist, or an unknown dep. setting 42710, 42723, 42P07 Duplicate object A role, endpoint, function, table or index that already exists 42804 Datatype mismatch REVEAL of a column that is not protected; a protected column that is not TEXT 42883 Undefined function A function that does not exist, or REVEAL with the wrong number of arguments 42P02 Undefined parameter A $n with no value 42P13 Invalid function definition A missing body, or a body whose columns do not match RETURNS TABLE 42P16 Invalid table definition A permanent table that references a temporary one 53200 Out of memory A query needs more than --memory-limit and cannot spill (a hash join) 53300 Too many connections More than --max-connections 55000 Object not in prerequisite state A function that uses a table dropped and created again 55006 Object in use The data directory is used by another DEP Engine; a role that cannot be dropped; the admin role must stay a superuser 55P03 Lock not available The write lock was not free within --lock-timeout 58030 I/O error A data file, key file or commit failure; a missing or invalid key file XX000 Internal error An error from DataFusion that DEP does not classify, or an internal inconsistency XX001 Data corrupted A stored row cannot be decoded, or a protected value cannot be decrypted with the current key DEP notes A DEP note is a sentence that says which DEP rule applied to a statement. Plain SQL produces none, so a note is a signal that DEP did something. Notes never contain a protected value. How a client receives them: Client How ------ DEP CLI, Hoopeo Studio Printed as DEP: ... lines before the result (DEP CLI: \notes off hides them) PostgreSQL drivers, psql NOTICE messages whose text starts with DEP: HTTP API The notes array of each result Any client SHOW DEP NOTES returns the notes of the last statement In the texts below, {x} stands for a name filled in by the engine: {col} is table.column, {domain} a match domain, {fn} a function. Reads Note When ------ PROTECTED column {col} is matched by equality through the blind index of MATCH DOMAIN {domain}. A protected column is compared with a value (matching): =, OR, CASE, NOT (col = v); also in UPDATE and DELETE PROTECTED column {col} is matched against a list of values through the blind index of MATCH DOMAIN {domain}. IN or NOT IN with a list Join of PROTECTED columns {col} and {col} (MATCH DOMAIN {domain}) is anchored to a single protected value. A join between two protected columns that the query anchors to one value Output column {name} is PROTECTED column {col} (MATCH DOMAIN {domain}) and is returned as NULL. A protected column is selected Output column {name} is disclosed: {description} (DISCLOSES {domain}). A column produced by REVEAL in a disclosing function is returned {fn}() is declared DISCLOSES {domains}: the columns it declares are returned in plaintext. A function declared DISCLOSES is called {fn}() is declared LINKS {domains}: it may join protected values without an anchor. A function declared for linking (LINKS) is called Writes and schema Note When ------ PROTECTED column {table}.{column} (MATCH DOMAIN {domain}) is stored as a blind index and ciphertext. INSERT writes a protected column Index {name} keys PROTECTED column(s) {columns} by their blind index entries: it answers equality only, and holds no plaintext. CREATE INDEX on a protected column Index {name} already exists; nothing was done. CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS finds the name taken {table} is a TEMPORARY table: it is kept in memory only, and is gone when the server stops. CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE {index}: {n} duplicate key(s); uniqueness is still not enforced. REINDEX of a unique key that still has duplicates {index}: no duplicate keys; uniqueness is enforced again. REINDEX after the duplicates were removed The master key was replaced: {n} protected values were indexed and encrypted again with the new key, and the indexes were rebuilt. The old key no longer opens this data. ALTER SYSTEM ROTATE MASTER KEY Transactions Note When ------ There is already a transaction in progress. BEGIN inside a transaction There is no transaction in progress. COMMIT or ROLLBACK outside one The transaction had failed, so it was rolled back. COMMIT of an aborted transaction Examples text reception_app@operational=> SELECT full_name, national_id FROM patients WHERE national_id IN ('123456782', '234567893'); DEP: PROTECTED column patients.national_id is matched against a list of values through the blind index of MATCH DOMAIN person_id. DEP: Output column national_id is PROTECTED column patients.national_id (MATCH DOMAIN person_id) and is returned as NULL. full_name national_id ------------+------------- Dana Cohen NULL Yossi Levi NULL (2 rows) reception_app@operational=> SHOW DEP NOTES; DEP: PROTECTED column patients.national_id is matched against a list of values through the blind index of MATCH DOMAIN person_id. DEP: Output column national_id is PROTECTED column patients.national_id (MATCH DOMAIN person_id) and is returned as NULL. note ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ PROTECTED column patients.national_id is matched against a list of values through the blind index of MATCH DOMAIN person_id. Output column national_id is PROTECTED column patients.national_id (MATCH DOMAIN person_id) and is returned as NULL.
