(2 rows) text doctors_app@operational=> SELECT p.full_name, m.diagnosis FROM patients AS p JOIN medical_records AS m ON m.patient_national_id = p.national_id WHERE p.national_id = '123456782'; DEP: PROTECTED column patients.national_id is matched by equality through the blind index of MATCH DOMAIN person_id. DEP: Join of PROTECTED columns medical_records.patient_national_id and patients.national_id (MATCH DOMAIN person_id) is anchored to a single protected value. full_name diagnosis ------------+------------------ Dana Cohen Asthma Dana Cohen Seasonal allergy (2 rows) text admin@operational=> CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE scratch (id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, token TEXT PROTECTED MATCH DOMAIN scratch_token); DEP: scratch is a TEMPORARY table: it is kept in memory only, and is gone when the server stops. CREATE TABLE admin@operational=> CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS scratch_token_idx ON scratch (token); DEP: Index scratch_token_idx already exists; nothing was done. CREATE INDEX admin@operational=> BEGIN; BEGIN admin@operational=> BEGIN; DEP: There is already a transaction in progress. BEGIN admin@operational=> COMMIT; COMMIT admin@operational=> COMMIT; DEP: There is no transaction in progress. COMMIT text admin@operational=> BEGIN; BEGIN admin@operational=> INSERT INTO patients (patient_id, national_id) VALUES (1, '999999990'); ERROR: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "patients_pkey": Key (patient_id)=(1) already exists. SQLSTATE: 23505 admin@operational=!> COMMIT; DEP: The transaction had failed, so it was rolled back. ROLLBACK

title: SHOW commands
text: SHOW statements describe the catalog, the privileges and the state of the connection. They are ordinary statements: they work in DEP CLI, in psql and from any driver, and they return rows. DEP CLI's meta-commands run them (\dt runs SHOW TABLES). Statement Needs Returns --------- SHOW TABLES One row per table SHOW COLUMNS FROM t One row per column SHOW INDEXES [FROM t] One row per index SHOW FUNCTIONS One row per declared function SHOW ROLES One row per role SHOW GRANTS One row per grant SHOW ENDPOINTS One row per endpoint SHOW PRIVACY MATRIX One row per protected column and role SHOW STORAGE t [n] superuser The first n rows of t as stored SHOW AUDIT [n] superuser The latest n audit records SHOW DEP NOTES The DEP notes of the last statement SHOW dep.path The access path of the connection SHOW ROLE, SHOW CURRENT_USER The current role SHOW SESSION AUTHORIZATION The role the connection logged in as SHOW TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL repeatable read Each statement below was run against the demo clinic as admin. SHOW TABLES Columns: table, protected_columns, rows, temporary. text admin@operational=> SHOW TABLES; table protected_columns rows temporary -----------------+---------------------+------+----------- appointments 10 medical_records patient_national_id 6 patients national_id, phone 6 (3 rows) SHOW COLUMNS FROM t Columns: column, type, match_domain (NULL for an ordinary column), primary_key, references, not_null, unique. text admin@operational=> SHOW COLUMNS FROM medical_records; column type match_domain primary_key references not_null unique ---------------------+--------+--------------+-------------+------------------------+----------+-------- record_id BIGINT NULL yes NULL yes yes patient_national_id TEXT person_id patients (national_id) diagnosis TEXT NULL NULL recorded_at DATE NULL NULL (4 rows) SHOW INDEXES [FROM t] Columns: table, index, columns, kind (primary key, unique or empty), enforced, made_by (engine or CREATE INDEX), keys (values, or blind index entries for a protected column). text admin@operational=> SHOW INDEXES FROM patients; table index columns kind enforced made_by keys ----------+--------------------------+-------------+-------------+----------+---------+--------------------- patients patients_pkey patient_id primary key yes engine values patients patients_national_id_key national_id unique yes engine blind index entries patients patients_phone_idx phone engine blind index entries (3 rows) SHOW FUNCTIONS Columns: function (with its argument types), discloses, links, owner, masked_path (yes when it can be called on the masked read path), comment, executable_by, body. DEP CLI's \df shows the first six without comment. text admin@operational=> SHOW FUNCTIONS; function discloses links owner masked_path comment executable_by body -----------------------------+--------------+-----------+---------------+-------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------+---------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ appointment_reminders(DATE) phone_number privacy_admin no Purpose: SMS appointment reminders. Owner: operations. reminder_job SELECT REVEAL(p.phone), a.starts_at FROM appointments AS a JOIN patients AS p USING (patient_id) WHERE CAST(a.starts_at AS DATE) = day monthly_fund_report(DATE) person_id privacy_admin no Purpose: monthly visit report to health funds. Owner: billing. billing_job SELECT REVEAL(p.national_id), CAST(a.starts_at AS DATE), a.visit_type, p.health_fund FROM appointments AS a JOIN patients AS p USING (patient_id) WHERE date_trunc('month', a.starts_at) = date_trunc('month', CAST(report_month AS TIMESTAMP)) diagnoses_per_fund() person_id privacy_admin yes Purpose: diagnosis statistics per health fund. Owner: management. bi_dashboard SELECT p.health_fund, m.diagnosis, COUNT() FROM patients AS p JOIN medical_records AS m ON m.patient_national_id = p.national_id GROUP BY p.health_fund, m.diagnosis fund_claims_report(DATE) person_id person_id privacy_admin no Purpose: monthly diagnosis claims to health funds. Owner: billing. billing_job SELECT REVEAL(p.national_id), m.diagnosis, m.recorded_at FROM medical_records AS m JOIN patients AS p ON p.national_id = m.patient_national_id WHERE date_trunc('month', CAST(m.recorded_at AS TIMESTAMP)) = date_trunc('month', CAST(report_month AS TIMESTAMP)) (4 rows) SHOW ROLES Columns: role, superuser, login, endpoints (those it may connect through), match_limit. text admin@operational=> SHOW ROLES; role superuser login endpoints match_limit ------------------+-----------+-------+------------------------+------------- admin yes yes analytics, operational app_developer yes operational bi_dashboard yes analytics billing_job yes operational doctors_app yes operational privacy_admin yes operational reception_app yes operational reminder_job yes operational scheduling_agent yes analytics (9 rows) SHOW GRANTS Columns: grantee, privilege. The privilege reads like the statement that granted it: SELECT (national_id, full_name) ON patients, EXECUTE ON FUNCTION monthly_fund_report, DISCLOSE ON MATCH DOMAIN person_id, CONNECT ON ENDPOINT operational. text admin@operational=> SHOW GRANTS; grantee privilege ------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- bi_dashboard SELECT ON appointments bi_dashboard SELECT (health_fund, patient_id) ON patients doctors_app SELECT ON appointments doctors_app SELECT, INSERT ON medical_records doctors_app SELECT (full_name, health_fund, national_id, patient_id) ON patients privacy_admin SELECT ON appointments privacy_admin SELECT ON medical_records privacy_admin SELECT ON patients reception_app SELECT ON appointments reception_app SELECT (full_name, health_fund, national_id, patient_id), INSERT, UPDATE ON patients scheduling_agent SELECT ON appointments scheduling_agent SELECT (health_fund, patient_id) ON patients privacy_admin DISCLOSE, LINK ON MATCH DOMAIN person_id privacy_admin DISCLOSE ON MATCH DOMAIN phone_number reminder_job EXECUTE ON FUNCTION appointment_reminders bi_dashboard EXECUTE ON FUNCTION diagnoses_per_fund billing_job EXECUTE ON FUNCTION fund_claims_report billing_job EXECUTE ON FUNCTION monthly_fund_report bi_dashboard CONNECT ON ENDPOINT analytics scheduling_agent CONNECT ON ENDPOINT analytics app_developer CONNECT ON ENDPOINT operational billing_job CONNECT ON ENDPOINT operational doctors_app CONNECT ON ENDPOINT operational privacy_admin CONNECT ON ENDPOINT operational reception_app CONNECT ON ENDPOINT operational reminder_job CONNECT ON ENDPOINT operational (26 rows) SHOW ENDPOINTS Columns: endpoint, path. text admin@operational=> SHOW ENDPOINTS; endpoint path -------------+------------- analytics MASKED_READ operational OPERATIONAL (2 rows) SHOW PRIVACY MATRIX One row for each protected column and each role. Columns: match_domain, column, role, paths (the endpoints it may use, with their paths), may_match (whether it may match on the column), discloses_via and links_via (the declared functions it may execute for that domain). It is computed from the grants and the declared functions, so it always agrees with what the engine enforces. The full matrix of the clinic has 27 rows; this is one table with one protected column: text admin@operational=> CREATE TABLE accounts (id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT PROTECTED MATCH DOMAIN email, name TEXT); CREATE TABLE admin@operational=> CREATE ROLE support LOGIN PASSWORD 'x'; CREATE ROLE admin@operational=> CREATE ROLE marketing LOGIN PASSWORD 'x'; CREATE ROLE admin@operational=> GRANT CONNECT ON ENDPOINT operational TO support; GRANT admin@operational=> GRANT CONNECT ON ENDPOINT analytics TO marketing; GRANT admin@operational=> GRANT SELECT (id, email, name) ON accounts TO support; GRANT admin@operational=> GRANT SELECT (id, name) ON accounts TO marketing; GRANT admin@operational=> SHOW PRIVACY MATRIX; match_domain column role paths may_match discloses_via links_via --------------+----------------+-----------+----------------------------------------------------+-----------+---------------+----------- email accounts.email admin analytics (MASKED_READ), operational (OPERATIONAL) yes email accounts.email marketing analytics (MASKED_READ) no email accounts.email support operational (OPERATIONAL) yes (3 rows) SHOW STORAGE t [n] The rows of t as the server stores them (a superuser only). A protected column appears as two columns: the blind index entry (ie1:...) and the ciphertext (col__ct, ct1:...). No plaintext is shown. text admin@operational=> CREATE TABLE secrets (id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, token TEXT PROTECTED MATCH DOMAIN token_domain); CREATE TABLE admin@operational=> INSERT INTO secrets VALUES (1, 'my-secret-token'), (2, 'another-token'); DEP: PROTECTED column secrets.token (MATCH DOMAIN token_domain) is stored as a blind index and ciphertext. INSERT 0 2 admin@operational=> SHOW STORAGE secrets 1; id token token__ct ----+--------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 1 ie1:a3f8833a9b1d6c1c8abc7d53381d77cf ct1:DlCrLM2SQ4X64ppl+shah5u5t4W3WRJ7QaZf6I8i4Va9WkQ6HnJltaulcCC67snctn2/F8MXSw== (1 row) SHOW AUDIT [n] Columns: seq, at (UTC), session_user, role, endpoint, path, kind, object, domain, count, detail. Newest first. See the administration guide for the kinds. text reception_app@operational=> SELECT full_name FROM patients WHERE national_id = '123456782'; DEP: PROTECTED column patients.national_id is matched by equality through the blind index of MATCH DOMAIN person_id. full_name ------------ Dana Cohen (1 row) reception_app@operational=> SELECT full_name FROM patients WHERE national_id LIKE '1%'; ERROR: LIKE is not supported for PROTECTED values (patients.national_id). HINT: PROTECTED values support only full-value equality matching. To release a value, use a disclosing function. SQLSTATE: ZD101 (DEP_PROTECTED_OPERATION) reception_app@operational=> \c operational admin You are now connected as "admin" through endpoint "operational" (OPERATIONAL). admin@operational=> SHOW AUDIT 2; seq at session_user role endpoint path kind object domain count detail -----+--------------------------+---------------+---------------+-------------+-------------+--------+----------------------+-----------+-------+------------------------- 2 2026-10-23T12:27:14.476Z reception_app reception_app operational OPERATIONAL denied SELECT NULL NULL DEP_PROTECTED_OPERATION 1 2026-10-23T12:27:14.476Z reception_app reception_app operational OPERATIONAL match patients.national_id person_id 1 NULL (2 rows) Other settings text admin@operational=> SHOW dep.path; dep.path ------------- OPERATIONAL (1 row) admin@operational=> SHOW ROLE; role ------- admin (1 row) admin@operational=> SET ROLE reception_app; SET reception_app@operational=> SHOW ROLE; role --------------- reception_app (1 row) reception_app@operational=> SHOW SESSION AUTHORIZATION; session authorization ----------------------- admin (1 row) reception_app@operational=> RESET ROLE; SET admin@operational=> SHOW TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL; transaction_isolation ----------------------- repeatable read (1 row) SET dep.path is always refused (ZD106): the access path is fixed at login. Any other SET that is not a dep. setting is accepted and ignored, so that drivers can send their usual settings. SET ROLE is the exception, and works as described in the DEP SQL guide.

title: Server options
text: dep-engine is the DEP Engine server. Every option can be given on the command line or in an environment variable, which is how the Linux service, the macOS launch agent and the Docker image configure it. A command-line option overrides the environment. dep-engine --help prints the same list. sh dep-engine --help 2>&1 text usage: dep-engine [--listen 127.0.0.1:5433] [--data-dir DIR] [--key-file FILE] [--init FILE]... [--admin-password PASSWORD] [--tls-cert FILE --tls-key FILE --tls-self-signed [--tls-host NAME]...] [--tls-required] [--http-listen 127.0.0.1:8433] [--match-limit 1000/minute] [--lock-timeout 30] [--memory-limit 4GB] [--cache-size 1GB] [--idle-in-transaction-timeout 300] [--max-connections 200] --data-dir keep the state in DIR (created if new); without it the server keeps everything in memory --key-file where the master key is kept (default DIR/master.key); keep it apart from the data --init a DEP SQL script run as admin, only when the database is new --admin-password sets the admin password; for a new database without one, a random password is printed --init-admin-password-file for a new database only: the admin password is read from FILE --tls-cert, --tls-key a PEM certificate chain and private key: clients may then connect with TLS --tls-self-signed create a self-signed certificate (DIR/tls/server.crt) for localhost and each --tls-host --tls-required refuse connections without TLS --http-listen also serve the HTTP API (HTTPS with TLS): /v1/query, /v1/health, /metrics --match-limit default limit on protected matches for roles that are not superusers, e.g. 1000/minute --lock-timeout seconds a writer waits for the write lock (default 30) --memory-limit memory for running queries; beyond it they spill to encrypted files (default: 1/4 of RAM) --cache-size page cache of the data file (default: 1/8 of RAM, at most 4GB) --idle-in-transaction-timeout seconds before a transaction left idle is rolled back (default 300; 0: never) --max-connections client connections served at once (default 200; 0: no limit) Options Option Environment variable Default Meaning ------------ --listen ADDR DEP_LISTEN 127.0.0.1:5433 Address of the PostgreSQL wire protocol. Use 0.0.0.0:5433 to accept connections from the network, with TLS --data-dir DIR DEP_DATA_DIR none Keep the database in DIR (created if new). Without it everything is in memory and is lost when the server stops --key-file FILE DEP_KEY_FILE DIR/master.key Where the master key is kept. Keep it apart from the data --init FILE DEP_INIT none A DEP SQL script run as admin, only when the database is new. Repeat the option for several scripts; in DEP_INIT, separate them with colons --admin-password PW DEP_ADMIN_PASSWORD random, for a new database Sets the admin password at every start. For a new database without one, a random password is printed --init-admin-password-file FILE DEP_INIT_ADMIN_PASSWORD_FILE none The admin password of a new database, read from FILE --tls-cert FILE, --tls-key FILE DEP_TLS_CERT, DEP_TLS_KEY none A PEM certificate chain and private key. Clients may then connect with TLS --tls-self-signed DEP_TLS_SELF_SIGNED (1, 0, false) off Create a self-signed certificate in DIR/tls (in ./tls without --data-dir), valid for localhost and each --tls-host --tls-host NAME DEP_TLS_HOSTS (comma-separated) none A host name for the self-signed certificate. Repeat the option for several --tls-required DEP_TLS_REQUIRED (1, 0, false) off Refuse connections without TLS --http-listen ADDR DEP_HTTP_LISTEN off Also serve the HTTP API, over HTTPS when TLS is on --match-limit N/UNIT DEP_MATCH_LIMIT none Default limit on protected matches for roles that are not superusers. Units: second, minute, hour, day. For example 1000/minute --lock-timeout SECONDS DEP_LOCK_TIMEOUT 30 How long a writer waits for the write lock before 55P03 --memory-limit SIZE DEP_MEMORY_LIMIT a quarter of RAM Memory for running queries. Beyond it they spill to encrypted files --cache-size SIZE DEP_CACHE_SIZE an eighth of RAM, at most 4 GB Page cache of the data file --idle-in-transaction-timeout SECONDS DEP_IDLE_IN_TRANSACTION_TIMEOUT 300 Seconds before a transaction left idle is rolled back. 0: never --max-connections N DEP_MAX_CONNECTIONS 200 Client connections served at once. 0: no limit A size is a number with an optional unit: 1048576, 512MB, 4GB, 2GiB. A malformed value stops the server with a message. In a container, the default memory and cache sizes follow the container's memory limit, not the host's. Behavior to know - --init runs only when the database is new. A server with a data directory runs the scripts the first time and skips them when it starts again on the same directory. A server with no --data-dir is new at every start, so it always runs them. - --admin-password is applied at every start, so it can also reset a forgotten password. - A data directory is locked: a second server on the same directory stops with 55006. - The server prints its settings and how to connect when it starts; see the getting started guide. Ports Port Used for ------ 5433 The PostgreSQL wire protocol (--listen) 8433 The HTTP API (--http-listen; the examples use this number, there is no default) DEP CLI dep-cli takes its own options: see the DEP CLI reference.

title: HTTP API
DEP CLI
text:
dep-cli is the command-line shell of Project Hoopeo, in the style of psql. It has DEP Engine built in, so it can open a local database directly, and it can also connect to a DEP Engine server over the PostgreSQL wire protocol. It prints the DEP notes of each statement. sh dep-cli --help 2>&1 text usage: dep-cli [-h HOST [-p PORT]] [-U ROLE] [-d ENDPOINT] [--data-dir DIR --memory] [--key-file FILE] [--init FILE]... [-c SQL] [-f FILE] [--sslmode disablerequireverify-full] [--sslrootcert CA.pem] without -h: a local database in --data-dir (default: ~/Library/Application Support/Project Hoopeo/data), or in memory with --memory with -h: a DEP Engine server, over the PostgreSQL wire protocol (password from DEP_PASSWORD, PGPASSWORD, or a prompt) Options Option Meaning ------ -h, --host HOST Connect to a DEP Engine server on HOST. Without it the database is local -p, --port PORT The server's port (default 5433) -U, --user ROLE The role (default admin) -d, --endpoint NAME (also -e) The endpoint, which fixes the access path (default operational) --data-dir DIR A local database in DIR (default: ~/Library/Application Support/Project Hoopeo/data on macOS, ~/.local/share/project-hoopeo/data on Linux) --memory A local database in memory, lost when the shell exits --key-file FILE The master key of a local database --init FILE A DEP SQL script, run as admin when a local database is new. Repeat the option for several. If the database already exists the shell says that --init was not run -c SQL Run the SQL (or meta-commands) and exit -f FILE Run a script and exit, printing each statement before its result --sslmode MODE disable (default), require or verify-full; also PGSSLMODE --sslrootcert FILE The CA certificate for verify-full; also PGSSLROOTCERT A local shell logs in without a password, like a local trusted connection in PostgreSQL: whoever can read the data directory and the key already holds the data. A remote connection always asks for one: the password comes from DEP_PASSWORD, PGPASSWORD, or a prompt. When standard input is not a terminal, the shell runs it as a script. History is kept in dep-cli-history.txt, next to the default data directory. The prompt The prompt names the role and the endpoint: reception_app@operational=>. Inside a transaction it is =>, and after an error that needs ROLLBACK it is =!>. A statement that continues on another line shows ->. Statements end with a semicolon. DEP CLI: a transaction with a savepoint, and the prompts of an open and a failed transaction Meta-commands A meta-command starts with a backslash, on a line of its own. Command Meaning ------ \c ENDPOINT [ROLE] (also \connect) Open a new connection through ENDPOINT, as ROLE (default: the current one). A remote shell asks for the password \conninfo Where you are connected, as whom, and on which access path \dt List tables (SHOW TABLES) \d TABLE Describe a table (SHOW COLUMNS FROM TABLE) \di [TABLE] List indexes (SHOW INDEXES) \df List declared functions \du List roles and the endpoints they may use \dp List privileges (SHOW GRANTS) \storage TABLE Show a table as the server stores it (superusers; SHOW STORAGE) \matrix Show the privacy matrix (SHOW PRIVACY MATRIX) \audit [N] Show the latest N audit records, 50 by default (superusers) 
otes [on\off] Print the DEP notes after each statement. On by default; 
otes alone turns them on \i FILE Run a script, printing each statement before its result \echo TEXT Print TEXT \q Quit \?, \h Help text reception_app@operational=> \conninfo Role "reception_app", endpoint "operational", access path OPERATIONAL, server local (in memory). reception_app@operational=> \d appointments column type match_domain primary_key references not_null unique ----------------+-----------+--------------+-------------+-----------------------+----------+-------- appointment_id BIGINT NULL yes NULL yes yes patient_id BIGINT NULL patients (patient_id) starts_at TIMESTAMP NULL NULL visit_type TEXT NULL NULL (4 rows) reception_app@operational=> 
otes off DEP notes are off. reception_app@operational=> SELECT full_name FROM patients WHERE national_id = '123456782'; full_name ------------ Dana Cohen (1 row) reception_app@operational=> 
otes on DEP notes are on. Done. reception_app@operational=> \c analytics bi_dashboard You are now connected as "bi_dashboard" through endpoint "analytics" (MASKED_READ). bi_dashboard@analytics=> \conninfo Role "bi_dashboard", endpoint "analytics", access path MASKED_READ, server local (in memory). Scripts -f FILE and \i FILE run a file that mixes SQL and meta-commands, which is how the guided tour works: \c operational reception_app switches role in the middle of a script. The tour is in the public repository, run from its folder: sh dep-cli --memory --init examples/clinic.sql -f examples/tour/all.sql -c takes a statement too: sh dep-cli --memory --init examples/clinic.sql -U doctors_app -c "SELECT p.full_name, m.diagnosis FROM patients AS p JOIN medical_records AS m ON m.patient_national_id = p.national_id WHERE p.national_id = '123456782';" text DEP: PROTECTED column patients.national_id is matched by equality through the blind index of MATCH DOMAIN person_id. DEP: Join of PROTECTED columns medical_records.patient_national_id and patients.national_id (MATCH DOMAIN person_id) is anchored to a single protected value. full_name diagnosis ------------+------------------ Dana Cohen Asthma Dana Cohen Seasonal allergy (2 rows) Connecting to a server sh export DEP_PASSWORD=demo dep-cli -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5433 -U reception_app -d operational -c "\conninfo" echo "SELECT count() AS patients FROM patients;" dep-cli -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5433 -U doctors_app -d operational text Role "reception_app", endpoint "operational", access path OPERATIONAL, server 127.0.0.1:5433. patients ---------- 6 (1 row)

title: DEP: Database-Enforced Privacy
text: > Design and future work. This document contains proposals and historical planning assumptions. For available software and current limitations, use Run the server. It is further reading for Inside the engine. Roadmap and Release > Design document — future and historical planning. This is not the feature list of the current binary. See Compatibility & limitations for DEP Engine 0.5.2 and the changelog for shipped releases. One possible path from idea to implementation Reuven Mandelovich > Status: v1.0 · October 2026 · Licensed under CC BY 4.0 > DEP is presented as an idea, and this document is not a commitment to build it. It records one way DEP could be built and released, for anyone, including the author, who decides to. Where it says "will", read "would". About this document. The companion document, the DEP design proposal, defines what DEP is, how it is written, and how it works. This document sketches how DEP could be built and released. Two appendices complete the picture: how the design maps onto Apache DataFusion and PostgreSQL (Appendix A), and how DEP relates to existing products and research (Appendix B). What actually ships will be recorded in a separate, living document (chapter 9). --- Contents 1. Strategy: one engine end to end, then a second 2. Project components 3. Milestones 4. Distribution 5. Before publishing: ownership, licensing, and naming 6. Publishing plan 7. Open questions 8. Publication text 9. After the release: what shipped Appendices - Appendix A: Mapping the design to real engines - Appendix B: How DEP relates to existing approaches - References --- 1. Strategy: one engine end to end, then a second Two full implementations of a database privacy model are two large projects. DEP therefore commits to one engine first, end to end, and treats the second as a later, conditional track. Track A: The reference server on Apache DataFusion. A DEP server built on DataFusion, wrapped in a server process that speaks the PostgreSQL wire protocol and listens on one endpoint per access path. It accepts the full syntax of the design proposal from day one, because in DataFusion the parser and the logical plan are under the project's control. Its job is to prove one complete path: declaring protected fields, anchored matching, matching rejected on the masked path, linkage and disclosure through declared functions, and no leakage through output or errors. Track B: PostgreSQL, later and conditional. PostgreSQL is reliable, familiar, and already trusted, and it remains the intended foundation for a production DEP Server. Track B begins only after Track A is complete and published, and it begins with a short gap analysis, not an implementation. Whether it proceeds, and how far, depends on what that analysis finds. Why DataFusion first - Control. In PostgreSQL, DEP's rules are inserted into an engine through hooks, and most of the effort goes into making sure no path was missed. In DataFusion, the rules for PROTECTED, REVEAL, anchoring, linking regions, and disclosed values are part of the logical plan from the first line of code. - Syntax. A PostgreSQL extension cannot add grammar. DataFusion's parser can be extended, so the reference server is the only place where the planned syntax can exist from the start. - Speed to a convincing demonstration. A working server that rejects attacks in front of the audience is more persuasive than any document. What the reference server proves, and what it does not It proves that the model is coherent and usable (the rules can be stated precisely, the syntax is natural, the errors make sense), and that the trust boundary holds: a client connected on the masked path cannot reach identifiers, because it holds nothing but a SQL connection. It does not prove that the rules can be enforced inside a production database without bypasses. Several leakage channels of a real database (server logs, persistent statistics, bulk export, backup and restore) simply do not exist in it. That claim requires PostgreSQL. Every public statement about the reference server says so plainly: > A reference implementation that proves the model and the trust boundary, not a production database. The PostgreSQL question Anyone evaluating DEP seriously (a database vendor, a cloud provider running managed PostgreSQL, a security team) will ask whether it fits an engine they already run. The answer at first release is honest and specific: the design maps onto PostgreSQL's extension mechanisms as described in Appendix A.2, and the gap analysis (Milestone 5) will establish where engine patches are required. Promising more than that before Track A is complete would split the project in two. --- 2. Project components Name Category Role --- --- --- Design proposal Document The DEP design proposal: what DEP is, why, and how it works. Explanatory, not normative. Normative contract Specification A separate, short document derived from the design proposal: exactly what is accepted, what is returned, and which error is raised. Versioned independently (contract 0.1). dep-conformance Engine-independent test suite Statements, roles, paths, and expected results or errors, derived from the normative contract. Any implementation can run it. dep-core Rust library The rules, the matching index, anchoring analysis, declared-function tracking, the output boundary, and the errors. Knows nothing about networking. dep-engine Server process on DataFusion Endpoints over the PostgreSQL protocol, authentication, roles, column and function privileges, the audit log, rate limits, and the catalog. The reference server. Contract explorer Optional interactive web page A small in-browser simulator for showing the rules side by side. Offers no protection (4.1). dep extension PostgreSQL extension (pgrx) Track B: implements the contract inside PostgreSQL. DEP Server Server distribution Track B: PostgreSQL, the extension, configuration, and any required patches, packaged for deployment. Client drivers Standard PostgreSQL drivers No custom SDK is required. A driver is never the enforcement boundary. DEP is not a new storage engine and not a new procedural language. --- 3. Milestones Milestone 0: Write the normative contract Derive a short, normative contract from the design proposal. It fixes the two access paths, the semantics of protected text, match domains, the rules for anchored and unanchored matching, the rules for DISCLOSES and LINKS, protected foreign keys, how column privileges govern matching, and the error codes. It must specify projection behavior, input normalization, NULL semantics, duplicate values, protected literals, and which predicates count as anchored. It must publish a supported-forms list: every SQL form the first version accepts on protected values. Everything else fails closed. Not every sentence of the design proposal becomes a rule. The contract contains only what an implementation must do and what a test can check. Deliverables: the normative contract, the supported-forms list, and the first version of dep-conformance, written in the final syntax. Exit criterion: every example in the design proposal that the contract covers has an expected result or a specific expected error, before any implementation begins. Milestone 1: Feasibility spike on DataFusion A short, time-boxed spike on the things most likely to go wrong: 1. The parser. A DEP dialect of sqlparser-rs that accepts the new constructs (PROTECTED MATCH DOMAIN, the DISCLOSES and LINKS function attributes, GRANT DISCLOSE, GRANT LINK, and CREATE ENDPOINT) while every other statement parses exactly as before. 2. A declared function. A LANGUAGE sql function returning a table, expanded into the calling plan, with the REVEAL marker and the linking region surviving expansion and optimization. 3. Anchoring analysis. Distinguishing an anchored join from an unanchored one on the resolved plan, including IN lists and subqueries. 4. An update by protected value. UPDATE ... WHERE national_id = $1 through a custom table provider with hidden internal columns. Deliverables: minimal working prototypes and a short written report. Exit criterion: each item works, or has a documented workaround (a parser patch, a pre-parsing step, a different expansion strategy). If one cannot be solved, the plan is revised before Milestone 2. Milestone 2: The reference server Build dep-core and dep-engine: protected columns and match domains, keyed-index matching, protected literals, two endpoints over pgwire, authentication with a fixed path per session, roles with column privileges, GRANT EXECUTE, GRANT DISCLOSE, and GRANT LINK, declared functions created without public execution, uniqueness and foreign keys on protected columns, anchoring analysis, disclosure and linkage tracking, the audit log for every protected match, per-identity rate limits, the output boundary, every error in the design proposal, and scrubbing of the engine's own errors. Data lives in memory, loaded at startup or through INSERT. Keys are loaded from a server-side location the client cannot reach. Out of scope: durable storage, transactions, full at-rest encryption, partial disclosure, deferred constraints, and every SQL form not on the supported-forms list. Deliverables: the reference server, the clinic demonstration from the design proposal, and a passing conformance suite. Exit criterion: - the same anchored lookup succeeds on the operational endpoint and fails with DEP_ENDPOINT_OPERATION on the masked endpoint; - an anchored join on protected columns succeeds on the operational path, and the same join without the anchor fails with DEP_UNANCHORED_MATCH; - diagnoses_per_fund returns counts on the masked path; - monthly_fund_report works, while joining its output to another table on the disclosed column fails with DEP_DISCLOSED_VALUE_USE; - a role without privilege on phone cannot match on it; - a table whose foreign key references a protected column without being PROTECTED is rejected with DEP_REFERENCE_MISMATCH, and an insert referencing a missing ID number fails without revealing the value and is counted as a protected lookup; - every error in the design proposal is reproduced by at least one test; - canary tests pass: synthetic protected values are planted in the data and also sent in queries, both as parameters and as literals, and an automated check confirms they never appear in any result, error, notice, audit record, query statistic, or server log, except through declared disclosures. Milestone 3: First public release (reference server v0.1) Release only after the ownership and licensing decisions in chapter 5 are made. Deliverables: the public repository, a container image, the documentation site, the demonstration script and a short screen recording, and the release notes with the list of known limitations. Exit criterion: a newcomer can run the demonstration in a few minutes with only a container runtime and psql, and see both the successful operational workflow and the rejected attacks. Milestone 4: Attack the reference server Test casts, aliases, function wrappers, views, CTEs, function inlining, subqueries that try to smuggle unanchored matching, prepared statements, role changes, connection reuse, nested results, binary output, error messages, EXPLAIN, and engine error paths. Add adversarial tests and fuzzing. Invite outside review through SECURITY.md. Deliverables: an adversarial test suite and an updated limitations document. Exit criterion: no known bypass remains within the supported-forms list, and unsupported cases reliably fail closed. Passing the suite is evidence, not proof of complete security. This completes Track A. Milestone 5: PostgreSQL gap analysis (Track B begins) A short, written analysis, with a minimal spike only where a question cannot be answered on paper, of how each rule in the normative contract maps onto one supported PostgreSQL major version, using the integration points in Appendix A.2. The hardest rules to check are the output boundary in both result formats, anchoring analysis on the analyzed query tree, the immutable path, and rejection of REVEAL outside declared functions. Exit criterion: for every rule, the analysis states whether an extension can enforce it or an engine patch is required. A decision follows: proceed with Track B, narrow it, or stop at the reference server. Milestone 6: The contract on PostgreSQL Implement the contract in a PostgreSQL extension, using an interim syntax (a protected type such as dep.protected_text and administrative functions), because an extension cannot add grammar. Add a thin translation layer so that dep-conformance can run against the extension. Exit criterion: the conformance results on PostgreSQL match those of the reference server, including the canary tests. Milestone 7: Attack the boundary on PostgreSQL Everything in Milestone 4, plus the channels a production database adds: RETURNING, COPY, server logs, optimizer statistics, query statistics, restores with function-body validation disabled, encrypted storage, backup recovery, restarts, and key-version transitions. Exit criterion: no known bypass remains within the supported-forms list. Decision point: Extension or fork If the missing checks require a small set of engine changes, maintain them as a documented patch set. If protection depends on pervasive changes, reassess the supported SQL subset and the implementation strategy before expanding the product. This decision determines the long-term maintenance cost of DEP Server. Milestone 8: Package DEP Server Package PostgreSQL, the mandatory extension, configuration, and any required patches as a reproducible server image. A missing or disabled DEP component must cause a startup failure. Exit criterion: a new developer can start the server and reproduce the documented behavior with a standard PostgreSQL driver and no custom SDK. Milestone 9: Measure usefulness and cost Benchmark lookup latency, join latency, throughput, storage, and index size against an equivalent plain PostgreSQL workload, on the same hardware, data, permissions, and query shapes. Performance targets are chosen before the evaluation, not after seeing the results. Exit criterion: reproducible results with stated limitations, an independent technical review, and one bounded pilot that genuinely benefits from the contract. Milestone 10: Native syntax on PostgreSQL Introduce DEP's syntax natively in PostgreSQL through engine patches, along with schema migration, introspection, backup behavior, and upgrade procedures. Exit criterion: native syntax and interim declarations produce equivalent behavior, and the conformance suite runs without its translation layer. Beyond the first release - Partial disclosure forms such as DISCLOSES person_id AS SUFFIX(4). - More protected types and operations, with a careful study of whether any comparison beyond equality can be offered without revealing too much. - Explicit linkage tokens, a separately designed capability for correlating results across queries. - A formal model of the rules, precise enough to reason about protection, not only test it. - A safe gateway for AI agents, exposing the database to agents exclusively through the masked path and approved linking functions. - Aggregation thresholds and differential privacy for linking functions called from the masked path, borrowing from data clean rooms (Appendix B.8). - A schema check for open paths: a tool that reads the foreign-key map and reports any path made only of ordinary keys between identities and sensitive data. - dep-core compiled to WebAssembly, so the contract explorer runs the real rules instead of a simulation. - Other engines implementing the contract and measured by dep-conformance. Immediate next actions 1. Decide on ownership and licensing (chapter 5). 2. Write the normative contract, the supported-forms list, and the first conformance tests. 3. Run the DataFusion feasibility spike. 4. Build the reference server until the conformance and canary tests pass. 5. Publish the first release with the clinic demonstration. --- 4. Distribution Package Form Audience Notes --- --- --- --- Reference server Container image Anyone who wants to try DEP and see it hold The first public artifact. Clients connect with psql or any PostgreSQL driver. dep-conformance Separate repository and Rust crate Implementers Lets any implementation prove it meets the contract. Contract explorer Web page Anyone, in thirty seconds Optional; labeled as a simulation. dep extension Built per PostgreSQL major version and platform; distributed through PGXN Teams running their own PostgreSQL Track B. Requires shared_preload_libraries, not only CREATE EXTENSION. DEP Server Container image Teams that want a ready configuration Track B. The convenient path for real use, and the only path if engine patches are required. A constraint to state openly: managed PostgreSQL services allow only the extensions their provider has approved. A compiled extension loaded at server start cannot be installed there unless a provider adopts it. In practice, DEP on PostgreSQL would first run only where teams operate PostgreSQL themselves. 4.1 The contract explorer > A first prototype exists: the DEP SQL Playground, a simulator built on sql.js that accepts DEP SQL, applies the rules of the design proposal, and shows the result an ordinary database would return for comparison. Unlike the explorer described below, it lets visitors create tables and declared functions. Like it, it is a simulation and protects nothing. A single web page in which a visitor writes a query and sees, side by side, what an ordinary database returns, what the DEP operational path returns, and what the DEP masked path returns, with a list of ready-made attempts: a lookup by ID, a CAST, an unanchored join, a join on a disclosed value. It is the fastest way to show the idea, and fits a launch post or a link sent to a reviewer. It can be built quickly with sql.js, SQLite compiled to WebAssembly, with a DEP rule layer written in JavaScript. That choice comes with constraints, which the explorer must respect: - It is a simulation, not a protection. Everything runs in the visitor's browser, so there is no trust boundary. Every page says so: a simulator. Everything runs in your browser; it illustrates the rules and protects nothing. - It is a third implementation of the rules, and could drift from the reference server. To keep it honest, the schema is fixed (the clinic), the visitor runs queries but does not create tables, declared functions are pre-defined, and the explorer passes the subset of dep-conformance it supports. - SQLite is not PostgreSQL. It lacks SQL-defined table functions, roles, and several types and functions used in the examples, so the explorer translates a curated set of queries rather than accepting arbitrary SQL. The long-term replacement is dep-core itself compiled to WebAssembly, so the explorer runs the same code as the server, still without a trust boundary, but no longer a separate implementation. DataFusion supports compiling to WebAssembly; bundle size needs to be evaluated. --- 5. Before publishing: ownership, licensing, and naming 5.1 Decide ownership first Publishing the design or the code under an open-source license gives the idea to the world. That is excellent for reputation and adoption, but afterwards there is little left to sell. If a patent or a company might ever be wanted, that decision must be made before the first public disclosure: in many jurisdictions, a public disclosure before filing harms the ability to obtain a patent, and publishing the design proposal counts as disclosure. If the project is carried out within the Technion (as a course, a final project, or with a faculty advisor) the institution's intellectual-property policy may give it rights in the work. This should be checked in advance, for example with the Technion's technology-transfer office. These are legal questions and should be confirmed with a qualified advisor. 5.2 Licensing Component License --- --- PostgreSQL PostgreSQL License (permissive, BSD/MIT-style) Apache DataFusion Apache License 2.0 pgrx MIT sql.js MIT All of them permit building on, modifying, and redistributing them, commercially as well. For DEP itself, Apache License 2.0 is recommended: it is compatible with all of them, and includes an explicit patent grant, which matters for a project that touches security and cryptography. "PostgreSQL" is a trademark; "based on PostgreSQL" is appropriate, but the product should not carry a name that sounds official. 5.3 Naming "DEP" is already a well-known security term: Data Execution Prevention in Windows. Searches for "DEP database security" will mostly find it, and some readers will misread the title. The concept can keep its name, but the repository, crates, and images need a distinctive identifier (the project is now named Project Hoopeo, with the identifier project-hoopeo), checked for availability on GitHub, crates.io, and container registries before the first release. Names are hard to change after publication. --- 6. Publishing plan 6.1 When DEP is published first as an idea: the design proposal, a short paper, and a post, in a public repository with a citable DOI. Publishing the idea does not depend on any implementation. A demonstration (the contract explorer, and later a reference server, if one is ever built) can follow and be added to the same repository. 6.2 Repository structure text project-hoopeo/ ├── README.md ├── LICENSE Apache-2.0 ├── NOTICE ├── SECURITY.md how to report a privacy bypass ├── CONTRIBUTING.md ├── CHANGELOG.md ├── docs/ │ ├── 01-dep-concept.md design proposal │ ├── 02-roadmap-and-release.md │ └── contract.md normative contract ├── crates/ │ ├── dep-core/ │ ├── dep-engine/ │ └── dep-conformance/ ├── explorer/ optional contract explorer ├── examples/ │ └── clinic/ schema, data, and the demonstration script └── Dockerfile SECURITY.md matters especially for a project whose central claim is protection. It gives anyone who finds a bypass a private way to report it, instead of a public issue. The people who find bypasses are exactly the audience the project wants. 6.3 The README Most visitors read only the README, so it must work in thirty seconds: 1. One sentence stating the promise: Protected values remain inside the database unless released through an explicitly declared disclosure. 2. A recording: the same query succeeding on one endpoint and failing on the other, and an unanchored join being refused. 3. Quick start: one container command and two psql commands. 4. What it proves and what it does not, honestly and briefly, with a clear label: reference implementation, not for production. Including: permitted matching can still reveal that a record exists. 5. Links to the design proposal, the contract, the explorer, and the conformance results. 6.4 Automation and versions - Continuous integration runs the unit tests, dep-conformance, and the canary tests on every change, and shows the result as a badge in the README. - Two version numbers: the contract version (contract 0.1) and the implementation version (dep-engine 0.1.0). The contract changes slowly, implementations quickly, and the separation allows other implementations of the same contract. - Crate names are reserved early, but crates are published only when their interfaces stabilize. - The documentation site is built from docs/ with mdBook and served from GitHub Pages. 6.5 Launch One concentrated launch day works better than a trickle: a post that explains the idea and links to the repository and the explorer, shared on Hacker News (Show HN), r/PostgreSQL, r/rust, the DataFusion community channels, LinkedIn, and a local PostgreSQL meetup if one is near. Be available that day to answer questions and criticism; the first hours shape much of the impression. After launch, label a few issues as good first issues and answer every report quickly. A responsive project attracts contributors; a silent one is forgotten. 6.6 Research and industry routes Large companies rarely accept unsolicited ideas, and many have explicit policies against it for legal reasons. The routes that work are public: - Open publication: the repository, a post, a talk at a PostgreSQL conference. Companies come to the project, not the other way round. - A demonstration paper: the main database conferences, SIGMOD and VLDB, have demonstration tracks that fit a project like this. A faculty advisor adds both guidance and credibility. - A portfolio: a project like this opens doors at database and privacy companies even if they never adopt it as is. In every route, what an organization is most likely to take is not the code but the contract: the rules, the error model, and the conformance suite, which it would then implement in its own engine. The documents deserve as much care as the code. --- 7. Open questions These decisions are left open for the normative contract, and are good topics for review. 1. Anchoring through another protected column. Does a join on national_id restricted by WHERE phone = $1 count as anchored? The proposal is yes. 2. Anchoring through an ordinary key. Does WHERE patient_id = 42 anchor a join on protected columns? The proposal is no, or at least that it counts against the rate limit. 3. Qualified access. Which tables should require every operational read or write to be anchored, and should that be the default for tables with protected columns? 4. Is NULL-ness protected? Knowing whether a person has an identifier on record is itself information. Should IS NULL and COUNT(national_id) be allowed, and on which path? 5. How is suppression signaled? Standard PostgreSQL result metadata has no field for "this value was hidden". Options include a catalog view, a companion function, or a protocol-level extension. 6. Normalization per match domain. Who defines normalization rules, and how are they versioned without breaking existing indexes? 7. Foreign-key checks and rate limits. Should a failed reference check count the same as a lookup, or more, given that it is a cheaper way to test identifiers? 8. Uniqueness and conflicts. How do UNIQUE constraints and ON CONFLICT behave on protected columns, and should the inference they allow be reduced? 9. Purpose as a clause. Is COMMENT ON FUNCTION enough, or should purpose become a first-class, machine-checked part of a declaration? 10. Nested declared functions. May one declared function call another, and how do disclosed columns and linking regions compose? 11. Rate-limit semantics. Per identity, per column, or per match domain, and how are anchored joins counted? 12. Naming of match domains. PostgreSQL already uses the word domain for CREATE DOMAIN. Should MATCH DOMAIN be renamed, for example to MATCH CLASS? 13. Interim syntax on PostgreSQL. How should a match domain be expressed in an extension that cannot add grammar? 14. Error-code class. The design proposal suggests the SQLSTATE class ZD. It must be confirmed against the classes PostgreSQL already uses. 15. Timing. Should a later version require constant-time matching, and at what cost? 16. Governance of the contract once other implementations exist. --- 8. Publication text One-sentence definition DEP is a database server in which PROTECTED is a built-in property of data: ordinary queries can match on protected values one at a time but never return them, whole datasets are linked through them only in declared LINKS functions, and they leave the database only through declared DISCLOSES functions. Short description DEP, Database-Enforced Privacy, is a proposed database server that separates four things ordinary databases fold into one privilege: matching a sensitive value, linking datasets through it, returning it, and disclosing it. A PROTECTED field supports lookups and joins anchored to a single value on an operational connection, while a masked read connection cannot match on it at all. Linking whole datasets and releasing values are allowed only in functions declared LINKS and DISCLOSES, the database's equivalent of Rust's unsafe, so every such place is explicit, reviewable, and listed in the catalog. Announcement We are introducing DEP, Database-Enforced Privacy: a database server that makes the permitted use of sensitive fields part of query execution. The idea starts with a practical distinction. A clinic's reception desk needs a patient's ID number to find her; her doctor needs it to see her diagnoses. That need does not mean either application must ever receive ID numbers back from the database, and it certainly does not mean either should be able to join every patient to every diagnosis in a single query. DEP proposes a PROTECTED declaration and two access paths. On the operational path, applications find, update, and connect records one protected value at a time, and every such match is recorded. On the masked read path (the natural home for analysts, BI tools, and AI agents) protected values cannot be matched at all. Ordinary queries on either path never return protected values. Linking whole datasets and releasing values are possible only in declared LINKS and DISCLOSES functions, the single places where those operations are legal. DEP is precise about its limits: permitted matching can still reveal that a record exists and associate it with the data returned. What it removes is the single query that exports a register or links two sensitive datasets wholesale. The first release is a reference server built on Apache DataFusion. It speaks the PostgreSQL protocol, so you can connect with psql, run the same query on both paths, and watch one succeed and the other refuse. It proves the model and the trust boundary; it is not a production database. We welcome technical discussion, criticism, and attempts to break it. --- 9. After the release: what shipped This document describes plans. What actually ships is recorded separately, in a living document maintained with each release, so that plans are never mistaken for results. It will contain: - Release notes for each version of each implementation. - Conformance results per engine and per contract version, including the canary tests. - The supported-forms list for each release. - Known limitations and open bypass reports, with their status. - Measurements, once they exist, with the scripts to reproduce them. - Security advisories, published through the process in SECURITY.md. --- Appendix A: Mapping the design to real engines The architecture in chapter 12 of the design proposal is engine-independent. This appendix considers the two engines on which it could be realized (chapter 1): how the design maps onto each, and what each lacks. A.1 The reference server on Apache DataFusion Apache DataFusion is an extensible query engine written in Rust: it parses SQL, plans, optimizes, and executes queries, and lets the embedding application control the logical plan. It is a library, not a database. A DEP reference server would wrap it in a server process that speaks the PostgreSQL wire protocol, using the Rust pgwire library, so that clients connect with psql or any standard PostgreSQL driver and the trust boundary of the design (12.1) is real. What maps naturally DEP component DataFusion mechanism --- --- Endpoints and paths One pgwire listener per endpoint; the session's path is fixed when the connection is accepted DEP analyzer and plan re-check Custom analyzer rules over the logical plan, and a final check after optimization Matching Predicates on protected columns rewritten to comparisons on internal index columns; joins become equi-joins on index entries Output boundary A final projection and a wrapper on the result stream, before encoding Parameters DataFusion's prepared statements with $1-style placeholders Errors with DETAIL, HINT, and SQLSTATE pgwire's PostgreSQL-format error responses What the reference server must build itself Gap Approach --- --- DEP's syntax A DEP dialect of the SQL parser DataFusion uses (sqlparser-rs), extending the PostgreSQL dialect with a small, fixed set of constructs: the PROTECTED MATCH DOMAIN column option, the DISCLOSES and LINKS function attributes, GRANT DISCLOSE and GRANT LINK, and CREATE ENDPOINT. REVEAL(x) and all queries parse unchanged. If the dialect mechanism cannot express a construct, a small parser patch or a pre-parsing step handles it. Users, roles, and privileges DataFusion has none. The server implements authentication, the mapping from identity to path and roles, column privileges (which decide who may match on which protected column), GRANT EXECUTE on declared functions without public execution, and GRANT DISCLOSE and GRANT LINK. Table-returning SQL functions Declared functions are stored and expanded into the calling plan, like parameterized views, with REVEAL markers and linking regions preserved (14.2). Hidden internal columns A custom table provider that exposes only the logical protected column. UPDATE and DELETE Implemented by the server's table provider where DataFusion's support is insufficient. Unique and foreign-key constraints DataFusion does not enforce them. The server's table provider enforces both on index entries, with each protected foreign-key check counted as a protected lookup. COMMENT ON and dep.declared_functions A virtual catalog table served by the DEP catalog. What does not exist, by design Transactions, durable storage, and crash recovery. The reference server loads data at startup or accepts it through INSERT, and loses it on restart. It also lacks several leakage channels of a real database (server logs, persistent statistics, bulk export) which is precisely why it proves the model and the trust boundary, but not resistance to every channel of a production engine. Engine-specific risks - EXPLAIN exists and can display constants and statistics, so it is rejected for statements involving protected values. - DataFusion's own error messages may quote literals or values, so every non-DEP error passes through the output boundary and is scrubbed or withheld. - Statistics such as column minimum and maximum must never be collected on internal protected columns. A.2 PostgreSQL PostgreSQL would be the natural foundation for a production DEP Server. The design maps onto its extension mechanisms as follows; whether they are sufficient is exactly what a gap analysis would have to establish (chapter 3). DEP component Candidate PostgreSQL mechanism --- --- Endpoints and paths ClientAuthentication_hook, storing an immutable per-backend path DEP analyzer post_parse_analyze_hook on the analyzed query tree Plan re-check planner_hook Output boundary ExecutorRun_hook, wrapping the destination receiver so values are replaced before text or binary encoding Declaration checker, COPY, SET, and other utility commands ProcessUtility_hook Log scrubbing emit_log_hook Protected representation and matching A user-defined type with input and output functions that never produce plaintext, plus an operator class for equality Protected foreign keys PostgreSQL's referential-integrity checks, running through the protected type's equality operator, with violation messages reduced to the constraint name Two constraints shape the PostgreSQL track: - An extension that uses these hooks must be loaded at server start, through shared_preload_libraries, not only with CREATE EXTENSION. Installing it requires control of the server's configuration. - An extension cannot add grammar. PostgreSQL's SQL grammar is compiled into the server. Until engine patches add native syntax, the PostgreSQL extension uses an interim form (a protected type such as dep.protected_text and administrative functions), while the reference server already accepts the full syntax of the design proposal. --- Appendix B: How DEP relates to existing approaches DEP is not built from new techniques. Using a column in a predicate without returning it, masking output, restricting joins, approving queries in advance, keyed equality indexes, and declaring privacy policy as code all exist today, in products and in research. This appendix describes what exists, what DEP borrows, and what it adds. It is written through one lens: Privacy as Code: where the privacy policy is written, where it is enforced, and what it actually controls. The descriptions of products below are based on their public documentation as of October 2026. B.1 Privacy as Code around the database The tools that use the name Privacy as Code work mostly around the database. - Fides (Ethyca) defines privacy policies in YAML over a shared taxonomy of data categories, data uses, and data subjects. Systems and datasets are annotated with the same taxonomy, and policies are evaluated in CI, so that a change that, for example, uses contact information for advertising is rejected before it ships. - Privado scans application code to discover which personal data is collected and where it flows (to third parties, APIs, and logs) and lets teams write policy guardrails over the results. - General policy-as-code engines, such as Open Policy Agent and Cedar, evaluate authorization rules written as code, and are called by applications or gateways. These tools make privacy policy reviewable and testable, and they are the direct inspiration for DEP's development method (chapter 10 of the design proposal). What they do not do is enforce anything at the moment a query runs. A query the scanner never saw, written by a new AI agent at three in the morning, is not covered. DEP takes the same idea (policy as reviewed, tested code) and moves its enforcement into the engine that executes the query. B.2 Output controls inside the database Several databases already separate using a column from returning it, at least for output: - Snowflake projection policies are schema-level objects that decide whether a column may appear in a query's final output. A constrained column can still be used in WHERE clauses and inner queries; projecting it either fails or, with ENFORCEMENT => 'NULLIFY', returns NULL. The constrained column also cannot be inserted into another table or passed to external functions. This is the closest existing mechanism to DEP's return decision. - Dynamic data masking in SQL Server, Oracle Data Redaction, and PostgreSQL Anonymizer replace values in the output while predicates run against the real values. Oracle's documentation states that the WHERE clause is never redacted. PostgreSQL Anonymizer declares its masking rules inside the database schema, with security labels, explicitly as an implementation of privacy by design. - Databricks Unity Catalog applies column masks and row filters, including policies driven by governed tags, so that classification drives enforcement. DEP adopts the core idea, and the suppression to NULL matches Snowflake's NULLIFY behavior. But these mechanisms are output controls, and their own documentation is candid about what that leaves open. Snowflake's documentation notes that a constrained column can still be used to target a specific individual with WHERE, that joins can expose values when the matching column in another table is unconstrained, and that error messages can contain a value. Masking leaves the real value available to predicates, which permits inference. None of them distinguishes looking up one record from linking two datasets, and none makes the places where values may leave into a reviewable inventory of code. B.3 Collaboration controls in data clean rooms Data clean rooms solve a neighboring problem: letting two organizations analyze their combined data without either seeing the other's rows. - Snowflake adds join policies, which can require that a table is always joined and restrict joins to allowed keys, and aggregation policies, which require every query to aggregate and drop groups below a minimum size. - BigQuery analysis rules, applied to views, enforce aggregation thresholds, differential-privacy budgets, join restrictions that limit which columns can be used in a join, and list-overlap queries. - AWS Clean Rooms attaches one analysis rule (aggregation, list, or custom) to each configured table, specifying join columns, columns that may not appear in output, minimum aggregation thresholds, and, for custom rules, analysis templates: pre-approved queries that are the only ones allowed to run. These systems are the strongest evidence that the problem DEP addresses is real and commercially important. They also contain ideas DEP shares: restricting how a sensitive column may be joined, preferring aggregates, and, in AWS's analysis templates, the principle that sensitive processing happens only in pre-approved queries, which is what DEP's declared functions are. The differences are in scope and in mechanism. Clean rooms are built for multi-party analytics in a data warehouse, not for the operational database that an application reads and writes every second. Their rules constrain which columns may be joined or how results must be aggregated; they do not distinguish an application finding one patient from the same application linking every patient. And their approved queries are governed as collaboration configuration, not type-checked against the provenance of each value. B.4 Cryptographic approaches - Client-side encryption (SQL Server Always Encrypted, MongoDB Queryable Encryption) protects data from an untrusted server or administrator. A client holding the keys receives plaintext. This is the opposite trust model to DEP, which protects data from clients and trusts the server; the two are complementary. - Encrypted query processing research, such as CryptDB, also protects data from the server. - Application-side blind indexes, as in the CipherSweet library, store a keyed hash next to each encrypted value so that applications can search by equality. DEP uses the same technique internally. The difference is where the key lives: with an application-side index, the application holds the key, can hash every possible value, and can enumerate them; in DEP, the key and the enforcement stay in the server. B.5 Research on policy enforcement in databases - Hippocratic databases (IBM Research, VLDB 2002, followed by Limiting Disclosure in Hippocratic Databases, VLDB 2004) proposed that databases take responsibility for privacy principles (purpose specification, consent, limited disclosure, limited retention) and enforce purpose-based disclosure inside the database. DEP's DISCLOSES functions, documented with a purpose, are a much narrower descendant of that vision. - Qapla (USENIX Security 2017) stores policies written in SQL in the database itself, and enforces them in a database adapter, so that policy compliance does not depend on application correctness. - Blockaid (OSDI 2022) sits between a web application and its database, verifies with an SMT solver that each query complies with the data-access policy, and blocks queries it cannot verify. - IFDB (EuroSys 2013) added decentralized information-flow labels to PostgreSQL, tracking how information moves between principals. This line of work established that policy can and should be enforced by the database rather than the application, and it is essential prior work to study. DEP applies a narrower, type-based idea to a specific practical problem, rather than general policy languages or information-flow labels. B.6 Side by side Use without returning One value vs. whole datasets Controls linkage Exits declared as code Enforced at query time, in the engine --- --- --- --- --- --- Fides, Privado, OPA, Cedar None No No Policies as code, outside the database No Snowflake projection policies Yes No No; joins can expose values No; role conditions Yes Dynamic masking, Oracle Data Redaction, PostgreSQL Anonymizer Partly; predicates see real values No No Rules declared in schema (Anonymizer) Yes Snowflake join and aggregation policies None No Partly: required joins, allowed keys, minimum groups No Yes BigQuery analysis rules None No Partly: join restrictions, thresholds, differential privacy No Yes, on views AWS Clean Rooms Partly: columns excluded from output No Yes, for collaborations Partly: analysis templates Yes Client-side encryption No; clients with keys see plaintext No No No Different trust model Hippocratic databases, Qapla, Blockaid, IFDB Varies No Varies Policies in the database or a proxy Yes DEP Yes Yes: anchoring Yes: LINKS Yes: DISCLOSES, LINKS, cataloged Yes The table simplifies. Each system does things DEP does not (differential privacy, multi-party collaboration, general policy languages) and its strengths should not be read as gaps. B.7 What DEP adds DEP's contribution is a combination, applied to the operational database that applications and AI agents query directly: 1. Protection as a property of the value, not of the output. A protected value cannot be cast, sliced, or passed to arbitrary functions anywhere in a query, not only in the final projection; protected literals in the query text are recognized and redacted; and protection is checked on referencing columns. 2. The distinction between one value and whole datasets. Anchored matching lets an application find, update, and connect the records of the value it was given, and nothing more. No existing mechanism we have found draws this line; projection policies explicitly permit targeted filtering and unrestricted joins. 3. Linkage and disclosure as declared, type-checked code. LINKS and DISCLOSES are function attributes whose bodies are analyzed when they are created, whose revealed values are tracked as terminal, and which cannot be executed by PUBLIC. This is closest to AWS's analysis templates, but expressed in the SQL of the database itself and checked by its type rules. 4. A complete inventory by construction. Because nothing else can reveal protected values or link datasets through them, dep.declared_functions lists every such place: an answer to "where can our ID numbers leave?" that no output-masking policy can give. 5. A development method in which the policy, the schema, and the tests are the same artifact. The privacy matrix becomes grants and declared functions, and its cells become conformance tests. This is the Privacy as Code idea of B.1, with the enforcement moved inside the engine. B.8 What DEP can borrow The existing systems also suggest improvements that are not yet part of DEP: - Aggregation thresholds from clean rooms and Snowflake aggregation policies could become a property of LINKS functions called from the masked path, so that statistics never report groups smaller than a minimum size. - Differential privacy, as offered in BigQuery and AWS Clean Rooms, could protect aggregate outputs of linking functions against repeated-query attacks. - Tag-driven policies, as in Databricks and Snowflake, suggest letting classification metadata drive which columns are declared PROTECTED, connecting Step 2 of the method to the schema automatically. The novelty of DEP's combination should still be confirmed by independent expert review. This appendix reflects a search of public documentation and well-known research, not an exhaustive survey. --- References 1. title: Privacy as Code
text: A privacy decision is easier to apply when a system can read it, test it and enforce it. Privacy as Code means expressing those decisions in artifacts that teams can version and review, alongside the software that handles the data. You do not need SQL knowledge for this introduction. Chapter 7: Privacy as Code & GDPR develops the ideas, technical controls and limits in detail. A simple example: finding a patient A receptionist needs to find the patient who presents an ID number. A dashboard needs statistics. A billing job sometimes needs to send an ID to an authorized recipient. These are three different tasks, and they need different permissions. Task What the application needs What DEP can make explicit --------- Reception Find the matching record Use the supplied ID for a lookup; return ordinary fields and NULL for the protected ID Analytics Read approved statistics An analytics connection and, when needed, an approved linking function Billing Release an identifier for a defined job A named disclosure function, granted to the billing role Hiding a number on a screen handles that screen. Database permissions, restricted views and stored procedures can also constrain access. DEP adds a language model that distinguishes using a protected value, linking records through it and releasing it. From a decision to an enforced rule 1. Describe the task. Record who needs which operation and why. 2. Express the decision. Put protection, roles and approved exceptions in the schema and grants. 3. Review and test. Check that required work succeeds and unwanted uses fail. 4. Enforce and inspect. The server applies the implemented rules; its audit and metadata support review. This is a way of engineering privacy decisions. A comment saying “billing” does not establish a lawful purpose, and a test passing does not prove that the decision itself was appropriate. How DEP applies the idea DEP stands for Database-Enforced Privacy. Applications can use a protected identifier to find a record without receiving the stored identifier in ordinary query output. Broader protected linkage and plaintext disclosure need declared functions with explicit permissions. The database provides a point of enforcement shared by its connected clients. Other Privacy as Code tools may check application code, configurations or policy decisions; DEP can work alongside those controls. Where GDPR fits Technical controls can support data minimisation, protection by design, security and accountability. GDPR also concerns the purpose and lawful basis of processing, people's rights and the organization's wider practices. DEP does not establish GDPR compliance, and protected identifiers do not make the rest of a record anonymous. Chapter 7 explains the relationship and what remains outside the database. Current capabilities and differences describe the available implementation. Continue at your own pace - Understand the complete model: start the DEP guide. - Read the privacy discussion: chapter 7: Privacy as Code & GDPR. - See one operation change: try the playground.

title: Install
text: Choose the environment that fits your task. For a complete local application, follow Build your first app. For a browser-only introduction, open the guided playground. Experimental Project Hoopeo is an experimental, conceptual project. See the terms of use . Installing a service? Engine packages can start a background server on port 5433. The application tutorial uses 5543 for an isolated manual instance, so the two do not conflict. Studio and CLI also have embedded modes that need no server. Current documented release: 0.5.2. Download buttons follow the latest upstream release. For repeatable evaluation, choose an exact release from GitHub Releases and verify its SHA256SUMS. Binary licenses and readiness are separate: read Compatibility & limitations. Hoopeo Studio The developer application, with a database of its own. The easiest place to start. DEP CLI The command-line shell, also with a database of its own. DEP Engine The database server, for applications, psql and other clients. DEP.js The playground, in the browser. Nothing to install. Hoopeo Studio SQL windows, an object browser, result grids, plans, the privacy matrix and the DEP notes of every statement. DEP Engine is built in, so Studio needs no server; it can also connect to one. macOS Linux Windows Download Hoopeo Studio for macOS macOS 11 or later, Apple silicon and Intel. 1. Open the downloaded package. If macOS says it cannot verify the developer, Control-click the package and choose Open, then Open again. (Or open System Settings > Privacy & Security and choose Open Anyway.) 2. Install. Choose Continue, then Install, and enter your password. 3. Start Hoopeo Studio from Applications or Launchpad. Download for Linux (x86-64) ARM (arm64) Ubuntu 22.04, Debian 12 or newer. 1. Open the downloaded file and choose Install (on Ubuntu, the App Center opens it). In a terminal instead: sh sudo apt install ./hoopeo-studio_amd64.deb 2. Start Hoopeo Studio from the applications menu, or run hoopeo-studio. There is no Windows build of Hoopeo Studio yet. Try DEP in the playground, which runs in any browser, or use DEP CLI in WSL. First steps in Studio 1. Create a database. Choose Session > New Local Database, give it a name, and choose Create. It is kept in a folder on your computer, or in memory if you prefer. The New Local Database dialog of Hoopeo Studio 2. Load the demo clinic. Download clinic.sql , open it with File > Open, and run it with Query > Execute (F8). 3. Run a lookup. Open a new SQL window (File > New SQL Window), and run: sql SELECT full_name, national_id, health_fund FROM patients WHERE national_id = '123456782'; The Output pane shows the result and its DEP notes: the ID number was matched through the blind index, and returned as NULL. Hoopeo Studio after a lookup by a protected value, with the DEP notes in the Output pane To work with a DEP Engine server instead, choose Session > Connect to DEP Server, and enter its host, port, role, endpoint and password. The Connect to DEP Server dialog of Hoopeo Studio Remove: on macOS, move Hoopeo Studio from Applications to the Trash. On Linux, sudo apt remove hoopeo-studio. DEP CLI dep-cli, the command-line shell. It connects to a DEP Engine server, or opens a database of its own in a folder or in memory. macOS Linux Windows Download DEP CLI for macOS 1. Open the downloaded package (Control-click and Open if macOS asks), choose Continue and Install. 2. Open Terminal, or the DEP CLI app the package adds to Applications, which opens Terminal for you. The examples are installed in /usr/local/share/project-hoopeo/examples. Download for Linux (x86-64) ARM (arm64) 1. Open the downloaded file and choose Install, or in a terminal: sudo apt install ./dep-cli_amd64.deb. 2. The examples are installed in /usr/share/dep-cli/examples. Or in one line, in a terminal (it picks the right file for your system and checks it): sh curl -fsSL https://mandelreouven2002.github.io/project-hoopeo.github.io/install.sh sh -s -- cli For a distribution without apt, the same command installs dep-cli in /usr/local/bin from the archive. There is no Windows build yet. In WSL 2 with Ubuntu, follow the Linux steps. First steps with DEP CLI sh dep-cli --memory --init /usr/local/share/project-hoopeo/examples/clinic.sql macOS dep-cli --memory --init /usr/share/dep-cli/examples/clinic.sql Linux This opens the demo clinic in memory, as admin on the operational endpoint.
