title: About
text: Project Hoopeo is an experimental concept: an implementation of Database-Enforced Privacy (DEP), a database in which privacy rules are part of the schema and of the query plan, so that the engine enforces them on every query, for every client. It consists of a specification, a database server (DEP Engine), a command-line shell (DEP CLI), a developer application (Hoopeo Studio), and a browser simulator (DEP.js, the playground). It demonstrates the model and its trust boundary. Experimental Project Hoopeo is an experimental, conceptual project. See the terms of use . The name is the project's own: Hoopeo is a play on the hoopoe, the bird of the logo, and the one that is spelled "Hoopeo" in the products' names. See Names and logos. The idea The principle is that the ability to use a value for an operation does not require the ability to read it. A column declared PROTECTED can be used by the database to find a record, update it, and connect it to related records, but an ordinary query never returns its value. Linking whole datasets, and releasing a value, are possible only inside functions that are declared for it, reviewable in the schema, and listed in the catalog. DEP on Privacy as Code explains the model and its limits, and the concepts guide defines its terms. The documents - The design proposal defines DEP: the problem, the idea, the language, declared functions, the architecture, and the guarantees and limits. Read the design proposal. - The roadmap and release plan records one way DEP could be built and released, and compares it with existing approaches. Read the roadmap. Both are licensed under CC BY 4.0: anyone may implement Database-Enforced Privacy, in any product, with attribution. History The history is in the changelog. In short: - 0.3: the name Project Hoopeo, with DEP Engine, DEP CLI and Hoopeo Studio. DEP notes, the privacy matrix and TLS. Installers for macOS, Linux and Docker. - 0.4: storage in redb, the transaction manager, the audit log, match limits and key rotation, the PostgreSQL extended protocol, and the HTTP API. - 0.5: storage on disk with indexes and constraints, savepoints and transactional schema changes, bounded query memory with encrypted spilling, and DEP.js following the engine rule for rule, checked by a compatibility test. 0.5.1 fixed two bugs. 0.5.2 changed the licensing and the way the products are distributed: DEP Engine, DEP CLI and Hoopeo Studio became binaries under an evaluation license, and the specification, the playground and the examples stayed open. The author Project Hoopeo is made by Reuven Mandelovich: lp.reuven.click. Licenses and a commercial license The layers have different licenses: CC BY 4.0 for the specification and documentation, Apache 2.0 for DEP.js and the examples, and the Project Hoopeo Evaluation License for the binaries of DEP Engine, DEP CLI and Hoopeo Studio. See Licensing. Production use and commercial use need a commercial license. To ask for one, contact the author through lp.reuven.click. Contributing and security Contributions are welcome to the open layers: the documents, DEP.js and the examples. See Contributing. A way around DEP's rules, in the design or in an implementation, should be reported privately: see Security. How to cite If you use, discuss or build on DEP, please cite the design proposal: > R. Mandelovich. DEP: Database-Enforced Privacy. A Design Proposal. Version 1.0, October 2026. To cite the software: > R. Mandelovich. Project Hoopeo: Database-Enforced Privacy (DEP). A Design Proposal}, year = {2026}, month = oct, note = {Version 1.0}, url = {https://github.com/mandelreouven2002/project-hoopeo.github.io} } The repository also has a CITATION.cff, which GitHub reads to offer a citation. title: Reporting a bypass
text: DEP's central claim is that protected values cannot leave the database except through declared disclosures, and that whole datasets cannot be linked through them except in declared linking functions. If you find a way around that in the design, please tell us privately first. What counts Anything that lets a client do something the design says is impossible, for example: - obtain a protected value outside a DISCLOSES function; - link whole datasets through a protected value outside a LINKS function; - match on protected values from the masked read path; - use a disclosed value as a key, filter, or argument; - learn a protected value from an error message, a log, a statistic, or any other channel; - change a connection's access path after authentication. Weaknesses that the design already documents as limitations (for example, that a successful match reveals that a record exists) are welcome as discussion in public issues. How to report Contact the author through and put "DEP security" in the subject. Do not post details in a public issue. Include the schema, the statements, the path and role, and what you expected versus what the design allows. You will receive an acknowledgment within a few days. Reporters are credited in the documentation and release notes unless they prefer to remain anonymous. Scope Reports about the design are in scope, and so are reports about the implementations: DEP Engine, DEP CLI, Hoopeo Studio (distributed as binaries) and DEP.js (open source). DEP Engine is an experimental concept that demonstrates the model and its trust boundary (see the terms of use). Design-level bypasses are especially valuable while the rules can still change.

title: Contributing
text: Project Hoopeo implements Database-Enforced Privacy (DEP): a specification, DEP Engine, DEP CLI, DEP.js and Hoopeo Studio. If a system or paper already does part of what DEP proposes, open an issue with a link. The comparison in the roadmap will be updated, and you will be credited. - Propose rules for the open questions listed in the roadmap. - Report a difference between DEP.js and DEP Engine. The playground should give the same result as the engine for every statement; a case that does not is a bug in DEP.js. - Find bypasses. Please report those privately, as described in SECURITY.md. title: Using the playground
text: Begin with the five-step guided tour. “Browse all examples” opens the complete example collection. Expand DEP notes to see why an operation was allowed or refused. Known native differences are documented in chapter 6. The DEP SQL Playground runs Database-Enforced Privacy (DEP) in your browser. New to DEP? Read Understand DEP first. You write DEP SQL against a small clinic, and you see the same statement run three times, side by side: in a regular database, on DEP's masked read path, and on DEP's operational path. Nothing is installed and nothing is sent anywhere: the page runs entirely in your browser. Open the playground. The page is also available as a single HTML file that works offline. > A simulator. The playground has no trust boundary, because everything runs in your browser, and its cryptography is a stand-in. It illustrates the rules and protects nothing. For real enforcement use DEP Engine, DEP CLI or Hoopeo Studio, which are distributed as binaries (see Install). The page The hosted page has four areas: the guided tour, the editable SQL, three result panes, and the database views. 1. Guided tour: Find one → Read IDs → Join one → Join everyone → Disclose. Each step explains the task and expected difference. 2. SQL editor: edit the syntax-colored query, then press Run or Ctrl/⌘+Enter. Colors aid reading; the query text remains ordinary SQL. 3. Results: compare the same operation in the regular database and both DEP paths. Expand the DEP notes to understand a result or refusal. 4. Schema and governance: inspect Tables, Functions, Access, Audit and Storage below the results. Chapter 1: Understand DEP explains why reading all IDs returns NULL, while an unanchored protected join is refused. The three result panes. Every statement you run appears in all three, with its DEP notes. - Regular SQL is an ordinary SQLite database with the same clinic, where ID numbers and phone numbers are plain text. It shows what a regular database does with your statement. SQLite has no CREATE FUNCTION, so in this copy the declared functions are views, and the examples that call them run the equivalent query on the views and show it above the result. It is a simulator of DEP Engine: a compiler and a server for DEP SQL, written in JavaScript, that runs the compiled statements on sql.js (SQLite compiled to WebAssembly). It targets DEP SQL rules, errors, DEP notes and audit records, with the implementation differences listed below. The source is open, under the Apache License 2.0. The repository includes compat.js, a suite comparing statements on a running DEP Engine and DEP.js. Its earlier 280-statement parity result predates the disclosed-sort correction. The current simulator rejects disclosed sort keys in accordance with the specification; a project review reports that native 0.5.1 accepts them. Native 0.5.2 has not been retested here for this issue. Name, alias and ordinal cases are included in the compatibility suite. See the known difference and examples. Where DEP.js differs from DEP Engine - EXPLAIN shows the SQLite statement DEP.js runs, then the engine's Read: lines. The engine shows DataFusion's plan there. - A second writer fails at once with 55P03, where the engine waits up to --lock-timeout. - Readers in a transaction see the latest commit rather than a snapshot taken at BEGIN. - Results come from SQLite: dates and times are text, and a few functions behave like SQLite's (division by zero gives NULL, for example). - current_date and now() are in the browser's time zone. The engine uses UTC. - \connect role [endpoint] opens a new connection inside a script. It is a simulator command, like \c in DEP CLI. - The cryptography is a stand-in. There is no trust boundary in a browser. Using depsql.js as a library depsql.js runs in a page or in Node. It needs sql.js. Download it from the latest release, or take playground/depsql.js from the repository. js const SQL = await initSqlJs(); // sql.js const server = new DepSQL.Server(SQL, { setup: clinicSql }); // a DEP server; clinicSql is a DEP SQL script const conn = server.connect('reception_app', 'operational'); // role and endpoint const [r] = conn.exec('SELECT full_name FROM patients WHERE national_id = $1', ['123456782']); // r: { ok, kind: 'rows' 'command', columns, rows, tag, notes, error: { message, code, sqlstate, hint }, session } conn.exec('BEGIN; ...; COMMIT'); conn.close(); // rolls back an open transaction new DepSQL.Server(SQL, { setup, matchLimit: '1000/minute' }) sets a default match limit for roles that are not superusers, as --match-limit does. server.describe(conn), server.storage(table, conn) and server.auditLog return the catalog, the stored form of a table and the audit records. DepSQL.parse(sql) returns the syntax tree. In Node, require('./depsql.js') returns the same object.
